Débats de la Chambre des communes

Content.ParaText: It being Wednesday, we will now have the singing of the national anthem, led by the hon. member for Argenteuil—Papineau—Des Collines.
[Members sang the national anthem]
Mr. Speaker, on Saturday, British Columbians voted for change. I would like to take this opportunity to welcome and congratulate Mr. Doerkson's government in waiting.
I would also like to welcome back Mike Farnworth, my own MLA in Port Coquitlam. It has been a pleasure to work with Mike these past 11 years.
I welcome Ryan Peterson, the new MLA for Coquitlam-Burke Mountain. Ryan and I have known each other for as long as I have been in office.
Another welcome goes to Matt Liang, the new MLA for Coquitlam-Maillardville, who I look forward to getting to know as well.

Lastly, let me thank outgoing MLAs Jodie Wickens and Jennifer Blatherwick, who have served with great conviction and great integrity these past years. Their contributions to our community will be noted for years to come.
All in all, let us all work together to build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, this week a great Quebecker was inducted into the Quebec sports hall of fame. I am talking about Luc Brodeur‑Jourdain, three-time Vanier Cup champion with Laval University's Rouge et Or and three-time Grey Cup champion with the Montreal Alouettes, twice as a player and once as their coach.

Six championships is quite the career. However, behind these achievements is a man with a big heart, a respected leader and a team player who believes in hard work, perseverance and commitment. Luc is the kind of guy who comes home after a Grey Cup victory and then spends the next morning giving the staff a hand and washing dishes at Pause Café, the café his wife Marie‑Élaine owns in Saint‑Hyacinthe. “As long as it helps,” he likes to say.
Luc is just an ordinary guy who is actually extraordinary. He is a man of the people, a true Maskoutain who is proud of his roots and stands up for his community.

No matter what challenge Luc takes on, he can be sure that the entire Conservative caucus will stand with him in his next victory. I congratulate him once again on his induction. He is now part of Quebec's sports history.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Judy A. Sgro (Humber River—Black Creek, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise today in solidarity with the courageous people and political prisoners of Iran and all those peacefully calling for freedom, dignity and human rights.

According to Amnesty International, 20 prisoners are at imminent risk of execution. The growing international support for the “no to execution Tuesdays” campaign, including the participation of United Nations special rapporteurs, sends a powerful message that the world is paying attention and that even prisoners' voices will not be silenced.
I commend those participating in this hunger strike and all those who continue raising awareness of the widespread human rights violations and executions carried out by the Iranian regime.

The persecuted men, women and children of Iran are not alone. Canada will continue to advocate for human rights, democracy and the protection of Iranians. Together, we must work toward a future of peace, freedom, justice and hope for all Iranians.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize Oxi Day, October 28, a defining moment in modern history and a day of immense pride for the Hellenic Canadian community and for all Hellenes worldwide.

On this day in 1940, when faced with an ultimatum from fascist forces to surrender their sovereignty, the people of Greece responded with the resounding word oxi, or “no”. That courage changed the course of World War II and stood as a beacon of resistance, proving that freedom and democracy are worth fighting for and prompting the great Winston Churchill to say that it is not that Greeks fight like heroes; it is that heroes fight like Greeks.
Today, the Greek community across Canada shares the same spirit of strength, honour and philotimo, a commitment that has helped build this country.
To all Canadians and to all Greeks across this great country and around the world, I say this:
[Member spoke in Greek and provided the following translation:]
Long live freedom. Long live Greece. Long live Canada.
[English]
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize one of my constituents, Alessia Commisso, an extraordinary young Canadian whose courage, determination and generosity are an inspiration to all of us.

Living with Leigh syndrome, a rare and progressive disease that has affected her mobility and sight, Alessia refuses to let challenges define her future. As a volunteer at Toronto's FIFA World Cup activities, she helped fans navigate the stadium and experience the excitement of the world's game. Her dedication earned her the recognition of being one of Toronto's FIFA World Cup 2026 Unsung Heroes.

Alessia is pursuing studies in event management at Humber Polytechnic and dreams of helping organize major events herself. She reminds us that true greatness is not measured by the obstacles we face, but by the difference we make in the lives of others.
I am proud to recognize Alessia Commisso and her remarkable contribution to our community and to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this scene plays out nationwide: desperate, addicted people using drugs openly in public. It is not fair to our communities, and it is not fair to people struggling with addictions, yet for too long, it has been tolerated, until now. The Edmonton Police Service has pioneered a bold new program. It does not allow open drug use. Instead, police take people who are high on drugs off the street. They bring them to a stabilization centre. There, they get clean clothes, medical care and a chance at recovery.
Our communities should not have to put up with open drug use, but we should not turn our backs on people struggling with addictions either. I believe this program could soon spread nationwide.
I congratulate Chief Warren Driechel and the Edmonton Police Service for making safer streets and for saving lives, with real recovery.
Mr. Speaker, today, Greeks around the world proudly commemorate the famous “No” or “Oxi”, a historic moment that symbolizes the courage, determination and spirit of resistance of the Greek people.

On October 28, 1940, Mussolini gave the Greek prime minister Ioannis Metaxas an ultimatum, demanding that Greece allow the Axis forces to enter its territory and occupy strategic positions under the threat of war. Faced with this threat, the Prime Minister responded decisively, “Then it is war.”

As Franklin Roosevelt alluded to, at a time when much of the world had lost hope, the Greek people dared to challenge the perceived invincibility of the Axis forces. The Greeks fought with extraordinary heroism, holding the Germans back for six weeks, significantly influencing the outcome of World War II. Their courage has inspired nations and serves as a powerful reminder that even in the darkest moments of history, the human spirit's determination to defend freedom can prevail.
[Member spoke in Greek]
[English]

Mr. Speaker, in Canada today, thousands of people are struggling to find a job. In just two months, 110,000 Canadians have lost their jobs, with 68,000 people losing their jobs in September alone. That is 110,000 families wondering how they are going to keep a roof over their head and food on their table.

A year and a half ago, the Liberal Prime Minister told us he would get us a bigger, better deal; all we had to do was put our elbows up. We cannot feed a family with empty promises or pay a mortgage with illusions. In Windsor last month, more than 1,000 people lined up at 3 a.m. just for a chance to work at the local Costco. The promise of Canada was not that government would make life easy for us. It was that hard work would give us a fair shot at getting ahead.

Conservatives are here to cut red tape and get projects moving. We know that Canadians have the determination and the ability to build a better future. What they need right now is for the inept Liberal government to get out of the way.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Société de recherches historiques de Pointe des cascades

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this year marks the 50th anniversary of the Société de recherches historiques de Pointe‑des‑Cascades. This historical society has developed vibrant historical sites, like the Centre d'interprétation et d'accueil du canal de Soulanges and the Parc des Ancres in Pointe‑des‑Cascades, a unique open-air museum.

During an event to mark this occasion, I was impressed to learn about the involvement of Jean‑Pierre Poirier. From the very beginning, he has embodied the passion, rigour and perseverance that have allowed the Société de recherches historiques de Pointe‑des‑Cascades to become a key component in the efforts to preserve regional heritage. He has devoted more than 50 years to documenting, protecting and passing on local history. Thanks to him and the loyal volunteers and partners, our precious maritime heritage is being protected.

The organization's 50th anniversary also coincides with Mr. Poirier's own celebrations. I want to thank him for his outstanding dedication, his passion and his public service. Thanks to him, our history lives on and is being passed on with pride.

Mr. Speaker, today I rise with great sadness to commemorate the sudden loss of a beloved community member, Maryam Muritala. Maryam's smile brightened every room she walked into. She was a vibrant part of our community in Brampton. She was an advocate, a leader and an entrepreneur whose hard work and dedication inspired those around her.

With her passion for leadership and business development, she founded Canada Vendors and Canada Business Forum, creating a place for making connections, creating business opportunities and supporting Black and Nigerian businesses across our country. Beyond her remarkable professional accomplishments, Maryam was a dear friend to me and to so many others. She was someone we could turn to for a conversation, a good laugh or a much-needed hug. Her passing leaves a tremendous void in our community, but her legacy will live on in the many lives she touched.
Maryam will be deeply missed. May she rest in peace.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister chose to borrow record amounts every year. Today, Canadians got the bill. The Bank of Canada has raised rates. A typical variable mortgage now costs $80 more a month, a line of credit costs $10 more and a car loan costs $5 more. That is more than $1,100 a year, on top of the $6,000 each family already pays toward interest on Liberal debt.

Growth is flatlining. Canada is growing at under 1%, Europe at 2% and the United States at 4%. Billions of dollars in industrial subsidies feed demand and inflation. Canada needs supply-side reform, competitive taxes, lighter regulation and a plan for transformational growth. Instead, the Prime Minister trafficks in promises of someday, maybe and never. What we are seeing is just the beginning.
How did the former central banker get it that wrong?

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to have been raised in a small fishing community on P.E.I. The fishing harbour is the centre of the community. Last week, I was in another fishing community, Miminegash, to announce a major reconstruction of the fishing harbour, the largest project ever announced for this coastal community.

For too many years, small craft harbours, the economic engines of coastal communities, have been underfunded by governments. I will express some disappointment that most members of the Conservative opposition, including those representing fishing communities, voted against the nearly $1-billion budget allocation in April, the largest budget ever for small craft harbours.

I want to express my thanks to the Prime Minister and my Atlantic caucus colleagues, who lobbied for and supported this major budget allocation. The Prime Minister recognized the economic value of the fishing sector, and his support was invaluable.

Mr. Speaker, today's interest rate hikes by the Bank of Canada are another blow to Canadians already struggling to survive. For seniors on a fixed income, this increase means choosing among mortgage payments, keeping a car on the road and putting food on the table. Maria, a senior from Vaughan, was forced from her home because she could no longer afford it. She now rents a basement from another senior who relies on that income to pay for her own mortgage, yet she also is struggling to survive. This is the reality of the affordability crisis under the Liberal government, which they voted against.

Liberals are making unkept promises while seniors are making the sacrifices. Conservatives are fighting for lower taxes, affordable homes and a Canada where seniors can retire with dignity and respect.
Mr. Speaker, tourism is Canada's second-largest service export sector, generating nearly $35 billion in spending by international visitors.

Today, tourism industry leaders are gathered in Ottawa for NorthStar, a national forum hosted by Destination Canada. In 2025, Canada welcomed 19.8 million international visitors, which highlights the importance of our tourism industry. We also have the privilege of welcoming 36 leaders in the House of Commons, and we welcome them to the national capital region.
Together, they form a true Team Canada for tourism, attracting visitors, creating jobs and helping diversify our economy.
Tourism is a core engine and key driver of Canada's economic growth and global competitiveness.
I thank these leaders who promote Canada around the world.

Mr. Speaker, Canada can be an energy superpower. Today the House has an opportunity to take concrete action toward that goal, not just give a speech, hold a press conference or make an announcement. Today the House will vote on repealing the west coast tanker ban, and I urge all members to do exactly that. The only effect of the tanker ban is to shut in Canadian oil production. It is time to recognize the value of our Canadian oil and gas industry, celebrate our world-leading responsible production, celebrate the men and women who produce energy for the world in all forms, and stop holding Canada back.

Some people say that the tanker ban protects the environment, but it does not prevent loaded oil tankers from sailing in the waters the ban covers. It is just ineffective legislation. The time has come to get it and the Liberal government out of the way of Canadian prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, teens today are awesome. Today I welcome 60 students from the Upper Grand District School Board who participate in the Beyond Borders leadership development program, an innovative grade 12 experiential learning semester that exemplifies how learning extends beyond books and classroom walls.

Through partnerships with businesses, universities, charities and community organizations, students tackle real-world challenges, explore future pathways and, most importantly, discover their own potential. Beyond Borders not only prepares students for what comes next but also teaches them the importance of giving back. Since the program's inception in 2012, participants have raised more than $1 million for community causes. I thank teachers Mike Parsons, Matt Mulhern and Cynthia McQueen.
Beyond Borders students prove that age is not a requirement for leadership, generosity or impact. The future is not waiting for them; they are already shaping it. Guelph and Canada are better for it.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Prime Minister spent, and now Canadians will have to pay. The Prime Minister has increased spending far beyond Justin Trudeau's irresponsible levels. In fact, he has doubled the deficit left by Mr. Trudeau, and we know that deficits fuel inflation. Inflation forced the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates on Canadians.
How much will Canadians have to pay before this Prime Minister stops spending recklessly?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for those questions regarding monetary policy. The Bank of Canada's message is that the impact on Canadian inflation is coming from outside Canada, but that the growth rate here in Canada will rise to 2% next year and the year after that thanks to the major policy changes implemented by the Government of Canada.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, he has just admitted that it is this government's policies, his government's policies, that have forced the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates at the expense of ordinary Canadians. Canadians already carry the most debt anywhere in the G7. Now they will be forced to pay more to the banks, while the Prime Minister celebrates. What a disconnect from the reality faced by ordinary people.
Will he acknowledge that Canadians are going to face hardship as a result of this increase?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if there is a disconnect, it is between my words and his. The Hansard is there to sort that out. What is clear is that the Bank of Canada says that the growth rate here in Canada will rise to 2% next year and the year after that. This will be the highest growth rate in the G7.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Prime Minister spent, and today Canadians are paying the price. He doubled the deficit that Trudeau left behind, increased government spending to the highest share of GDP since 1996 and is threatening to add $700 billion more in debt. More deficits cause more inflation, which today caused the Bank of Canada to bring in more interest on Canadians.
How much will Canadians have to pay before the Prime Minister finally hits the brakes on his out-of-control Liberal spending?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada was very clear about the global causes of inflation and why it acted. It was very clear that our growth is going to pick up next year and the year following, the strongest in the G7.

Let us be clear about the fiscal record of the government: the lowest net debt in the G7, the second-lowest deficit in the G7, operational spending down from 8% to 2%, a 10% cut in the civil service and a 20% cut in consultants, $60 billion of savings. That is even before the budget next week. We are building Canada strong—
The hon. Leader of the Opposition.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, how completely out of touch that is. Canadian families are the most indebted anywhere in the G7, and today they will go home to learn that their mortgage payments, car payments and line of credit payments will go up because the Prime Minister could not control his spending. He doubled Trudeau's deficit and has imposed a new fuel tax that is driving up the cost of diesel to 30¢ higher than in the U.S., which is one of the causes the Bank of Canada cited in raising rates on Canadians today.
Will the Prime Minister get his hands out of the pockets of Canadians so they do not have to pay more in their rates?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I repeat: Spending is down from 8% per year to 2%. This is new information. The operational budget will be closed next year, one year ahead of schedule. There is a 10% reduction in civil service, a 20% reduction in consultants, the strongest growth in the G7 in the coming years, and mortgage affordability down every month in the current government's time.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister says affordability is better. Everybody out there knows that is false, and it is worse today. The Bank of Canada governor said that food price inflation will be even higher next year: “Higher diesel prices raise freight and operating costs in fuel-intensive sectors such as food processing [and] agriculture”.

The Prime Minister is not to blame for world prices, but he is to blame for the fact that our prices are much higher than the world's, in part because of what the Nova Scotia Energy Board calculates is 16¢ a litre in extra fuel standard taxes that the Prime Minister is imposing at the pump.
Will the Prime Minister reverse this tax so that we can reverse the inflation and reverse the rate hikes?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is a problem with starting to quote the Bank of Canada. It is all on the public record. If we look at the Bank of Canada and affordability metrics, there was 54% of disposable income affordability before this government came into place, and it is now at 41%. For 24 straight months, asking rents have gone down. We are improving affordability in a tough housing market. Next time the Leader of the Opposition goes through Edmonton, he might want to confirm that the price of diesel in Edmonton is the same as in the United States.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, could he be more out of touch? That sounded just like his statement back on March 25, that affordability is the best it has been in a decade. The same month he said that, Food Banks Canada registered a record-smashing 2.35 million visits, 9% higher than when he took office, with fewer Canadians believing they will ever be able to afford a home than in the other 21 countries polled by Habitat for Humanity.
Will the Prime Minister admit that affordability is not the best it has been in a decade?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us talk about affordability and steps that governments can take to improve affordability. The Canadian dental care plan benefits over 17,000 people in the riding of Battle River—Crowfoot. The Canada child benefit supports over 14,000 families. There are EDC summer job grants. I could go on. They have two things in common: first, that this government proposed them and passed them; and second, that the Leader of the Opposition voted against them every single time.

Mr. Speaker, this week, the Prime Minister hosted a grand banquet for the Crown Prince of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed, arranged a photo op on Parliament Hill and even provided a mounted escort. Let us not forget that the United Arab Emirates is currently funding violence in Sudan, including violence perpetrated by a group that commits torture, rape and summary executions.
This week, that same Prime Minister also refused to allow the Premier of Quebec to speak at the Canada-European Union summit in Montreal.
How can the Prime Minister justify bestowing such honours on the United Arab Emirates while offering nothing to Quebec?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I look forward to welcoming President von der Leyen and President Costa of the European Union.

We offered the Premier of Quebec the opportunity to officially welcome both presidents. I invited him to join me at my table for a private conversation with them. Those are honours befitting the beginning of a process, a process with the European Union.
Mr. Speaker, Paul Saint‑Pierre Plamondon is no less the premier of Quebec than the Prime Minister is the prime minister of Canada.

Entering into agreements with the United Arab Emirates is no obstacle for the Prime Minister, and neither is going to Turkey to support Erdoğan. Visiting Erdoğan and telling him that we share common values is no problem, even though he is an enemy of human rights and targets his country's LGBTQ community and free press. However, giving the floor to the Premier of Quebec to talk about Quebec in Quebec is out of the question.
Does the Prime Minister realize the kind of message and images he is sending around the world?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we work with a range of countries to improve the situation during the most difficult wars, including wars in Ukraine, the Middle East, Gaza and Sudan. Every time, I have raised issues and solutions with these countries' leaders, and I have offered Canada's assistance.
Mr. Speaker, more importantly, he wanted to befriend them in order to make money.

Yesterday, all the parties condemned the Prime Minister's refusal to accept Quebec's request to speak at the summit in Montreal. The Prime Minister promised to co-operate with Quebec, but he is off to a very bad start.
Will he listen to reason and, quite simply and courteously, offer the Premier of Quebec the opportunity to address the European guests in Montreal, Quebec, in French?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Right Hon. Mark Carney (Prime Minister, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would say, “in Montreal, Quebec, Canada”.
I have made offers to the Premier of Quebec.

As for co-operation with Quebec, there have already been four meetings with Quebec's official delegation to discuss the terms of the new agreement for the future. This week is just the beginning of a process.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's 16¢-a-litre fuel standard tax is bad enough, but what is even worse is where the money goes. To quote energy expert Heather Exner-Pirot, “To meet their carbon intensity targets, many Canadian refiners blend biofuels into their petroleum products. But Canada is not self-sufficient in their production. More than half of Canada's biofuels are imported, predominantly from the United States.”
The Government of Canada forces the people of Canada to pay 16¢ a litre more to buy American biofuels. Why?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada understands and acknowledges the challenges in the global economy. However, it is Wednesday, and I have good news. In fact, Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7, the lowest net debt to GDP in the G7 and one of the lowest deficits to GDP in the G7. The Bank of Canada has seen that we are going to have the second-fastest growth in the G7. On top of that, we are investing to be an energy superpower. We are going to build Canada strong together.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, not only did the Prime Minister not answer the question, but the finance minister did not even seem to hear it. The question was about the 16¢-a-litre diesel and gasoline tax charged at the pump. Now, it is bad enough to tax the Canadian people. It is even worse to force them to pay that money to the United States of America to buy U.S. biofuels.
While Canadians cannot afford groceries, while they must empty their bank to fill up their tank, why is the Prime Minister forcing them to pay a 16¢-a-litre tax at the pump to Trump?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have some good news for the member opposite. Canola prices are up 8% this year. The amended clean fuel regulations will create significant new demand for canola. Rather than fight against canola farmers, why does he not help us build Canada strong?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: No, Mr. Speaker, the minister wants to build America strong, because the cost of the majority of the biofuels that the government is forcing refiners to purchase with this 16¢-a-litre tax is not going to Canadian farmers. It is going to megacorporations south of the border. On this day when the Bank of Canada governor says that food prices are rising because of higher diesel costs, the Prime Minister is imposing a tax on Canadians at the pump and on truckers who deliver us our food.
Why is he putting that money in the pockets of the Americans?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to correct my last statement. Canola prices are up 8% because of clean fuel regs, but they are up 30% this year. Thirty per cent, and the Leader of the Opposition is trying to talk us down. We have been helping the farmers. We have been helping the people in Alberta. He is talking against them. We should work together and build Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, at Trump Tower, they will be popping the champagne today, knowing that this government is defending a 16¢-a-litre tax that sends Canadian money south of the border to subsidize large U.S. corporations selling us overpriced biofuel. That single mother who is turning back items at the grocery store, because it costs too much for the trucker to deliver those items, or the family who cannot quite fill up the minivan can take comfort in knowing that the Prime Minister has a “make America great again” tax at the pump.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we all know that the Leader of the Opposition likes to talk, but he should listen. He should listen to the voices in this House, like when we extended the suspension of the excise fuel tax. That is helping Canadians. That is helping families. That is helping truckers. That is helping farmers. That is helping fishers across this nation.
I hope Canadians are watching at home today because this gentleman has voted against supporting Canadians.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this Prime Minister could not be more disconnected from reality. Today he said that things are going well for Canadians.

After Canada experienced the worst food inflation in the G7, after 2.35 million visits were made to food banks, and after the Bank of Canada was forced to raise interest rates today because of his inflationary spending, this Prime Minister is now looking to add another $735 billion to our national debt over the next five years.
Will he hit the brakes before we hit a wall?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canadians can see the bigger picture. They understand that there are external factors that obviously affect the economy and prices in Canada.

What the people at home want to know is why, when we introduced the Canada groceries and essentials benefit that will help 12 millions Canadians and provide up to $1,891 per family, the Conservative leader voted against this measure and convinced all his colleagues to vote against it. That is the question.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister not only doubled the deficit left by Justin Trudeau, he also increased annual government spending to the highest share of GDP since 1996, outside of COVID. He has now driven inflation above target and forced the Bank of Canada to increase interest rates. Canadians are going to be hit hard on their mortgage and car loan payments as of this evening.
Will he stand up and announce that he will stop this irresponsible spending?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what Canadians are hearing is an opposition leader who is always criticizing the Canadian economy, and I am sure they are sick of it.

Members on this side of the House are confident. Canada is attracting talent from around the world. Canada is one of the rare countries in the world that can build a ship, build a car and certify a nuclear power plant. Canada is a country that has the critical minerals needed for the 21st century. We are producing more energy. Canada is the only G7 country with a free trade agreement with every other G7 country.
Rather than criticizing, the Leader of the Opposition should be celebrating the hard work of Canadians across the country.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is never too late to do the right thing. The Prime Minister decided to hold another summit with the Europeans on Quebec soil without including the provincial premiers, even though some changes might affect areas of provincial jurisdiction.
Will the Prime Minister show some respect for Quebeckers and at least let their Premier speak?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, doing the right thing means strengthening our ties with the European Union, which represents 450 million consumers and 18% of the global economy. That is exactly what we are doing in the interests of Quebec and in the interests of Canada as a whole.

I want to commend the Quebec delegation for the work it did in preparation for this summit. I also want to point out that the Premier of Quebec and all the other premiers are invited to this very important event. I hope that the Premier of Quebec will be there in the best interests of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Quebec is right to demand an opportunity to speak at the Canada-European Union summit.

He could even claim a seat at the negotiating table, because the federal government is negotiating with Europe on labour mobility, energy, critical minerals and more. All of these areas fall, in whole or in part, within Quebec's jurisdiction. Excluding Quebec violates the Gérin-Lajoie doctrine. It is an insult to all Quebeckers.
Will the Prime Minister grant the Premier of Quebec the opportunity to speak that is rightfully his on his own turf?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when I get up in the morning, I am certain of three things: The sun will rise in the east, the leader of the Bloc Québécois and Bloc members will be outraged by anything and everything, and Bloc members will claim to speak on behalf of all Quebeckers. Those are certainties.
Quebeckers are asking for closer ties with the European Union. Obviously, they want that to be done in partnership with Quebec, as it was in the lead-up to this summit.
Closer ties with the European Union are good for Quebec and good for Canada. I sincerely hope that Quebec will be there with us.
Mr. Speaker, there is a fourth certainty: the federal government's lack of respect for Quebec.

Whether a certain minister likes it or not, geopolitics is not a matter of federal jurisdiction. Quebec has the right to conduct its own international relations in all areas that fall wholly or partly under its jurisdiction. That is the Gérin-Lajoie doctrine. The Prime Minister's insulting attitude and his Minister of Industry's outlandish statements undermine decades of Quebec and Canadian foreign policy.
Will the Prime Minister reconsider, respect the Quebec nation and invite the Premier of Quebec to speak at the summit?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us talk about the Bloc Québécois's outrage over everything. All summer long, the Bloc criticized us for doing too much for Quebec: too much for infrastructure, with $10 billion in investments; too much for the Davie shipyard in Lévis, with 5,000 jobs in Quebec; too much for Alstom in La Pocatière and Saint‑Bruno‑de‑Montarville. The Bloc Québécois criticized us for supporting the Churchill Falls project, which will ensure prosperity for generations of Quebeckers. It is criticizing us for going ahead with the high-speed rail project, which will help build Quebec. The Bloc Québécois is busy stoking division and outrage. Our government is busy building Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised to move at speeds not seen in generations, but Canadians did not realize that what he meant was accumulating debt at speeds not seen in generations. In five years, he plans to add more debt than all prime ministers before Justin Trudeau combined. Today, because of the Liberals' inflationary spending, the Bank of Canada has raised interest rates, making government debt even more expensive.
Can the Prime Minister explain who will repay this mountain of debt and how?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Evan Solomon (Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, all the opposition members do is talk down our economy and our workers, but they do not realize that criticism does not create jobs. Their negativity does not make life affordable.

Did the Conservatives vote for the groceries and essentials benefit? No. Do they vote to make life more affordable? No. In the member's own riding, when we support Technical Steel Corp or Exco Engineering, do they support that investment in businesses to create jobs? No. They should get with the program, and we should build this country strong together.

Mr. Speaker, the member did not answer my question. My question was about the vicious cycle that the Prime Minister is building, which is more debt, more interest and more borrowing. In fact, he is borrowing to pay for the interest he already owes on the debt that he already took on. Today, the Bank of Canada raised interest rates. Now, the government pays more to borrow, families pay more on their mortgages and more taxes go toward interest instead of services.
When will the Prime Minister break his vicious cycle and finally get this borrowing under control?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Evan Solomon (Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canada has the fastest growing economy in the G7 and the lowest debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. We are creating jobs.

The Conservatives talk about making life more affordable, but they do not do anything about it. Do they vote for affordable child care? No. Do they vote for national school food lunches? No. Do they vote for dental care? No. All they know how to say is no to Canadians. We will continue to say yes to building Canadian, yes to building strong and yes to making life more affordable for everybody.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister assumed in his first budget that interest rates would stabilize and go lower, except they have actually been going up, including at the Bank of Canada. That means that Canadians will pay more when they renew their mortgage, but it also means taxpayers are on the hook for billions more. Why is that? It is because the Prime Minister chose to double the size of the deficits he inherited, and he has pushed borrowing to record numbers, including nearly $600 billion this year alone.
Will the Prime Minister tell Canadians how much his mistake has cost Canadians with higher interest rates?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rechie Valdez (Minister of Women and Gender Equality and Secretary of State (Small Business and Tourism), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will share that we have chosen to be there for Canadians. In fact, thanks to our government, we have cut taxes for 22 million Canadians. This means more money stays in their pockets. While things are challenging at the grocery store, we have delivered the national groceries and essentials benefits so that the average family of four in our ridings receive close to $1,900. That is real support, and we are going to continue to be there.
The good news, also, is that we have increased the Canada child benefit. That is an additional $160 per child this year.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada says inflation is going to remain high and exceed 3% until the end of 2027. As a result, the cost of living will continue to rise, putting even more pressure on Canadian families and farmers. Furthermore, the government intends to increase the federal fuel excise tax. The bank itself admits that this increase will drive up inflation. This is completely irresponsible.
When will the government put an end to its inflationary decisions that are driving up the cost of living?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the MP rose to speak about affordability, yet time and again she has voted against measures designed to help Canadians, to help the people in her constituency. Whether it is dental care, the Canada child benefit or the groceries and essentials benefit, she has consistently opposed any support for Canadians. She will have to explain those choices to her constituents.
Mr. Speaker, I am quoting the Bank of Canada, which is confirming the Liberal government's failure on the economy.

Our growth has plateaued at 1%, which is less than half the rate in the United States and barely one-third of the global growth rate of 3.1%. Worse still, half of this result comes from government spending alone. According to the Bank of Canada, “Finding work continues to be challenging”. This situation is untenable, especially in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis.
When will the government stop adding to the tax burden and adopt our Conservative plan to create stable, well-paying jobs?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anna Gainey (Secretary of State (Children and Youth), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we understand the challenges Canadians are facing. That is why we made the national school food program permanent. That is why we lowered the fuel tax. That is why we brought in the groceries benefit. More recently, we announced the national heat pump rebate of $10,000 for low-income families.
We are there for Canadians. It would be nice to have the support of the members across the way on these issues.
Mr. Speaker, Hamilton is proud to be Canada's steel city. It is part of who we are. This is—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Let us try to be fair. Let us try again.
The hon. member for Hamilton West—Ancaster—Dundas.
Mr. Speaker, we are talking about real jobs for real people, and this disruption is extremely disrespectful.
Hamilton is proud to be Canada's steel city, and thousands of families depend on steelmaking. It—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
We will give it one more shot from the top. The hon. member will understand that there is only so much I can do.
The hon. member for Hamilton West—Ancaster—Dundas has the floor. Let us try again.
Mr. Speaker, this is a critical issue for all Canadians, and it would be nice if the opposition were interested in what is happening. In the face—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Members have to co-operate. I would ask them to help me out.
I want to finish today as close to three o'clock as possible, and I do not know if that is going to be possible now, but let us try.
The hon. member for Hamilton West—Ancaster—Dundas, from the top.
Mr. Speaker, Hamilton is proud to be Canada's steel city. Thousands of families depend on steelmaking for their livelihood.

In the face of the illegal and unjustified American tariffs, can the Ministry of Industry give the House an update on what our government is doing to protect Canada's steel industry and support steelworkers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we know that the steel industry helped build this country. We have it as a pivotal industry as we are building Canada strong.

Last week, I joined the Prime Minister and the Premier of Ontario to announce an additional $5.2 billion to support the steel industry from the unjustified American tariffs. We will make sure that people in Hamilton get that support, that we create growth in the country and, more importantly, that we create jobs across the steel industry.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday, the industry minister said she would provide the demand letter she sent to Cleveland-Cliffs, because it outlines the way in which the company has breached its contractual commitments. Yesterday, I stood up in the House and asked her for a date on which she would provide us with that letter. She did not answer the question. Meanwhile, we hear from Cleveland-Cliffs repeatedly that it is not in violation of any of its contractual commitments, and workers are still awaiting some transparency.
I will ask the minister this again: Will she provide us today with the demand letter that she sent to Cleveland-Cliffs so workers can get some transparency?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the question is not that. The question is whether the Conservatives are in favour of protecting the jobs at Stelco. I have not heard that from them. My question to my colleague is—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I will have to ask the minister to go back a little further and start a little closer to the beginning, because I could not hear what she was saying.
Mr. Speaker, the question is not that. The question is, are the Conservatives in favour of protecting the jobs at Stelco and Hamilton, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, Cleveland-Cliffs's CEO admitted that he bought Stelco because Canadian steel was hurting his American business. He admitted to blocking Stelco from selling steel to the United States, and now 350 Hamilton steelworkers are losing their jobs.
Conservatives demand that the Liberals take Stelco to court, stop illegal steel dumping and secure a tariff-free steel deal. Instead, the Liberals keep sending love letters and extending deadlines.
Stelco's CEO is protecting American profits and his American workers. What are the Liberals doing to protect ours?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us be serious. There are people hurting because of these layoffs. There are people who are wondering whether they will be able to—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I am sure that people in Hamilton would like to hear this debate.
The hon. Minister of Industry.

Mr. Speaker, let us be serious here. There are people right now who are asking whether they can pay their mortgage. There are people who are asking themselves whether they will be able to pay their bills. That is why we did not stop. We did not wait. The Conservatives are late. We have been at it and starting the legal process for more than 10 days now. They should, basically, read the news.
Mr. Speaker, the only thing late is the minister filing a lawsuit to protect Hamilton workers.

This is the third pay cycle that Hamilton steelworkers are missing. I spoke with Stelco workers this morning and they want action. The CEO admitted yesterday that he bought the company as a defensive measure to protect his American profits. We also know he supports Trump and his unjustified steel tariffs. The Liberals approved this takeover. Now they are watching Canadian steel jobs disappear.
Will the Prime Minister stop being bullied by Trump's buddies and file the lawsuit today?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I met with and I have been in contact in the past two weeks with the head of United Steelworkers, Marty Warren. The union is fully supporting the position of the government. Of course, I was in the studio at CBC when Cleveland-Cliff's CEO made the admission regarding the fact that he bought Stelco to get rid of a competitor. We take that admission very seriously and will act.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, today's hike demonstrates the government's economic plan is not working. Inflation is taking hold.
According to the Globe, today's hike means that the cost of a typical variable mortgage will rise $82 a month and a typical home equity line of credit $12 a month, or over $1,100 a year.
When is the government going to introduce supply-side reforms to the economy to increase productivity and wages and to make life more affordable?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have had a display in question period today where the Conservatives are trying to catch up with my colleague with respect to steel. I note the member's question over there.

Why can the Conservatives not just once stand up and say that there is a war in the Strait of Hormuz or that there is a trade attack that is illegal and unjustified on Canada. Yes, we are facing economic headwinds, and the G7 is going to be led by Canada despite all of that. The Conservatives should stand up and celebrate Canada's success and its—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michael Chong (Wellington—Halton Hills North, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the government's plan simply is not working. It is focused on the demand side of the economy. It is spending more and more and driving up the cost of interest, which is the fastest-growing line item in the budget that is projected to chew up almost 14¢ of every dollar by decade's end. Now the Bank of Canada is hiking the interest rate, driving up interest costs on mortgages, lines of credit and car loans. For a typical family, this amounts to more than $1,100 a year.
Again, I ask the question, when will the government start focusing on supply-side reforms to increase productivity and increase wages to make life more affordable for Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, every time we propose a measure to make life easier and more affordable and to make conditions for Canadians just a little better, whether it is reducing fuel taxes, whether it is a Canada food and essentials benefit or whether it is the Canada child benefit, these Conservatives, led by that finance critic, get up and oppose it. When we grow the economy, they decry that. When we protect jobs in Hamilton, they—
The hon. member for Calgary East.

Mr. Speaker, like a typical Liberal elitist, the Prime Minister is sending more money to his banker, bondholder and Brookfield buddies in debt interest than what goes to provinces in health care transfers. Just this year, a family of four will pay $6,000 in debt interest. Justin Trudeau doubled the debt. The Prime Minister took that as a challenge. He doubled down and doubled his deficit.
Will the Prime Minister show up at the finance committee and tell Canadians exactly why he is so out of touch and why Canadians are so out of money?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us just think about this for Canadians. That member and that party voted against targeting the Canada child benefit to families that need it the most. They think a family that makes $500,000 should get the same as a single mother who makes $20,000 a year. They voted against a school food program; voted against feeding hungry children. They voted against a dental program that gives dental care to seniors who need it the most. That side has no credibility when it comes to affordability. On this side of the House—
The hon. member for Calgary East.

Mr. Speaker, the measure of a success in this country should be how many government programs Canadians get off, not get put on to. Debt interest is the fastest-growing expense, more than health care and more than the military. It is the money that gets sent to the Prime Minister's banker, bondholder and Brookfield buddies every single year. This guy said he would spend less, but he is all talk and no results. That is why 2.35 million Canadians visit a food bank every single month.
The Prime Minister doubled Justin Trudeau's deficit. Is he looking to double food bank lines too?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on this side of the House, we are going to continue to focus on affordability measures for Canadians. The groceries and essentials benefit will put up to $1,900 in the pockets of families. We cut the taxes, and they voted against it, of course, for 22 million Canadians. We paused the federal excise tax on gas. We will continue to focus on and deliver for Canadians. That side can continue with the empty rhetoric.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians can see that the Prime Minister is using creative accounting to manage the country's finances. He is dividing a monumental deficit across three different credit cards: one for current expenditures, another misleadingly labelled “investments”, and a third hidden within Crown corporations. Stephen Harper and Justin Trudeau never hesitated to appear before parliamentary committees.
Will the Prime Minister support the Conservative motion and come explain his creative accounting practices before the Standing Committee on Finance?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are always prepared to answer questions before the Standing Committee on Finance.

What is strange is to see the Conservatives talk down the Canadian economy in every one of their questions, even though international institutions and the Bank of Canada recognize that there are external factors at play. The good news is that Canada has the second-fastest growth rate in the G7. One would think the Conservatives would celebrate our workers, our industries and Canada.
If they do not want to do that, we will always be here on this side of the House to stand up for our workers and our industries.

Mr. Speaker, what is clear is that we need to hear the truth. The truth is that deficits have doubled and the debt has doubled. Even the Parliamentary Budget Officer is struggling to understand the creative way in which this government and this new Prime Minister are managing the country's finances.
We are seeing staggering expenditures hidden across different credit cards. We just want him to come and explain himself before the finance committee.
Will he accept our motion today and appear before the Standing Committee on Finance, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, occasionally, we like to rise in the House to remind the Conservatives that they have never defined what they mean by inflationary spending.
Is it the Canada child benefit?
Is it equalization?
Is it our military spending that has increased and will continue to increase to reach 5% of GDP?
What does my Conservative friend consider to be inflationary spending?

Mr. Speaker, we live in an era when global events have local impacts. The people of University—Rosedale understand that there are forces affecting our economy that are beyond our control. They do not want to hear parliamentarians talk down our economy, our businesses and our workers. They want us to address affordability by building on our strengths and our shared values.
Can the Secretary of State for the CRA and Financial Institutions tell us about the work under way to make life more affordable for people in Toronto and across this great country?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for University—Rosedale for her strong advocacy on the disability tax credit and automatic federal benefits. We are going to build a strong, resilient economy for all Canadians. We are attracting outside investment. We are going to build Canada strong. We are cutting taxes for 22 million Canadians. The groceries and essentials benefit is offering $1,900 for families. We will continue to focus on and deliver on affordability measures for Canadians. On this side of the House, Canadians know who stands with them. It is our side.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has the oil the world needs, the workers to produce it and the rail lines to get it to the Pacific. Strathcona Resources is ready to ship up to 250,000 barrels per day through Prince Rupert to global markets. This would mean more jobs, a stronger Canadian economy and more customers for our oil, and the best part is that no government subsidies are necessary. In fact, this is a company that is ready to bring in its own private dollars and make it happen. The only thing standing in the way is the Liberals' tanker ban.
Will they do the right thing, advocate for the well-being of Canadians and remove it?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let me share what the new Conservative Premier of British Columbia just said: “Our government’s focus is on the project in front of us.... Pacific Link has been declared in the national interest, it takes a southern route, and it will create...jobs [for] British Columbia.” Other Conservatives seem to be able to get on board and support Pacific link. These guys just look for opportunities to fight. We are interested in building, not fighting. Why do they not join us?

Mr. Speaker, this is not an either-or decision, and at the end of the day it is a federal matter, so it is up to this government to make the choice. Will it take the tanker ban and remove it or, at the bare minimum, at least grant an exemption so that this private investment can go through, so that Canadian jobs can be created, so that oil can get to world markets and so that we as a country can be proud of what we produce here at home? The government is more than happy to give handouts to corporations that come begging. This one is not. It just needs this obstacle out of the way.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, here is what this government is doing: expanding the Taylor to Gordondale pipeline; expanding the Sunrise pipeline; building Pacific link, a million-barrel-a-day pipeline to the west coast; building LNG Canada phase one; supporting Woodfibre; supporting Tilbury; and supporting Ksi Lisims.
All the Conservatives do is complain and look for things to fight about. Why do they not help build Canada with us?

Mr. Speaker, under the Liberal tanker moratorium, up to 34 tankers can be approved every month on the southern route, yet the northern route is equally safe, has less marine traffic and can have the same protections as the south. Having navigated the navy's tanker on the B.C. coast for years, I know what it takes to operate tankers safely, and the northern route can also meet the same standards as the south. This is a Liberal embargo on Canada and companies like Strathcona Resources that are standing by to ship Canadian oil overseas.
Will the Prime Minister immediately grant an exemption for the northern route, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is so much going on on the west coast that is driving up economic growth and opportunity for that member's constituents that it is hard to name them.

In addition to what my colleague, the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, just laid out, let me just congratulate the port of Vancouver for an all-time record of shipments going out of that port that is building our country strong and diversifying our trade markets. It has us on the path to double non-U.S. exports over the next 10 years. We are building British Columbia and we are building Canada—
The hon. member for Burnaby Central.

Mr. Speaker, workers and unions in my riding have emphasized the importance of protecting workers' rights and ensuring their voices are heard at the bargaining table. Our government shares this commitment and believes meaningful collective bargaining leads to better agreements. This is why we are giving workers and employers more time to negotiate and greater support to resolve disputes.
Could the minister explain how Bill C-39 will protect workers' rights, strengthen collective bargaining and ensure government intervention is reserved for exceptional circumstances?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anna Gainey (Secretary of State (Children and Youth), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our government believes that the best agreements are reached at the bargaining table. Bill C-39 strengthens the bargaining process by providing employers and unions with more time to negotiate, earlier access to dispute resolution tools and additional support to help the parties reach agreements before disputes escalate.

At the same time, the bill preserves the fundamental right to strike while introducing important guardrails around the use of section 107, ensuring that government intervention remains exactly what it should be: rare, exceptional, transparent and a measure of last resort.

Mr. Speaker, last week, Parks Canada announced it is cutting the 55-year search and rescue K9 program in Banff National Park. This program is essential to park visitor safety, responding to thousands of calls. Leroy, the last rescue dog, tracked 156 individuals and found 57 people over seven years. This is a small team that has a huge impact on visitor safety. These dogs cover areas 30 to 50 times faster than human rescuers. They are essential to the safety in our parks.
Why is the minister cutting vital safety programs while her executives received millions of dollars last year?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Wade Grant (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we thank the federal public service employees for their dedication and deeply value their critical role in protecting Canadians. We need to continue to protect Canadians' nature, environment and emergency preparedness. We continue to ensure Canada's national parks and heritage are preserved, safe and managed right to serve both Canadians and our environment, and we will continue to do that.
Mr. Speaker, I have good news. Today, the Liberals have a chance to vote for our NDP bill to repeal section 107 and protect the right to strike. Unions and workers everywhere have supported it.

The government has a clear choice, continue its unconstitutional attacks on workers in Bill C-39 or vote in favour of our NDP bill. Which is it? Will the Liberals finally respect the demands of workers or continue caving to CEOs by violating the right to strike?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, obviously, we honour the role of workers, honour the role of organized labour and recognize that, in fact, there are rights to collectively bargain, but sometimes those rights, in order to be exercised, need federal support, especially in Canada Labour Code situations. We will, under Bill C-39, put in place new, expanded measures in order to support parties that find it difficult to achieve a collective agreement. We want to make those strikes all too rare.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order regarding what happened earlier when a colleague in the House—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I cannot hear the hon. member.
The hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order regarding what happened earlier when a colleague, who represents his community here in the House, was trying to ask a question to a minister. There was a lot of noise, purposely to stop him from—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I am going to finish hearing what the hon. member has to say, one way or the other.
The hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, maybe this time they will listen.

Members purposely made noise to try to stop the member from speaking. I think we are getting into the territory of privilege. If a member cannot speak and ask a question in the House on behalf of the people he represents, there is a potential question of privilege.

It was difficult, but we did get through it. This is why I ask members sometimes to try not to be provocative, because it creates an unparliamentary ruckus. I would ask members to make it easier next time.
I thank the hon. member for her point of order.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Bill C-41—Proposal to Apply Standing Order 69.1

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to request the division of Bill C-41 for voting purposes, pursuant to Standing Order 69.1. Standing Order 69.1(1) says the following:

Quote.QuotePara: In the case where a government bill seeks to repeal, amend or enact more than one act, and where there is not a common element connecting the various provisions or where unrelated matters are linked, the Speaker shall have the power to divide the questions, for the purposes of voting, on the motion for second reading and reference to a committee and the motion for third reading and passage of the bill. The Speaker shall have the power to combine clauses of the bill thematically and to put the aforementioned questions on each of these groups of clauses separately, provided that there will be a single debate at each stage.

Content.ParaText: Bill C-41 seeks to do two fundamental things. That is to say, the bill stands for two separate principles. The bill seeks to stop the forthcoming expansion of medical assistance in dying to people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness. It also seeks to allow medical assistance in dying for people who have no capacity to consent but who requested MAID before they lost capacity, otherwise known as advance requests. These are two fundamentally different questions that must, I submit, be voted on separately. The bill, as worded, would also fundamentally change the nature of the MAID regime by partially removing it from the realm of criminal law insofar as advance requests are concerned. This is another matter that speaks to both the complexity of the bill and its omnibus nature, which I believe warrants your prerogative to divide the question pursuant to Standing Order 69.1.

Based on my preliminary reading of the bill, there should be two separate questions: one on the mental health expansion in clauses 9, 10 and 14, which concern a statute passed in 2021, An Act to amend the Criminal Code (medical assistance in dying), as amended in 2023 and 2024, together with subclause 4(2) of Bill C-41 on the same subject matter; and the second question on MAID for people who cannot consent, otherwise known as advance requests, in the remaining provisions of Bill C-41, which propose amendments to a different act, the Criminal Code, plus consequential cross-references in three other statutes.

I recognize that these matters concern medical assistance in dying. However, the question under Standing Order 69.1 is not simply whether the provisions fall within the same broad policy area, but rather, whether they are sufficiently distinct so as to warrant separate votes. Speaker Regan addressed this contrast in a bill containing multiple principles while addressing a singular field of policy in his March 1, 2018, ruling at page 17551 of the Debates. He stated:

Quote.QuotePara: In presenting arguments relating to Bill C-63, the hon. member for Calgary Shepard raised an interesting concept from the practice in the Quebec National Assembly. Quoting from page 400 of Parliamentary Procedure in Québec, he stated:

“The principle or principles contained in a bill must not be confused with the field it concerns. To frame the concept of principle in that way would prevent the division of most bills, because they apply to a specific field.”

While their procedure for dividing bills is quite different from ours, the idea of distinguishing the principles of a bill from its field has stayed with me. While each bill is different and so too each case, I believe that Standing Order 69.1 can indeed be applied to a bill where all of the initiatives relate to a specific policy area, if those initiatives are sufficiently distinct to warrant a separate decision of the House.

Content.ParaText: To that end, Mr. Speaker, I submit that you should approach Bill C-41, legislation which quite literally concerns life and death, in a fundamentally different way from how you might consider a request to, say, separate a transportation bill with respect to its rail clauses and its aviation clauses. Stopping the expansion of MAID to people with mental illness was the subject of Bill C-218, which the Liberal government voted against earlier this session, citing an intention to bring forward the legislation it tabled yesterday, Bill C-41. In the absence of legislation, this expansion will go into effect March 17, 2027. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that this deadline has been twice delayed by the Liberals, citing the need for further study and further readiness.

In this Parliament, the Special Joint Committee on Medical Assistance in Dying was re-established, with the narrow mandate of exploring the forthcoming mental illness expansion. The culmination of the study was a singular recommendation, supported by Liberal and Conservative members of the committee, that the expansion not proceed. This was an incredibly important act of bipartisan co-operation on what, I reiterate, is a life-and-death matter. This work underscores the importance of allowing parliamentarians to consider the mental health expansion of MAID on its own merit rather than marrying it to the separate and also consequential question about advance requests.

During the course of the committee's hearings, we heard from many experts, including MAID practitioners, who oppose MAID for people with mental illness but support MAID itself. There are those who support MAID for people with mental illness but not MAID for people without the capacity to consent, just as the inverse is undoubtedly true. On these questions of conscience, members should be free to vote individually on each of these two distinct questions.

In approaching the exercise of your authority under Standing Order 69.1, Mr. Speaker, I would encourage you to draw inspiration from the way in which the Chair uses its discretion on the selection of report stage amendments when a matter of conscience comes before the House. While on most bills, the criteria are applied in a clinical manner, the Chair will, on matters of conscience, approach the exercise in a more generous fashion.
Two such cases concern earlier iterations of medical assistance in dying legislation. On the original MAID bill, Bill C-14, Mr. Speaker Regan said, at page 3485 of the Debates on May 17, 2016:

Quote.QuotePara: The Chair appreciates the arguments put forward by hon. members as to why they consider these amendments to be of such significance as to warrant further consideration at report stage. I recognize that this is an important issue on which many members have strong and varied opinions. The Chair notes that the bill before us is unique, in its far-reaching social, moral and constitutional implications. The Chair also notes that, given the variety of opinions expressed by various members in all parties in relation to the provisions of this once-in-a-generation bill, the Chair is open to the argument of exceptional significance as contemplated in our Standing Orders. For these reasons, the Chair is prepared, on this occasion, to give members the benefit of the doubt....

Content.ParaText: Similar views were expressed concerning the later Bill C-7, by the Assistant Deputy Speaker, on November 27, 2020, at page 2603 of the Debates:

Quote.QuotePara: As with the original medical assistance in dying legislation four years ago, I recognize that this is an important issue with profound legal, moral and constitutional dimensions and that members have strongly held and varied points of view on these matters.
For these reasons, the Chair is prepared on this occasion to give members the benefit of the doubt....

Content.ParaText: To return to the threshold for dividing votes set out in the relevant standing order, I submit here that there is a sound basis for you to find that, despite the common element between the key questions involving MAID itself, the measures are fundamentally distinct from one another, with separate political, moral and legal implications, and for that matter, distinct levels of support and opposition among Canadians and, I suspect, Parliamentarians as well.
In closing, the disparate objectives of Bill C-41 warrant your prerogative as Chair to divide the question for the purposes of voting.
I thank the member for his intervention. Of course, the Speaker will take it back to make a decision on it.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to indicate that we would like the opportunity to respond to the point of order that has been raised before you make your ruling.
It is noted.
I wish to inform the House that because of the deferred recorded divisions, the time provided for government orders will be extended by 73 minutes.

It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Nanaimo—Ladysmith, Finance; the hon. member for Yellowhead, The Economy.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the fifth report of the Standing Committee on National Defence, entitled “The Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces Contaminated Sites”.
Pursuant to Standing Order 109, the committee requests that the government table a comprehensive response to this report.
Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to table petition e-7590.

As members are likely aware, I often like to tell individuals in the chamber that my riding has the highest percentage of Korean Canadians out of all 343 ridings in our country. Bearing that in mind, and given that some of them are here in the gallery today, it is a great honour—

I have to interrupt the member. A member cannot mention a presence or absence, and especially of people who are in the gallery. Only the Speaker can make reference to those who are in the gallery. I will allow the member to continue and to finish, but the member has to remember not to make reference to people in the gallery.
Mr. Speaker, the petition is regarding the Korean War armistice of 1953.

As we are all aware, one of the proudest moments in our current history was when Canada contributed to the Republic of Korea during the Korean War. In fact, we were the third-largest contributor to that effort. Over 26,000 Canadians served in the Korean War, and of course, 516 gave their lives. As a result of that, and given the flourishing relationship between the Republic of Korea and Canada, and the sizable community of Korean Canadians from coast to coast to coast, petitioners are presenting this petition. It is about how the absence of a peace agreement will certainly fuel military tension and humanitarian suffering in the Korean region.

Petitioners have requested that we publicly support international efforts to negotiate a formal peace agreement replacing the 1953 armistice. They are requesting that we work with allies, including the Republic of Korea, to advance multilateral diplomacy toward durable peace and stability on the Korean peninsula. They also ask for the tabling in Parliament of a report outlining our strategy for a permanent peace settlement. Finally, they ask that we demonstrate global leadership by advocating in international forums for peaceful conflict resolution and a formal peace settlement on the Korean peninsula.
Mr. Speaker, today I am tabling a petition from Greenpeace Canada, Oceans North and MiningWatch Canada that calls for the protection of deep seabeds; it is signed by 10,398 people.

In 2023, Canada announced its support for a moratorium on deep sea mining in international waters. However, a business registered in Canada, The Metals Company, holds exploration contracts in the Pacific. This Canadian company also responded to the Trump administration's call to seek authorization to mine the seabed under U.S. legislation, in breach of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

Deep seabeds are mankind's shared heritage. We have a responsibility to protect our oceans for future generations. Accordingly, this petition calls on the government to clearly prohibit any Canadian individual or company from undertaking deep sea mining activities.
I am honoured to table this petition in the House.
Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to rise on behalf of petitioners in Simcoe—Grey.
An individual, Erin Small, started a petition that has quite a few signatures on it. The petitioners are very disappointed in the judicial system with respect to intimate partner violence.

They are calling for the implementation of strict conflict of interest rules requiring investigating officers to disclose any personal or professional relationship with either the accused or the victim, with mandatory reassignment where a conflict exists. They also call for reform of mandatory charging policies to prevent survivors from being criminalized when the accused attempts to countercharge the victim. Third, they ask us to ensure that sexual assault charges cannot be resolved through peace bonds, diversion agreements or other non-conviction resolutions without judicial oversight and clear public interest justification.

They also ask that we remove barriers to victim impact statements by allowing survivors to provide statements, regardless of the final judicial outcome. Finally, they are asking for the creation of independent civilian oversight bodies to review investigative failures, wrongful countercharges, mishandled cases and systemic bias within police and prosecutorial systems.
