Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present a petition on behalf of concerned Canadians.
Since October 2023, Health Canada has prohibited all pentachlorophenol wood preservative products used to treat Douglas fir utility poles. Basically, all the stock had to be used by this month.

The petitioners highlight that DCOI is an arsenic-free, chromium-free and dioxin-free preservative that has been standardized by the American Wood Protection Association since 1989 and has been approved by the United States and Europe for use in wood preservatives. Of the four pole preservatives registered in Canada, only creosote is oil-borne, leaving utilities without a modern oil-borne option, causing fir logs to be uncoated and hence unusable as utility poles.

There are only three processing plants left, and this has resulted in Canadian fir being exported to the United States for further processing, which could have been done right here in Canada. There is a loss of jobs, and it is not really helping the environment in the long run. This is an important issue the petitioners are bringing forward.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I ask that all questions be allowed to stand at this time.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.
[For text of questions and responses, see Written Questions website]

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I ask that all notices of motions for the production of papers also be allowed to stand at this time.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from October 21 consideration of the motion that Bill C-34, An Act to enact the Digital Safety Act and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my comments, I will emphasize that the government, coming out of the last federal election, made commitments to Canadians in regard to the Internet and how we can protect children. That is really what Bill C-34 is all about.

If we were to canvass and talk to the constituents we represent, we would find that there is genuine concern in regard to some of the harmful things that are on the Internet. The bill is not meant to replace parents but is rather to support parents. The Internet is 24-7. There are things on it that are very harmful, particularly for children 16 and under, and there is a role for government to play.

We have seen other countries take action, as we are taking action. I appeal to my colleagues across the way to listen to what is being expressed through our constituents, which is genuine concern over the harmful things that take place on the Internet, and vote accordingly in regard to Bill C-34.

The bill is a solution, in good part, that would protect and complement what parents have to go through in raising a child. The Internet did not exist when my children were young, and I can only imagine what parents today have to go through given the seven-day-a-week, 24-hour availability of the Internet. The Internet is going to power our economy and society in many positive ways; there is no doubt about that, but to ignore the potential harm, particularly to our children, would be irresponsible.

We have had other private members' bills on the issue of our children and what is on the Internet that causes problems. I made a note of some of those things. We can think of what harmful content is. I have heard Conservatives talk about it, and obviously many members of the Liberal caucus have had opportunities both inside and outside of the House to talk about it. These are the types of discussions that take place in our communities.

There are things such as sexually victimizing a child, revictimizing a survivor, using intimate content without the consent of the person and inducing a child to harm themselves. Just the other day, a Conservative MP was talking about an incident where committing suicide was being promoted. Unfortunately, these are the types of things we see. They are things that promote extreme hatred or violence, or that deal with issues like terrorism and the promotion of terrorism. One could easily classify these things, I would suggest, as harmful content.

It is one thing to talk about harmful content. I suspect if we were to canvass the House, we would find virtually unanimous consent that there is harmful content on the Internet. The challenge I put across the way to my Conservative friends in particular is, what are they prepared to do about it? Bill C-34 has an action that would protect children and support parents. That is why I believe it is time for us to not only talk about this, but look at taking substantial action.

The establishment of an independent digital safety commission is long overdue. It would have a profound, positive impact on the children of Canada no matter where they live. If members believe that there is harm on the Internet and we have a role to play in Ottawa, I suggest that supporting an independent digital safety commission is something they ought to be voting in favour of. If they cannot vote in favour of it, I believe they owe an explanation to their constituents as to why they do not see the merit in doing that.

Having a commission that has the ability to ensure there is a higher sense of responsibility and duty to act responsibly is critically important. We could regulate service providers, as an example, to assess and mitigate risks in the form of a report, with a sense of accountability and transparency. We could enable the commission to do the follow-through, to the degree that it would have the ability to go after the major players, not only here but also abroad, and levy fines.

These are all ways in which we can play a role in protecting the children of Canada by having a ban on social media content for children under the age of 16, with the opportunity for some exceptions if they are proven to be safe for our children. This is good legislation. I hope every member of the House will get behind it and vote for it.

Mr. Speaker, the Bloc Québécois definitely believes that social media needs to be regulated. It is a new sector, and we are already seeing serious harms emerge. Most recently, in August, Meta agreed to a settlement and paid $16 billion in compensation for the harm caused to young people.

Quebec has already undertaken a collective review with the aim of protecting our young people from screen time, and it has made significant progress in that endeavour. The Select Committee on the Impacts of Screens and Social Media on Young People's Health and Development tabled a report recommending a ban on social media for children aged 14 and under, rather than 16 and under, as proposed in Bill C-34.
My question for my colleague is this: Will the government respect Quebec's jurisdiction over youth protection? Has the report been consulted and has the question been asked—
I must interrupt the member to give the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader the opportunity to reply.

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to chat with the minister responsible for the legislation earlier today. He amplified and explained in great detail the degree to which there is a high level of expertise.

The age has been well documented. If the member believes that the age should be lowered, he should attend the standing committee and make his case. If he is inclined to suggest that he has the evidence and science that demonstrate that it would be better to lower it, he should share it with the minister.
There are certain aspects of note in the legislation, but I will wait for my next question.

Mr. Speaker, I am very concerned about the implication of children being exposed in particular to pornographic content online. This is a major and still underdiscussed issue and problem. Many children are exposed to pornography online at the age of nine, 10, 11 or 12 years old, and it has significant negative implications for them, their understanding and their expectations.

In looking at this bill, my understanding is that it deals with some of this content if it is on social media websites. It does not deal with other situations outside of social media where young people may encounter this content. I think it is incumbent on us to work together to look at this and/or other legislation that addresses it.
I wonder if the member could comment on ensuring that children are not accessing this material not only on social media but anywhere else.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has made very clear that he wants to work collaboratively. The simple message that needs to get across is that there is a role for the Parliament of Canada to protect the interests of our children from the negative side, the very hurtful side, of social media and the Internet. I would suggest to the member opposite, who I know has a number of young children, that this is not to take away any sort of parenting from the child, but is rather to complement the parent's role. At the end of the day, there is a wonderful opportunity to have that dialogue. The minister is very much open to it, and I look forward to ongoing discussions both here and at committee.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Wade Grant (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I too grew up in an era that did not have the Internet. All we had was a land line, which we used to phone our friends to talk to them. However, I am the father of two young children. My daughter is now 15, and, of course, she is exposed to things like social media. I have seen things that I have never had to deal with. I wish I could protect her 24 hours a day, seven days a week, but unfortunately we cannot do that.

The member talked about protecting children. I have heard it from a lot of parents. He has probably heard it from a lot of parents. Can he expand on how he feels this bill would protect them going forward?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question, because it is important to recognize that Bill C-34 would create the digital safety act. It would regulate major social media services, AI chat services and some other online services. Through those regulations, we would have the opportunity to have them enforced by the safety commission.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to split my time.

In 1965, The Who sang The Kids Are Alright. In 1998, The Offspring answered that with The Kids Aren't Alright. That was before Instagram and Snapchat and before strangers across the world could come into a child's bedroom.

Today, that answer is truer than ever, and I think most would agree in the House the kids are not all right. They are being hooked by algorithms engineered on purpose to keep them scrolling past midnight because every extra minute they scroll is worth money to somebody on the other side. They are being bullied in ways that never log off, and they are being hunted in their own bedrooms by predators who never have to pass a parent's bedroom. A generation ago, a child's bedroom door was a wall, and now it is a window to the entire world.

There are no Liberal kids and there are no Conservative kids. There are no NDP kids. There are just kids, so I want to approach this bill, Bill C-34, in a way that any parent would: not asking whether it sounds good, but whether it actually keeps people safe.

Every member of the House knows the name Amanda Todd. She was 12 years old when a stranger in the Netherlands hiding behind 22 different aliases found her online. He coerced her. He captured images of her. He threatened to send them to everyone she loved, and then he did. Weeks before she died, Amanda held out flash cards to a camera one at a time and told the world what was happening to her. She was 15 when she took her own life, and she carried all of that alone. Then it took 10 years to put the man responsible behind bars, and by then he had been convicted of crimes against 33 other young people.

We told ourselves that this would not happen again. Then came Carson Cleland, 12 years old, from Prince George. A sextortionist found him on Snapchat, an app whose own rules said that he was too young to be on there. Nobody stopped him from signing up. Nobody stopped the stranger from finding him. My colleague from Cariboo—Prince George told the House it was just 12 hours from the first threat to his death. His father said it best when he said our kids are “not built for adult problems in a kid's world.”

For Amanda, justice took a decade. For Carson, the harm took half a day. The predators get faster and the laws do not keep up. Amanda and Carson are not rare. They are just names that we know. Behind them, there are thousands of names that we do not know of thousands of other cases.

In 2023, Canadian police recorded almost 20,000 incidents of online sexual exploitation, up 59% in a single year. That is more than 50 cases a day. Sextortion reports to Cybertip.ca rose 300% between 2020 and 2025. Where the victim is known, more than four out of five are boys, boys like Carson. Nearly two-thirds of cases happen on Instagram or Snapchat or some app on some kids' phones tonight. These companies have the data, the engineers and the billions, but they have lacked will.

One in four Canadian youth has been cyber-bullied. In a classroom of 28 people, that is seven kids. Every one of those numbers is a child on the edge of their bed at two in the morning with a phone glowing in the dark, scrolling and too ashamed to wake their parents up to tell them what happened. Here is a number I want every member of the House to remember: Nine in 10 Canadian teens who were sexually victimized online were harmed in private messages. It was not the public feed and not in the DMs, but behind a closed door on a screen that no parent can see.

There are ideas in this bill that deserve our attention, there is no question, such as a duty on platforms to act responsibly, a 24-hour takedown of child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate images and a duty on AI chatbots to connect a child in crisis with an actual real person.

For years, we let these platforms police themselves. They buried the safety fixtures six menus deep. Self-regulation has had its chance and it has failed kids. Parents were too busy maybe to find it six menu items deep. An idea on paper has never really protected a child. What matters is how the law works on an ordinary Wednesday night like tonight when a stranger sends that first message. Those questions cannot be settled just on the floor in a short debate. The committee has to do some work on this.

These are some of the questions. First, would it reach the harm where it happens? Private messaging where nine out of 10 victims are harmed would be expressly excluded from the bill's duties. We want to know why. Committees should ask what safety-by-design duties, like stopping strangers from messaging minors by default, could protect kids in the DMs without anybody reading their messages.

Second, what would the rules actually say? This has not been clear in the legislation. Roughly 50 key decisions in this legislation are left until after passage: 19 of them for cabinet and 31 of them for a commission that does not actually exist yet. Which platforms are covered? What is safety by design? Are gaming platforms in there or at all, or will that only come later? Parliament should vote on the whole house, not just a framework of it.

Third, we all have seen the example of Australia. We want to know what it teaches us. Australia went first, so we do not really have to guess. Platforms there shut down 4.7 million children's accounts in the first month, but three months in, its own regulator found that teen social media use had barely moved. It went from 86% to 81%. About half of the teens still online said that nobody even checked their age. As a result, parents became less aware about what their kids were doing because of it. A ban with a weak age check is not really a ban at all. It is like leaving the key under the mat at the front door. It does not really keep kids out. It moves them out of their parents' sight, or it moves them, in the case of Australia, to other platforms that are not captured within the legislation.

Fourth, we want to know if the penalties are strong enough. The last online harm bill, which was a terrible bill in this House, set the minimum fees at 6% of global revenue. This one would cut that to 3%. There are some questions about why. For some of the richest companies in history, a fine that they can budget for is not really a punishment. It is like a licensing fee that they work into the cost of doing business.

Fifth, does it touch the actual business model? On these platforms, kids are not the customers. Their attention is actually the product. That is the problem. Our own heritage committee recommended banning targeted ads and data harvesting aimed at minors. The government declined, while admitting that the algorithmic feeds drive the actual addictive designs. We want to know more about that, certainly.

Finally, most importantly, the member before me spoke about the digital safety commission, but who will watch the watchdog? Who will write these rules? What judge would enforce this? Is it five people? Is it one person? The legislation really is not clear on any of that, so we would like to hear more from the government. Hopefully we will get that in the course of this debate in this House. What recourse does a family have when the platform fails a child?

Through all of this, there is one principle that should guide everyone here: Parents know their kids better than any government or tech company ever could. A mother can tell her son to put his phone down and go to sleep, but what she cannot do is out-muscle an algorithm built by thousands of engineers to keep him awake at night. A good law does not take her place. It stands beside her.

I hope that we have that conversation in this House. There must be a law that protects all privacy. It is the work of the committee not to blindly support something that needs clarity, but to hear from the experts and parents like Carson's parents. It must be a law that protects adults' privacy too. We cannot find every user under 16 without checking every user over 16, so there are some real questions about what that could mean for every parent and grandparent who would have to give their identification to a platform. Who stores that data and for how long? What happens when it is breached? It is not a question of if, but it is a question of when.

I will end with this. A paper tiger does not keep a child safe. It does not stop a predator and it gives no parent peace of mind, so it is important to get this right. We owe it to the families of Carson and Amanda and thousands of others.

I started by saying the kids are not all right and I mean it. The kids are not all right today, but if we ask the hard questions and put down good legislation to keep kids safe, then maybe they will be all right.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what I like about the legislation is that by establishing the commission it does not just talk to it. My understanding is that there would be between three to five members on the commission who would have the ability through regulation to put in fines, and so forth. The commission would actually have teeth. I think that is so critically important.
Does the Conservative Party in principle support the concept of having that commission?

Mr. Speaker, the legislation is really unclear about the commission, and that is the answer we are trying to seek in the House. It could be three to five and it could be one, and that one is left up to regulation after the legislation.

The question that we have in the House is to make it clear. I know the member opposite has read the legislation so I am not suggesting that he has not, but he has not made it clear to this House, the legislation has not made it clear to this House and the minister has not made it clear to the public.

Mr. Speaker, the member made mention of Amanda Todd. I have met the mother. Amanda lived in my community, Maple Ridge, and also in Port Coquitlam. At 12 years old, she was persuaded to expose herself, then she was blackmailed, went through years of bullying and ended up killing herself. What happened was terrible. I know that Conservatives want children to be protected online because they are vulnerable.

I just responded to a letter today from a constituent. She said her 12-year-old granddaughter received communication through social media from two young men who, in their posts, threatened to kill and rape her 12-year-old granddaughter and said that she should kill herself. This is happening. This was reported to the police. Parents, families and children are feeling very vulnerable.

I wonder if the member could talk a bit about this bill in the sense that we want something to happen, we want them to be protected, but how much bureaucracy is going to be involved as opposed to really getting the job done of protecting our kids?
Mr. Speaker, Amanda Todd held up flashcards because she believed that the people who would know her story would then act.

In the case of Carson Cleland, also from B.C., his parents spoke out during the hardest days of their lives because he had hoped that people would act. They did their part. I think it is incumbent on this House to truly look at this legislation very carefully and make sure that it is not just words on paper, that it has teeth, that we do not follow the example of Australia where it does not work, that we give parents the tools to parent, that we stand side by side with parents rather than letting the government parent their kids. That is what parents want to see from this legislation, and it is incumbent on the House to take this to committee and really study it.
Mr. Speaker, I commend my colleague on her speech. I believe we share the same point of view on the need to regulate digital safety, particularly for children.

I would like to hear her thoughts on the new digital safety commission that will be established. We do not know the parameters or what powers it will have. We also do not know which platforms it will regulate.
Does my colleague not think that the government is doing things a bit backwards?
As legislators, we are being asked to pass a bill, but we do not have a full understanding of the parameters involved.

Mr. Speaker, there is very much agreement with the member who just asked the question. It is hard to vote on something that you know halfway. We do not know anything about this commission. We do have a very live example in one of our country's closest allies, where pieces of this did not work. We know that putting 20 different social media companies into a piece of legislation just drives people into other ones where they are not actually off and it drives parents to put trust in the government where it does not deserve trust.
There are a lot more questions than answers in this legislation and that is exactly where we are on it.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-34, more commonly known as the safe social media act.

I believe that everyone in the House agrees that the rapid development of social media has created enormous challenges for families across Canada and the world. What is the answer to this challenge? The vast web of global connection it has brought us has also created serious mental health and addiction challenges for children and teens.

As a mother of two grown children, I saw the beginnings of this phenomenon, with the Internet's opening and expansion into digital spaces, when my children were very young. As early as the mid-1990s, the centre for online addiction was established and Internet addiction disorder was first recognized. In 1997, the New York Times wrote that psychologists are beginning to treat patients who spend 40, 50 or 60 hours a week in chat rooms and online games, ignoring spouses, children and jobs. They described the classic cycle of tolerance, withdrawal and a desperate reliance on the glowing terminal for emotional gratification.

This could well describe the same challenges we face today but, instead of just addicted adults, it is children whose health and development are being harmed. The Internet's uniquely absorbent nature, along with chat rooms and online games, has only become more dangerous because of smart phones, algorithms and AI models. Nowadays, these addictive and mind-altering spaces have become available anytime, anywhere.

Ask any parent or teacher, and we will find that children view their digital lives as intertwined with their everyday lives. Purely online friends and hangouts have become commonplace. These spaces let them educate and express themselves. It is why children and teens report the longest screen time and highest social media use of any age group. We know that spending seven-plus hours on personal screen time is significantly more likely to lead to anxiety, depression and suicidal thoughts. These platforms were never designed for children, yet children are vulnerable to their design.

Recommendations for algorithms, push notifications, endless scrolling and autoplay can repeatedly direct them toward content that keeps them engaged. These design choices can amplify exposure to harmful material and make it difficult for young users to disengage. At the same time, AI chatbots and digital companions are becoming increasingly integrated into the platforms young people use, creating new and largely untested risks.

Parents who once set computer time now know that these barriers do not exist when children under 10 can readily access TikTok, Instagram and ChatGPT. They cannot control their children's algorithms or be notified when harmful material appears.

One of the most tragic case studies on this subject involves the death, last year, of 13-year-old British Columbian Maddy Croswell. Her parents and the coroner's office found this case of teen suicide to have occurred after a social media platform she was using repeatedly pushed hundreds of hours of harmful content onto her feed advocating self-harm and eventual suicide.

Her parents thought they had done everything right. They had parental controls on her phone. They monitored her screen time. They believed they had created a safe, loving home environment, but it was not enough. Sadly, many more cases like this exist across Canada. Parental involvement is not enough to challenge the enormous reach of social media algorithms that can push dangerous and harmful content to young children and teens.

According to Stats Canada, one in four children aged 12 to 17 experienced cyber-bullying. Police reported that online child sexual exploitation incidents reached 16,000 in 2024, up 347% from 2014. I have heard from many parents about the helplessness they feel and the fear they have for their children. They feel they are in a David versus Goliath battle with Meta, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.

AI companies and their algorithms are also increasingly dangerous in this respect. Reports that the shooter at Tumbler Ridge was assisted in planning this deadly shooting by ChatGPT is sickening for all Canadians. OpenAI's failure to report clear warnings of violence has left a community devastated for generations to come.

Parliament must act on this, but as lawmakers we must ensure that what we pass is good law, not just good intentions. For myself, I would like to see legislation that accomplishes three main goals: protect children and teens from harmful content online; set clear rules on tech giants that affect all our lives; and put more control in parents' hands, not the government's.

Canada also has the opportunity with this legislation to review other jurisdictions that have established similar measures and see what has worked and what has not. Australia, which was the first to move forward with the social media ban for those under 16, has found that the measure it chose to restrict access has frequently been circumvented. Surveys by Australia's eSafety Commissioner showed that 61% to 70% of young Australians aged 12 to 15 who previously used restricted platforms still have active accounts. Children still using the apps report that it is easy to bypass the restrictions and still have active accounts. If we were to ask children nowadays what they think about this type of bill, they would say that they would find a way to get through if they have to. Teens easily dodge the rules by lying about their birth year, having older teens create new accounts or using facial recognition workarounds.

Platforms also do not always enforce regulations consistently across their sites. We have also had concerning evidence that bans in other countries led to a spike in teenagers using virtual private networks, VPNs, to mask their country of origin when accessing social media platforms. Using VPNs often means youth are accessing unregulated underground platforms that could lead them to more unsafe content rather than less.

What can we do to get ahead of this? We have to consider the downstream consequences. If we ask any teenage visitor to the House of Commons today whether a ban we enacted would discourage them from accessing Instagram or TikTok, they would probably laugh and say no. That is why we need to ensure the bill has real teeth, not just vague regulation for future bureaucrats to interpret. For example, Bill C-34 leaves the definition of “regulated social media services” to future regulations, but will it be based strictly on active Canadian user accounts, annual revenue or specific platform features? Will the age restrictions be determined by facial recognition, ID uploads or credit cards?
What about privacy? Who will be asked to store this information? Would it be government, third parties or tech giants themselves? How long can they store it, and how secure will it be?

The bill's regulations for chatbot services will soon face open-ended AI models that let almost any website create a functioning chatbot service for everything from customer service to online shopping.

Given the Liberals' poor track record on online regulation and censorship, the House must move carefully as it considers Bill C-34. Previous failures and fiascos, such as Bill C-11 and Bill C-63, infringed upon Canadian civil liberties. This cannot be allowed to be repeated when so many parents are asking us to help them hold dangerous digital platforms and addictive social media companies to account.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would go back to the comments I put on the record in seeing the bill. In my mind, there is no doubt whatsoever that the vast majority understand that there are harmful things on the Internet that have an impact on children under the age of 16. We have had endless examples provided to the House.

To me there is a responsibility to not only put something into legislation, but also ensure that the legislation has some form of enforcement, that the commission being proposed would ensure there are consequences and that regulations are put in to protect our children.
Does the member support the principle of protecting our children through legislation and having a commission?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the member's passion for this. I know how important it is to him that this bill passes, that this bill goes through and becomes legislation, but he must also understand that, if we do not do this right, it is not just something we can do a redo on. There are children's lives at stake here. There are families' lives at stake. We need to do this right, which means we need to bring it under careful scrutiny, and we need to make sure this is brought under careful scrutiny in committee.
Mr. Speaker, the issue of jurisdiction absolutely must be addressed in the bill. Matters relating to social protection and the protection of youth fall under Quebec and provincial jurisdiction.

I would like to ask my colleague whether she agrees that the federal government should work in collaboration with Quebec and the provinces. Once the bill is passed, they are the ones who will be responsible for intervening directly in an area that does not fall under the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I think everyone in the House knows that this could be one of the most important bills during our mandate that could affect the most people, in particular children and families. Yes, we need to get input from all provinces, including Quebec. We need to get input from parents. We need to get input from children. We need to look at what other countries have done, because we are not the first to approach this situation. We need to make sure we learn from past mistakes, from countries like Australia, to learn from them and, again, make sure this legislation is done right for the sake of our children.

Mr. Speaker, I do appreciate the response I got from the member, but I really want to talk about the principle of having the commission, because the commission, from my perspective, is what gives it real teeth. We are talking about three to five members who would sit on a commission and ultimately be responsible for administering regulations. They would have the power, for example, to give fines. They would have the power to hold some of these Internet service providers responsible through regulation. They would have the authority necessary to protect the interests of our children and protect them from harmful content.
Is that something she supports in principle?

Mr. Speaker, we need to have commissioners. We need to have oversight, but we cannot take oversight away from parents. We need to make sure parents keep their oversight over their own children. If there is one commissioner who is making the decision, it can be problematic, so we need to make sure there is a lot of oversight, not only from the House, but also from parents themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I have a concern about this bill. Why are so many actual issues in this bill being left to regulations, rather than us deciding at this point in Parliament, as representatives of the people, that these are the minimum requirements? Why are we not doing that, and instead leaving it for regulations?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague also knows how important this bill is and how important it is that it is scrutinized. In particular, we need to make sure that what he is asking is discussed in committee and that something like this is not just pushed through quickly, like many other bills that have been brought forward by the Liberals have been. I believe they have the children of Canada at heart in this bill, but there is no way this can go forward without being heavily scrutinized in committee by everyone in the House.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessTitle: Protecting Young Persons from Exposure to Pornography Act

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from September 24 consideration of the motion that Bill S-209, An Act to restrict young persons’ online access to pornographic material, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what purpose do the laws we pass here serve? They serve to civilize society. That is what I have always loved about the law and the body of legislation built over time. Obviously, when new sectors emerge, the law often lags a little behind. The government has to catch up and figure out what is happening.

With the development of digital and virtual technology, we have work to do as legislators. Last week, one of the topics we discussed was the digital services tax. A little while ago, we discussed Bill C‑34, which also seeks to regulate the social media sector. Now, we are now discussing Bill S‑209, which is a worthwhile bill. The Bloc Québécois supports it, because what is happening online should be regulated more.

More and more people are living their lives online. The online world is increasingly becoming the place where people communicate, interact, meet and learn. It is crazy. I was looking at some statistics earlier. Young people spend more than three hours a day online. The law must adapt. One of the risks children face online is coming across pornographic material, and we know that exposure to such material can have damaging effects on their healthy sexual development. Bill S-209 seeks address that issue. That is why we support it.

I want to say from the outset that the Association des pédiatres du Québec also supports this bill and believes that this initiative must be commended. I think that this bill will transcend party lines.

Now that information technology makes pornographic content more widely available, the government has a duty to restrict minors' access to such material as much as possible. Bill S-209 makes it an offence for organizations to make pornographic material available to young persons on the Internet. Furthermore, it enables a designated enforcement authority to take steps to prevent pornographic material from being made available to young persons on the Internet in Canada. This bill is motivated by a desire to better regulate online access to pornographic material through age verification, which is currently limited to a mere declaration. In fact, that is the main purpose of this bill.
We should commend Senator Miville-Dechêne for laying the groundwork in Bill S-203, which is moving forward under a new name.

The bill does not answer every question, but it sets forth the general principles of verifying the age of customers seeking access to pornographic content. Once enacted, the bill will authorize the relevant authority to make regulations establishing a specific framework to be implemented. The bill also sets out the consequences for pornographic websites that violate the law, whether or not they are hosted in Canada. People may be wondering whether we can still civilize the virtual world when everything is hosted overseas. The answer is yes, we can still take action within our own borders.

The bill allows the government to block sites that fail to comply with the future age verification regulations. Is this a silver bullet that will ensure no child ever gains access to pornographic content? Probably not. There will always be ways to circumvent age verification measures, whether through VPNs or other workarounds. Nonetheless, we believe the bill will have beneficial effects because it will make access more difficult and, ultimately, protect children.

In our view, supporting Bill S‑209 is common sense. It means standing up for measures designed to protect the public and promote healthy lifestyle choices. This bill addresses a real concern in our communities. That is why we will support this bill and recommend that it pass second reading.
Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour to rise on behalf of the great people of southwest Saskatchewan.

I want to thank my colleague from just north of me in the province, the member for Battlefords—Lloydminster—Meadow Lake, for sponsoring this Senate bill to address the issue of kids accessing pornography online. As a father of three, including two teenagers, I appreciate seeing all the good work she has done over the years to support children and families. She lives with the modern reality facing parents because she is a mother of young children herself. Raising children who are minors is something each of us has in common with many others in the House, from all parties. That is the most important thing we should be focusing on here today.

As parents, we want the best for our kids. We try to give them everything they need to have their best start in life. Our goal is to help them become adults who can reach their full potential for health, happiness, success and good character. While they are in the process of growing up, we want to keep them away from anything that is harmful to their development. It is an important part of our job to protect them when they are most vulnerable and too young to fully understand how certain things can negatively affect them and sometimes have a permanent impact, for life. As children enter their teen years, parents have to guide them through new challenges, including relationships and sexual development.

I'll quickly quote something from a book called Every Young Man's Battle, which is written from a faith-based perspective to help teens think about these issues. The authors say to the young reader, “One of the most difficult assignments you’ll ever have is to integrate your sexuality with the emotional, spiritual, social, and relational person you want to be.” They goes on to talk about having a healthy outlook on sexuality, which is integrated and balanced with other parts of our lives, including our emotional, relational and spiritual needs. This is a special part of how we are made. We know it is supposed to be a beautiful expression of love, which should lead us toward personal fulfillment, but instead of following that type of path, pornography easily takes a young person in the opposite direction and quickly creates some distorted impressions.

Especially during early puberty, or even before it begins, the damage of exposure to pornography can cause serious problems. One of those problems that can develop at a more formative time is addiction. As time goes on, now with more than one generation growing up with online pornography, we hear from professional and popular discussions about things like porn addiction and sex addiction. Like other forms of addiction, it has negative effects on the person experiencing it, but there are also ways for other people to be harmed, not only relationally but physically as well. That is why Bill S-209 starts off by saying that its purpose is to protect public health and public safety. To do that, it would bring forward a simple solution by requiring age verification. This is really nothing new. The law already has an age limit of 18 years old for selling or distributing sexually explicit material.

We do not allow minors to access these things at a physical store in the real world, and having this rule in place has helped to achieve some good in the process. In some ways, it is similar to the idea of setting an age for people to buy alcohol, but everybody knows that in practice, the situation is very different when it comes to the Internet. The Canadian Centre for Child Protection has said that children as young as eight and nine years old can easily come across sexually graphic material online. In Alberta, a separate study of adolescents found that one-third had been exposed to pornography by the age of 10. There are people who will simply say that this is just boys being boys, and their curious minds will find this material regardless, but many people's experience, and a huge amount of research, shows that it is a bigger problem than that, and I am going to explain why.

The human brain is growing and not finished developing until the age of 26 or thereabouts. To put it simply, while a person's brain is being wired and developing until they are 26, everything that happens in those first 26 years of their life goes a long way to determining who they are, because it can make a difference in how they develop at the biological level. Along with the psychological effects on mental health, we are also talking about experiences that can result in physical changes in the brain while it is still in the middle of development.

Viewing pornography is obviously very different from having sex with a real person. Besides the direct experience, there is something different happening with the brain. Studies have shown that people who are addicted to pornography have a similar brain pattern to people who are addicted to cocaine. Now, take that brain pattern and place it in a preteen or teenage boy or girl, and we have a recipe for disaster. It creates an addiction and a dependency that they will continue to seek from now on, and this is happening at a crucial stage when they are forming their self-image or dealing with insecurities. At the same time, they are learning new ways to handle relationships with their peers and having their first experiences, which shape how they will handle intimate relationships when they are older.

Here are some more stats. When intentionality is questioned, 44% of teens say they looked it up on purpose, but as many as 58% say they encountered porn accidentally. The rates of intentional consumption are actually higher among respondents who identify as LGBT. For that group, some studies show it was 50% higher or could even be 66% higher. We have these youth, who are already vulnerable and seeking affirmation for who they are, exposed to sexually explicit, graphic and violent material while working through deeply personal questions of identity. That higher rate of consumption actually puts them at even more risk than their peers of being victimized.

Pornography also creates erratic behaviour and false expectations of what sex is. I am going to give a couple of examples of such behaviour, and what I am about to say is quite disturbing. There was a case of a 12-year-old schoolboy who raped his seven-year-old sister after watching hard-core porn with his buddies on an Xbox. After viewing this content, he wanted to try to do the things in real life that he was watching online. There was another instance in 2019 of a 14-year-old boy sexually assaulting his eight-year-old stepsister after watching pornography on a regular basis. These are both very shocking and disturbing cases, and it is a mistake to dismiss them as a couple of isolated incidents. They are alarm bells for a much larger problem. Stories like this are less surprising if we realize what is happening beneath the surface.

When studies on this issue have been done, they have found that 38% of teens reported viewing porn that depicts rape, choking or deliberately causing someone pain; 21% agreed that “most people” like to be spanked, hit or slapped during sex; and the numbers get worse among those who purposely watch violent pornography. Those numbers skyrocket to 80% for teenagers who watch porn at least three times a week, yet only 30% say that some form of consent was given by the people in the videos.

Pornography is destroying how healthy relationships are viewed. It is creating massively false expectations for intimate partners about what is deemed to be normal conduct in the bedroom. This is something that is hard to overcome. We could ask any cocaine addict how hard it is to overcome that addiction and then imagine what it is like dealing with this addiction. When we have expectations and ideas being influenced by violent pornography, it is not difficult to imagine how this can contribute to abusive relationships or domestic violence.

All of this is why I support Bill S-209 to restrict access to pornography for young people. We can take action and require age verification. We can help to prevent and reduce early exposure among the future generations. We can take a simple step to fight some of the worst impacts of online pornography. It is impossible for government to replace the role of parents, and it should never try to do that, but it is also true that parents are looking for help to protect their kids online, and the government knows that. It says as much when it promotes Bill C-34 to restrict access to social media. I find it interesting that we are debating both of these bills at the same time. Hopefully, it helps my colleagues on the government side understand where this bill is coming from and support this one as well.

There are real concerns with young people using social media, which I share as a parent, but it is also likely that the negative effects of online pornography are even substantially worse, yet Bill C-34 would do nothing to address an issue of protecting the innocence of kids and youth from material that they should never see. Parenting has always been a tough job, but it has only gotten more complicated in a digital world. The least we can do for them is to pass Bill S-209.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak to Bill S-209 on an issue that affects us all: our children's safety online.

A week ago, I welcomed my 17-year-old nephew, Charles André, to the Hill. He wanted to deliver a message to the Minister of Health and the Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture. He came to talk about how he became addicted to porn at the age of 10 and suffered psychological and physical harm as a result. Fortunately, my nephew has a strong support network and managed to break free from this vicious cycle. However, he wanted to make sure that our government puts measures in place to protect children.

I want to commend him for his leadership and courage in speaking out publicly about his experience. The post about his meeting with the ministers went viral, and he had to deal with a lot of hateful and violent comments, which is another problem that comes with social media. However, he also received a lot of kind comments. Young people, mothers and fathers expressed their support for Charles André's call for action, which strikes me as a clear message that people want to see the government take the necessary measures to protect our young people.

Children across Canada use online services every day to learn, to express themselves and to connect with their friends, their family and their community. However, these services can also expose children to inappropriate and harmful content and interactions. These harms are very real. They can harm young people's mental health, their development and their understanding of what healthy, respectful relationships look like.

Too many children are exposed to measurable and preventable harms online, and our laws have not kept pace. Pornography is a big part of that challenge. Children are exposed to it, whether they are looking for it or not, including on services that many of them use every day, such as social media. All too often, it only takes a few clicks, without any verifications, for a child to access such content. Parliament is right to examine how we can reduce that exposure. Protecting children from such harm is a responsibility we all share, across party lines.

I would like to acknowledge the work of Senator Julie Miville‑Dechêne, who brought this issue to Parliament's attention through Bill S‑209, as well as the member for Battlefords—Lloydminster—Meadow Lake, who is sponsoring it in the House. This bill reflects a legitimate and widely shared concern that children should not have unrestricted access to online pornography. Let me be clear. Our government fully supports the principle underlying this bill, which is the protection of children. That is why I am pleased to confirm today that the government will support sending Bill S‑209 to committee for study.

This bill is closely aligned with the work we are undertaking through Bill C-34, the safe social media act, but that alignment is not an obstacle. On the contrary, it is exactly why we should move forward with Bill S-209. Bill C-34 is based on a simple premise: A child's online experience is shaped by the content they see, by the way these platforms are designed and by the interactions these platforms enable. These risks rarely exist in isolation. The content, the design and the interactions can combine to amplify the effects on children. That is why Bill C-34 proposes comprehensive measures to make online services safer from the design stage onwards. Furthermore, together with Bill C-36, it establishes a new framework to better protect Canadians online.

Rather than relying on voluntary commitments from platforms, our government is proposing to enshrine clear legal responsibilities for operators of regulated social media services and AI chatbot services.

Their duties would be brought together under a single framework based on transparency, accountability and independent regulatory oversight. Operators would have a duty to act responsibly by assessing and mitigating risks associated with harmful content. They would have a duty to protect children by incorporating age restrictions into the design of their services. They would have a duty to make content that sexually victimizes a child as well as intimate content communicated without consent, including deepfake sexual images, inaccessible within 24 hours. The bill would also prevent children under the age of 16 from opening accounts on regulated social media platforms unless those services can demonstrate that they are safe for them.

As for chatbots, they will be required to direct users to support services when users express thoughts of suicide or self-harm. One important point is that Bill C-34 directly addresses children's exposure to pornographic content. Under this bill, if the operator of a regulated service has reasonable grounds to suspect that its service is making pornographic content accessible, it would be required to implement age verification or age estimation measures. These measures should be sufficient to mitigate the risk that children will be exposed to pornographic content on the service in question. This requirement is also part of the broader duty to protect children set forth in the bill.

The bill also provides clear safeguards by establishing a framework for these measures. Among other requirements, the regulator would be required to ensure that the measures are effective. Personal information could be collected or used only for age verification or age estimation purposes. It would have to be protected while it is being retained and then destroyed once the verification or estimation is completed. These requirements are set forth directly in Bill C-34. They are intended to ensure that the measures designed to protect children also respect privacy. To ensure that these protections are effective, the bill also provides for ongoing independent oversight. It recognizes that protecting young people online requires binding rules and a regulator capable of enforcing them.

Bill C‑36 would create the digital safety and data protection commission of Canada, an independent, permanent regulatory body made up of members with proven expertise. For the first time, the major online platforms would be accountable to a Canadian regulator with real power. The commission would be able to conduct audits and inspections, issue compliance orders and impose administrative monetary penalties of up to $10 million or 3% of an operator's gross global revenue, whichever is higher. It would review the digital safety plans that operators would be required to publish to explain how they are identifying and mitigating risks on their services. It could also make regulations to issue guidelines. The commission would offer support to victims of online harm. It would also serve as a recourse for users who are dissatisfied with a platform's response to more serious content. It would operate independently. Platforms would no longer be able to get by on mere promises. They would have to demonstrate convincing results.

Bill S‑209 and Bill C-34 are both grounded in a well-established principle: Children deserve to be protected, including online. Both bills recognize the importance of protecting children from being exposed to online pornography. This common objective presents an opportunity for us to consider how these two approaches can complement one another and strengthen our efforts to protect children online. That is why our government supports sending Bill S-209 to committee for study. Our commitment to protecting children is clear. The committee is the appropriate forum to examine Bill S-209 alongside the new framework proposed in Bills C-34 and C-36 and to ensure that these initiatives work together toward the shared goal of creating a safer online environment for children and families across Canada.

By protecting our children, we are protecting Canada's future. The experiences young people have online today will help shape the citizens, workers, innovators and leaders they become tomorrow. We have a responsibility toward them and toward Canada's future.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to stand today in support of Bill S-209. I certainly want to thank the members of the other chamber, who have worked hard to get the bill this far. I also want to thank the member for Battlefords—Lloydminster—Meadow Lake for her leadership in keeping this bill going and bringing it to our chamber. It has been discussed for quite some time in Ottawa, and I am pleased to see that it is moving forward.

Very simply, Bill S-209 is about protecting Canadian children. I am certainly in no position to speak for all members of the chamber, or even all members of my party, although I am sure all members of this place would agree that children must be protected from harm and that parents should have the tools they need to protect their children online. Bill S-209 would protect children by requiring commercial pornographic websites to implement effective age verification or age estimation measures while including safeguards that protect Canadians' privacy. I believe this is truly a targeted, common-sense approach requiring websites that host pornographic material to take reasonable steps in verifying or estimating their users' ages.
Before I get further into some of the specifics of what the bill would do and how it aims to achieve its objectives, I want to speak about the “why”: the issue the bill aims to address.

We have heard some quite remarkable comments already from members on all sides about some of the challenges we are facing as a country regarding this issue. Research has associated minors' exposure to pornography with harmful attitudes and beliefs regarding sexual consent, including those of violence and degradation toward women, in particular, as well as coercion and exploitation. We also know that early exposure to pornography has been found to lead to increased rates of peer-to-peer sexual abuse among youth, meaning in part that a lot of the problematic narratives and actions depicted in some of this content are leading to many youth having troubles in their relationships, especially as they begin to grow older and begin dating.
There have been many studies about the impact that the exposure of youth to pornography has on their self-esteem. I would like to speak about that for a few moments.

Studies note that pornography consumption is associated with a negative body image and self-comparison in both sexes. Research links porn consumption to feelings of anxiety and depression in young girls, which is an alarming statistic to read. When looking at the impact on young boys, a report from Australia notes that viewing pornography can create or exacerbate feelings of loneliness, anxiety and body dissatisfaction in young boys in particular.

With all that knowledge being stated, there are also surveys that show that by the age of 16, over 70% of boys view pornography multiple times per week. If we put that into perspective, to step back and look at that alarming stat, we see that 70% of boys up to 16 not only have viewed some of this harmful content, but are regularly viewing content that can cause them to feel lonely, anxious and dissatisfied within their own bodies. This is unquestionably a great concern for the mental health of young girls and boys alike, and something that we should all be concerned about in this place.

The concerns that I highlighted and just shared are among the reasons that pornographic material is subject to age restrictions in Canada. However, despite the extensive research proving how harmful the material can be to young people, there is no effective enforcement of these age restrictions. This leads to the reality that many underage children are accessing pornography.

In fact, the average age of first exposure to pornographic material is 12 years old, with one-third of children exposed to pornographic material by the age of just 10. Further, for youth aged 14 to 18, there are studies showing that more than 70% report having viewed pornography. The fact that so many young Canadians are viewing content that, as I just highlighted, negatively impacts their mental health, their relationships, the way they view the world and the way they view their relationships should be of great concern to all of us.

Again, I do not speak for all members, but I am sure all members would agree with respect to having these age restrictions in place. That is the right thing to do. It only stands to reason that these restrictions should be enforced effectively. Of course, having a law in place but failing to enforce the law makes the law essentially useless. That would apply to any law we have in place in Canada. Bill S-209 seeks to fix that inconsistency. The bill, if passed, would require websites hosting pornographic material to implement effective age verification or age estimation systems. As I mentioned, the bill would also establish financial penalties for non-compliance, of up to $250,000 for a first offence and up to $500,000 for subsequent offences.

Further, Bill S-209 would give court authority to order Canadian Internet service providers to block access to non-compliant websites. The rules set out within Bill S-209 would apply equally to all sites accessible in Canada, including those based outside the country. I do understand that throughout discussion and debate on this, there have been some people who raised concerns about privacy and data collection, and I do not disregard those concerns.

I would note, however, that Bill S-209 also does not disregard those concerns. Set out in the bill are very specific criteria for age verification. Among others, the bill would require that the age verification method be operated by a third party organization, maintain user privacy, protect personal information and destroy any personal information collected once the age verification is completed. To me, this is a common-sense proposal being brought forward.

I think about the consistency of the laws we have in place. When Canadians purchase alcohol, tobacco, cannabis or lottery tickets, they must present valid ID at the discretion of the vendor. If we are to allow, as a Parliament and as a country, an entire industry that offers age-restricted materials to bypass that accountability simply because it exists online rather than in a brick-and-mortar storefront, to me that is nonsensical.

Further to that, it is presently an offence for a retailer and also for an individual employee to sell age-restricted products, such as alcohol and tobacco, to minors. This means that in Canada right now, we are essentially holding minimum-wage workers such as those selling tobacco products at a gas station, for example, to a higher standard of accountability than we are holding multi-million-dollar companies providing pornography online. It only stands to reason that all age-restricted products should have more consistent enforcement.

Companies that profit from providing pornographic content should be responsible for keeping it out of the reach of children, and the websites that fail to protect children should face serious consequences. That is why I support Bill S-209 and the goals set out within it. I believe this would be an important step in keeping kids safe and in ensuring that our laws are consistently enforced. I hope the House chooses to vote in favour of Bill S-209 and move it forward to the next stage of discussion.
As always, Conservatives will stand with parents and families and will continue to fight for an online environment where all children are safe.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to Bill S-209, the protecting young persons from exposure to pornography act. I want to begin not only as a member of Parliament in the chamber but also from the perspective of a former educator and as a mom.

Before I entered politics, I spent almost two decades working with young people. I saw their potential, their curiosity and their struggles. Every day, I was reminded that the adults in a child's life have a responsibility to create conditions where they can learn, grow and thrive safely. Today that responsibility extends far beyond the classroom. It extends into a digital world that is available to our children 24 hours a day, seven days a week. That reality should concern us all.

In rising here today as a mom, like parents across the country, I have watched technology transform childhood. Many of us remember growing up in a world where childhood had limits, where certain materials were difficult to access and where adults acted as gatekeepers. Today a child can stumble across explicit and violent sexual content in a matter of seconds, and not because they were looking for it, not because parents have failed and not because teachers have failed but because the online world has been built in a way that makes that exposure possible, and where, instead, they are learning from an industry designed to generate profits. That should alarm every one of us.

As an educator, one of the most important lessons I tried to teach my students was the difference between reality and performance, yet when children encounter pornography at a young age, often before they are emotionally prepared to understand what they are seeing, that distinction becomes very blurred, as their expectations are shaped, their perceptions are shaped and their ideas about relationships are shaped. In some cases, those consequences can be quite profound. Our laws have not kept pace. Our Parliament is right to examine ways to reduce that exposure, because protecting kids from these harms is a responsibility we all share, regardless of party.

I want to take a moment to also thank Senator Miville-Dechêne for her work and service by keeping this issue before us here in Parliament, as well as my colleague from Saskatchewan, with whom I sat on HUMA, for her undying support in protecting children. I am happy to also be a seconder to the bill.

Our government is committed to keeping Canadians, especially children, safe, including online. We agree on the objective of preventing children from accessing online pornography. Bill S-209 shares this objective very closely and aligns with Bill C-34, the safe social media act. Let me be clear. Our government fully supports the principle behind the bill. Its alignment with Bill C-34 is not an obstacle. It is precisely why we support sending Bill S-209 to committee for study, as the bill asks the right questions and demands action to prevent children from accessing online pornography.

At its core, the bill would require commercial providers of online pornography to take concrete steps to restrict access by people under 18 years of age The status quo is not acceptable. Online services must take greater responsibility to protect children from being exposed to harmful content on their platforms. The remaining question is not whether action is needed but how to build a framework that works in practice, protects privacy, can be enforced effectively and remains responsive as technology changes.

Bill S-209 closely aligns with the work of our government that we are advancing through our safe social media act, Bill C-34, which would place an affirmative obligation on operators of regulated services. This would ensure that safeguards are put in place to mitigate the risk before children are exposed to harmful content, rather than after the situation has occurred. If an operator has reasonable grounds to suspect that its service makes pornographic content accessible, it would have to implement age verification or age estimation measures to mitigate the risk of children's being exposed to this content. Adequate protection is the first consideration.

The digital safety and data protection commission of Canada, an independent, permanent regulator that would be created through the safe social media act together with Bill C-36, would have to be satisfied that the measures implemented by an operator will meet that requirement. This is so essential, as the objective is not merely to demonstrate that an age assurance measure has been implemented. Its objective is to mitigate the risk that children will be exposed to pornographic content.

This approach recognizes that regulated services do not all operate in the same way, as their designs, users and methods of providing access to content might differ. Bill C-34 would establish the required outcome and assign responsibility for assessing the adequacy of the measure to the regulator with the necessary technical expertise to do so.

Second, Bill C-34 would also set clear limits on the collection and use of personal information for age assurance so that personal information could only be used to verify or estimate a person's age, and it would have to be protected and destroyed as soon as the process is complete. These safeguards are built directly into the safe social media act because protecting children should not create new privacy risks.

The digital safety and data protection commission of Canada would provide the continuing institutional capacity needed to apply this framework. As the body responsible for administering and enforcing that legislation, the commission would also assess the measures used by regulated operators and determine whether they satisfy the applicable requirements. This commission could establish guidelines concerning the protection of children in relation to regulated services. It could also make regulations specify design features that operators must integrate into regulated services as part of their duty to protect children.

While this authority also extends beyond age assurances, it demonstrates the central role that the commission would play in giving practical effect to the duty to protect our kids, much like our senator's bill. That continuing role is particularly important because age assurance technologies and industry practices will evolve. Different services might require different measures, and new evidence might identify more effective, privacy-protective approaches. The framework would therefore permit this flexibility and innovation without leaving adequacy entirely to the discretion of its regulators.

As we know, the Internet has created some extraordinary opportunities, but it has also created unprecedented access to harmful content. The question before us is whether we are willing to acknowledge that reality and then take action. As a former educator, I want young people to learn about relationships through respect, empathy and healthy human connection. As a mother, I want children protected during the years when they are most vulnerable. As a woman, I want girls growing up in a society that values their dignity, equality and humanity.

Those goals should be uniting all of us. This debate is not about politics. It is about children, families, the kind of culture that we are going to build for this next generation, and whether we are willing to say that the safety and well-being of our children matter more than a convenience of an online industry. I believe they do.
For those reasons, I am pleased to support Bill S-209 and these objectives of protecting young persons from exposure to pornography online.
I will give the floor to the hon. member for Battlefords—Lloydminster—Meadow Lake for her five-minute right of reply.
Mr. Speaker, protecting children from harm should always be a priority. As legislators, we have the responsibility to protect the vulnerable and put reasonable safeguards in place.

I want to thank members from across party lines who have spoken in support of Bill S-209, which seeks to protect children from online pornography. Many members who have taken part in this debate are parents themselves. They understand the challenges of raising children in a digital age, when so much content is available at the click of a button.

Children are being exposed to pornography at very young ages. Sometimes they come across it accidentally. Other times, curiosity leads them to content they are not mature enough to understand. The concern is not just how young children are when they encounter this content, but what they may see. Age checks are often absent or ineffective on websites that host pornography. Children can encounter videos that portray aggression, degradation and sexual violence. Some depict acts that can cause serious physical harm, including choking, while presenting them as healthy or even desirable. Children's brains are still developing. They are learning to understand relationships, consent and appropriate behaviour. Repeated exposure to this content can shape how they understand sex, consent and expectations in relationships.

Parents have a very important role to play. They set boundaries. They have difficult conversations and use parental controls, but in reality, they cannot monitor every search, every link or every video. They should not have to carry this responsibility alone.

During this debate, the member for Vancouver Granville raised Bill C-34 as another way to address children's exposure to online pornography, but that is not correct. Bill C-34 does not have the same explicit reach as Bill S-209. Bill C-34 would require age verification to user-generated pornography on sites like OnlyFans. Just so members know, OnlyFans is a site where users generate pornography and upload it. However, Bill C-34 does not stipulate age verification for pornography websites. The government has provided Bill C-34 to the House, a bill that is supposed to protect children, but it does not cover pornography websites. The Liberal government has not clearly stated that it intends to use the powers in Bill C-34 to ensure that all commercial pornography websites restrict children's access.

If we agree that protecting children from online pornography is important, we cannot just leave it to Bill C-34. We need a direct approach, and that is what Bill S-209 is. It is a targeted approach that would require all commercial pornography websites to use prescribed age verification or age estimation methods to restrict children's access to it.

To be clear, Bill S-209 would not ban pornography for adults. It would establish an additional safeguard to help keep this adult content away from children. It also would not come at the expense of Canadians' privacy. This bill includes safeguards governing the collection, use and destruction of personal information used for age checks. We can protect children from content they are not ready to see while also protecting Canadians' personal information.

This issue has been before Parliament since 2016, when the House unanimously supported Motion No. 47, which called for a study on the public health effects of easy access to online sexually explicit material. This is the third version of this legislation being considered, yet children still lack these safeguards. Other jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom, France, Germany and more than 25 American states, have taken steps to restrict minors' access to online pornography.
We cannot keep debating this issue without taking action. Our children deserve safeguards, and I urge all members in the House to support Bill S-209.
The question is on the motion.

If a member participating in person wishes that the motion be carried or carried on division, or if a member of a recognized party participating in person wishes to request a recorded division, I would invite them to rise and indicate it to the Chair.
Mr. Speaker, I ask that it be carried on division.

I declare the motion carried on division. Accordingly, the bill stands referred to the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities.
Content.ProceduralText: (Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to a committee)

Content.ParaText: The hon. parliamentary secretary to the government House leader is rising on a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that if you were to check, you would find unanimous consent to call it 6:30 p.m. so we can get on with government business.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill C-34, An Act to enact the Digital Safety Act and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise to speak to Bill C-34 today. I will be sharing my time with the member for Winnipeg South Centre.

This bill is long overdue. This is not the first time this House has tried to legislate to protect children in particular from online harms, but hopefully this time we will get it done. Based on the speeches I have heard from colleagues across parties in the House, it seems like there is finally consensus to protect our children online.

When I was preparing for this speech last night, I stumbled across an article in the New York Times. It gave me pause and crystallized for me why it is so crucial that we put this legislation forward and get it right. The article was about a young woman living in the United States who had epilepsy and decided to talk about her medication with ChatGPT. What ended up happening is that ChatGPT counselled her on how to reduce her epilepsy medication and hide it from her doctor, which ultimately led to her death.

Bill C-34 deals with chatbots. It deals with AI. We need to ensure that there are protections in place. There are vulnerable people and children using these tools in a way that is harmful to them. This woman's story is an absolute tragedy and is something that I think all of us want to ensure does not happen again. What it crystallizes for me is that, left to their own devices, these companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

We have only to look at the whistle-blowers from Meta, Frances Haugen and Arturo Béjar, who both testified in front of Congress in the United States and said that Facebook and Meta have knowingly not put forward safety mechanisms because they want increased profits. We have heard that when it comes to protecting children, there are studies at Meta showing that young women are particularly vulnerable when it comes to bullying, body image issues and eating disorders, yet consistently they choose profits over safety.

We have all heard stories from constituents and people across this country whose children have experienced online harms. Unfortunately, there are cases like that of Amanda Todd, who was so severely cyber-bullied that she ended up taking her own life. We have a responsibility to act in this House.

I had the opportunity to meet with her mom, Carol, who has met with many of us in this place over the years and has been asking all of us, as members of Parliament, to act responsibly. Bill C-34 would do just that.
