It is there to protect our children from online harms and would come forward with a digital safety commission that would make sure the big tech companies are putting in safety by design as their principle. It would have real teeth and a real ability to fine companies that do not uphold their obligations to protect our children.

If these things were happening in a playground, it would be unacceptable and the police would be called. There is no reason for these harms to be allowed online. The companies and people who perpetuate them need to be held to account.

What I like about the digital safety commission is that it is based on principles, values, laws and protecting our children, but it is flexible for the future. When I hear colleagues say that we need to write these laws right now, I challenge them on it: Do we know what those harms are going to be five, 10 or 15 years from now?

I am going to date myself a bit, because my first year of university was the first year that Facebook came out. In 2006, nobody knew that Facebook would become Meta. Nobody knew that Meta would effectively become the Internet in some parts of the world and have the kind of reach and control it does now.

We do not know what the next thing is going to be. We do not know exactly how ChatGPT, Claude or any of these AI companies are going to transform our experiences and what existing or new harms they could potentially cause. I am not saying there is nothing good about any of these things. There certainly are. There are ways people connect that are great, but we have an obligation as members of Parliament, as legislators, as citizens, some of us as parents, to make sure we are doing everything we can to protect our children, the children of this country and people in this country from those potential harms.

What would be good about the digital safety commission is that, for the first time, we would not just be legislating in the rear-view mirror; it would actually be forward-thinking and would give Canadians the tools to ensure that we can protect against some of these harms.

Bill C-34 would also impose an age limit when it comes to social media. In her testimony to Congress, Frances Haugen suggested that, in fact, platforms like Instagram should raise their minimum age from 13 to 16, or even to 18. I think this is a really good step. We know there are age limits for a number of things in this country, whether it is drinking, voting, driving, or being able to buy cigarettes or cannabis. There are always people who are going to get around those age limits, but that does not mean it is not the right thing to do. It gives parents the tools to also help protect their children.

A journal for the Canadian Medical Association talks about the fact that when children have constant access to online content, their levels of depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation increase. Just reducing that from three hours a day to one hour a day has incredible benefits for their mental health. It is why the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Mental Health Association, organizations like Unplugged and Raise the Age, Children First Canada and a wide range of pediatricians, etc. support Bill C-34, as it is about providing opportunities for healthy and safe lives for our kids.

AI is changing the way in which we interact, just as social media has done over the past 20 years. We need to ensure that, as Canadians, we can take control of what is happening in the online world and have the tools to enforce protections for our children. This is important work that would build off legislation like Bill C-16, which already made it illegal to share content like deepfakes, revenge porn, etc. We need to make sure we are protecting everyone from an image that can go around the world in seconds.

As a mom of two young kids who are not quite at the age where they would be engaged in social media, I cannot say how much I want this to pass right now. I talk to young people who tell me about their anxiety, their depression, the challenges and the bullying. They cannot turn social media off. When I was younger, maybe some of these things existed in magazines and we had these kinds of images, but I could put that down. I could put that away, and I could walk outside. When we are connected all the time, there is no escape.

Bill C-34 would not solve all the problems. There are always going to be challenges, but this is such an important piece of legislation at this moment in time to do what we can to protect our children, protect future generations and make social media and the Internet a safer place for everyone.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Karim Bardeesy (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, my colleague pointed to the flexibility around the digital safety commission. I wonder if she could expound on why it would be important for the digital safety commission to have the powers and the flexibility it needs to adapt to new and emerging technologies.

Mr. Speaker, it is exactly as I said in my speech. We do not really know what is coming next. We did not predict 20 years ago so many of the harms we are seeing happen right now, and we do not have the laws in place to deal with them. If we are constantly trying to keep up with technology, we are always going to fall behind. Technology is always going to be ahead of what we are legislating, so having a digital safety commission would enable us to have the flexibility and the agility to respond, hopefully in real time, but if not, hopefully quickly enough to actually deal with these harms as they emerge.

Mr. Speaker, I think that there is broad consensus around this bill and that it has unanimous support in the House. Nevertheless, some people have raised concerns about privacy, particularly when people are required to show ID to prove their age. I think those concerns are legitimate. We have to figure out how to strike the right balance between inconvenience and risk reduction.
I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on this specific risk. What are the best ways to reduce it?

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question. I think we have the advantage of being able to learn from Australia's experience. We have introduced this bill, but we will also have the opportunity to observe what is happening elsewhere and make improvements.

Personally, I have some concerns about age verification technology. Showing a piece of ID is something we have to do in many everyday situations, but we do not do it online. I think we need to talk about it, but we also need to listen to the experts to ensure that privacy and personal information are protected.
Mr. Speaker, the bill appears to put off 50 decisions until later. Of those 50 decisions, 19 will be delegated to a minister, and 31 will be referred to a commission that does not exist yet.

Given that this bill is so important and so eagerly awaited by Canadians, should we not ensure that these questions already have answers, rather than postponing them and relying on “maybes”, especially when it comes to something as important as protecting our young people online?

Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned in my speech, there will always be factors that we cannot foresee, and I believe it is important to allow the commission to exercise its judgment. As I noted, 20 years ago, no one could have predicted what Meta would become. Likewise, we cannot know what platforms and technologies will look like in five, 10 or 20 years.

For that reason, I believe it is important to provide the commission with a degree of flexibility. That said, the principles and objectives that will guide its work have now been clearly established, and that is what matters most.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of those I represent in Winnipeg South Centre. I do want to begin by thanking my colleague from Burlington for an exceptional speech. She did a great job of providing a framework and a foundational conceptualization of what we are facing here and why this piece of legislation is so necessary.

I have talked often, when I have had the honour of rising in the House, about my time as a teacher. I started as a grade 6 French immersion educator at École Robert H. Smith. I can still remember at 3:30 on the first day of school putting my head down on the table and wondering how I was going to get through it. It turns out I did, and I had the privilege of going on from there to be a high school teacher and a high school principal. It was through about a decade in the public education system that I got to know what mattered to kids, what they were interested in, what they were curious about, what challenges they faced and their opportunities. Of course, by extension, I had the privilege of being able to work with so many of their families as well.

I stand here today as well, as a very proud uncle, not only to my own niece through blood, but to so many of my friends' children, many of whom are growing up now, in an age that looks very different than it did when my colleague from Burlington and I were young. That reality is one that is constantly shifting.

The nature of the threats faced in our society, particularly by young people, are more dynamic, they are more sophisticated, and they are more targeted and complicated than they were in the past. By virtue of changes in technology, and the emergence of social media and the strong role that it is playing in our society, we have had to re-evaluate the safeguards that we must put in place as a society to ensure that, while we have access to these incredible technologies that have the potential in so many ways to do good, we are aware of the harms that they can create and are creating.

I am mindful of an indigenous scholar named Dr. Martin Brokenleg, whom I studied a bit when I was the principal of a school called Maples Met in Winnipeg. The circle of courage is based on these four ideas of what is important in the lives of young people. They are focusing on mastery, generosity, independence and belonging. In relation to what we are talking about here, it is independence and belonging that are so critical in the frame of Bill C-34.

Young people want to belong, and at the same time, they want to be independent. Anyone who is around young people, particularly teenagers, will know that there comes a time when they no longer want mom or dad to drop them off at school in sight of kids, or a time when they want to be able to go to the mall alone with their friends, and they want to have that independence. However, there is a variety of different things out there in the online world in particular, that we ought to be mindful of when we are engaging with young people about that independence that they are seeking.

I can remember a superintendent of mine once telling the story of a fight that broke out in the school, and although in the early moments of the fight the kids were all cheering and doing what young teenagers often do when there is a physical altercation, which was ego and bravado taking place, when the principal finally did show up, the students asked what took them so long. In other words, it happens often with young people that, at the same time as they are holding our hand tightly to tell us to stay, they are pulling away from us.

This reminds me of the tension that exists in terms of the responsibilities that we have as adults and as lawmakers in our country to provide the guidance, support and love that is necessary for young people to grow and develop into independent young people, while at the same time ensuring that we are responsible for keeping them safe. This brings me to what we have heard in relation to some of the challenges that are ongoing right now vis-à-vis social media and online platforms.

I have received calls from countless parents, men and women, regardless of the demographic that they may represent socio-economically, who have called to say that they are scared for what their children are exposed to online, and that they expect the government is going to do something about it.

I have received calls from students, many of whom I have met with in the hallways, libraries and theatres of their schools, who have talked about their resistance to social media and to a variety of other online platforms that they feel are actually taking away from the authenticity of their lived experiences.

I have heard from experts. Just this past weekend in my office, I was really proud to welcome an expert panel of unbelievable community members to talk about the different challenges we face. I want to take the opportunity to give credit to Dr. Michelle Warren, a clinical psychologist who was there and who spoke about the work she does with young people in particular who are facing anxiety and depression by virtue of some of the harmful things they are exposed to online.

There was also Monique St. Germain, who represents the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, which is located in my riding and is something I am very proud of. It is a world leader in eradicating the distribution of illegal and damaging sexual images of children online. It is fully behind the government in terms of its support for the measures embedded in Bill C-34. I was also joined by Cordella Friesen, who serves as the head of the YMCA in Winnipeg. They work with young people on a daily basis and were there to share stories they have heard from folks who use their services. Sharon Labossiere, Colleen Nelson and Laura Thomas are each great educators in their own right who took time to tell us about what they are seeing in schools and who reinforced the need for us to act.

The question then becomes what we should do about this. We have heard the calls from parents, from young people and from experts that it is time for us to act. Bill C-34 would do this in a number of ways. One that has often been talked about in the context of this debate and outside the walls of the chamber has to do with placing limitations on social media.

I know that there have been some criticisms of other jurisdictions, most noteworthy being Australia, that have taken some steps in order to limit the harms that are being caused by too much time online, and that there have been some instances where young people are finding ways around them. I think my colleague, the member for Burlington, did an excellent job of explaining that notwithstanding those challenges, which of course will evolve over time, they cannot alone be the justification for why we do not start to move forward today. I think ensuring that there is less time spent on these platforms for people at vulnerable ages is going to be very important.

I will note that I come from a province that has put a policy in place to ban cellphone use in schools. I have heard overwhelmingly from teachers, principals, parents and young people that this has had a positive impact on their experience in school. I think there is something for us to take from that feedback and from those experiences in relation to Bill C-34.

Bill C-34 is also about accountability that would lead to real penalties and that will hold accountable in the way they ought to be held accountable those who are responsible for designing and maintaining unsafe platforms online, which is to say that we would create a regulator. Of course, through a regulatory framework and ongoing dialogue in the chamber and beyond, after the passage, I hope, of this legislation, we would figure out exactly how that would come to be.

The important piece is that there would be accountability. Social media platforms and other online platforms that care more about the bottom line than they do about the health, well-being and safety of our children would be held accountable. They would be held accountable not just through the proverbial slap on the wrist but through real financial and other lawful penalties that would send the very strong message that is necessary for them to understand we are serious.

I am very proud to be part of a government that is putting forward a bill that would address these serious concerns at a moment in time where it is incumbent upon us, as the Parliament of this wonderful country, to take action that will keep our young people safe.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his contribution to the debate. My question is as follows: Before drafting Bill C‑34, did the government carry out consultations, particularly with Quebec, which has already made significant progress on the issue of regulating access to social media for minors?

Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely important bill. There have been conversations across Canada, of course, with parents, with groups representing children and mental health, as well as other stakeholders that have something to say in this context. I cannot speak to which discussions took place between governments, but I certainly know that conversations are ongoing between governments. The people on our side, in the Government of Canada, are developing the bill here and will continue their efforts with the regulations to follow.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member for Winnipeg South Centre brings a very interesting point of view, given his background as an educator and working with young people for as long as he has.

It is important that this is not about replacing parents, or anything of this nature. It is something to support the current structure of parents and teachers. However, I believe the need for it, given how the Internet is, and the harmful content out there, is easily justified.
Can the member provide his thoughts on that from a teacher's perspective, possibly?

Mr. Speaker, as I made reference to during my remarks, it is critically important we understand that young people need to go through experiences in life. It is very important, as they develop the skills for independence, that we allow opportunities for them to fall and to learn lessons, sometimes difficult ones, and then to get back up, but of course that has to be done with our love and support.

One of the things I noticed in the years I spent in the public education system is that as much as young people feel as though they are capable of moving through the world on their own, they recognize the importance of having that love, support and guidance from the adults in their life, inclusive of their parents of course, but also their teachers, friends and others. This bill is a really important step in the right direction of ensuring that we find the balance between allowing young people to participate in the world around them and making sure we do so in a safe way.

Mr. Speaker, one of the things that give the legislation teeth is the proposed digital safety commission that would have the power to give fines and make sure the regulations are in fact being enforced in many different ways.
I am wondering if my colleague could provide his thoughts on the importance of having a commission, because it would actually provide action.

Mr. Speaker, one thing the Province of Manitoba has done that I am fully supportive of is that it has created a body that can oversee disciplinary measures for educators. The person who heads that up goes by the name of Noni Classen. Where did she come from? She came from the Canadian Centre for Child Protection. The whole reason the disciplinary board exists is for there to be accountability and for there to be real consequences when inappropriate or unacceptable actions are taken.

I see this as no different. It is about protecting young people. However, if it is going to work, it has to be created in a way that ensures that there are consequences. I have full confidence, based on the way the legislation is currently written, and I am sure as the legislation will be strengthened throughout the legislative process, that we will land at a place that will ensure that if a social media company or other online platform is not abiding by the law, as it is written in Bill C-34, they would have a price to pay for that.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to share my time with the member for Cambridge.

Every parent in Montmorency—Charlevoix and, I suspect, across all of Quebec and Canada has gone through the same experience. It is 10 p.m. and our teenager's bedroom door is closed. We see a faint blue light under the door. Sometimes we hear them laughing to themselves, or we hear strange noises from a video. When that happens, every parent starts wondering the same thing. What are they watching? Who are they talking to? We wonder how long they have been online. We also want to know who is on the other side of the screen. I think that is a completely reasonable question to ask.

Today, we have to be clear. Phones are not the enemy, but they come with problems and challenges that we have rarely encountered in our lifetimes. In fact, our generation may have no experience with that kind of thing at all, and the generation before us has even less. Few of us here have lived in the kind of world our children are growing up in. This is what Bill C‑34 addresses.

We have to be clear from the outset. From the start, we have to be clear about the fact that protecting our children online is non-negotiable. It is not a partisan issue. We all agree on that, and so we should. However, we are not going to give the government carte blanche when it asks for powers in the name of protecting our children. More power for a good reason is how these things always start.

Our role as opposition members is to challenge the government, ask questions, seek out the little details hidden in the legislation and make them public knowledge. Two things can be true at once: We have to protect our young people, but we must not close our eyes and hand over unrestricted power. I think we understand that, and parents, of all people, understand that the best.

Why is this discussion important right now? It is because things are changing at a pace we have rarely seen before, and the numbers are really heading in the wrong direction. In 2024, the police reported 17,000 cases of online child sexual exploitation. That is four times as many as in 2014. In the span of a decade, there was an exponential increase. Behind each of these cases, there is a child, but there is also a parent who never saw it coming.

Let us read this bill the way a parent would read it, and I am going to talk about it the way a parent would, focusing on two questions. Will this really protect my children? For me, that is the first question I ask myself. We can certainly pass laws, but will they really protect children? The second question is this: Who will get to decide?

The most prominent provision in Bill C-34 is the proposal to prohibit young people under the age of 16 from having social media accounts. This is what has been highlighted in the media, namely that this is a major initiative to protect young people and that social media is being banned for those under 16. Many parents see this minimum age as the right age to regulate access. In fact, an Angus Reid poll found that three in four Canadians support the measure. That is 75% of the population.

However, the poll reveals another very important fact, and that is that 72% of Canadians believe that parents, not the government, are primarily responsible for what teenagers look at on social media and how they use those platforms. Canadians want both. They want something that protects their children, but they also want to have the final say at home. They want clear guidelines, but they want to remain in control.

Now let us look at what happened in Australia. My colleagues talked about this earlier today in the House. Australia banned social media for children under the age of 16. This happened last December, so it is a very recent thing. Three months later, Australia's own online safety regulator found that eight in 10 children were still using at least one platform that had been banned or age-restricted, and more than half of those who had kept their accounts said that no one had checked their age.

That does not mean that we should do away with this, but clearly we can look at what other places are doing, draw inspiration from their approach and try to improve on it. If we have a ban that does not work, that does not protect anyone. It just creates a false sense of security. That is what we need to stop doing. We need to stop making laws that only create more bureaucracy.

Then there are video games. If we ask a 10-year-old where they meet up with their friends after school, the answer is often online, playing a video game with a live chat feature. That is where the young people talk to one another. However, video game platforms are not covered by this bill. If we lock the door but leave the window open, are we really protecting young people?
My second question is one that requires us to really look at the details: Who gets to decide?

If we are going to prevent young people under 16 from accessing social media, we will need a way to verify everyone's age. That means asking everyone for proof of age: me, my grandmother, my grandfather, my parents. We will have to ask all of them how old they are. How exactly will that work? Will people be expected to upload their driver's licence and send it to companies they have never heard of? Will they have to submit to facial analysis software? This raises questions once again.
The bill does not provide the answers. Instead, it says regulations will be made later. We have not yet seen the regulations. What I just talked about is not an isolated example.
Under the bill, 50 major decisions will be put off until later, with 19 reserved for the minister responsible and 31 referred to a commission that does not exist yet.
Which platforms are covered by the ban? Cabinet will decide that. Moreover, the bill does not currently identify any criteria for that.
Which platforms could be exempt? The commission will decide that upon request.

The 24-hour deadline for taking down content can be changed by cabinet. That way, a minister can personally choose the time frame. We are told that the ban is temporary, but that is not indicated anywhere in the bill.

This commission would draft rules, conduct investigations, hold hearings and impose fines. That is absolute power, and it is not bound by any rule of evidence. Once again, it is total control. This is the kind of detail that is important to raise in bills that have a nice catchy title.
Until the other members are appointed, the chair of the commission will make all decisions on their own. Again, there is a problem here.

That is not all. Five days after introducing Bill C‑34, the government introduced Bill C‑36, which makes that same commission a super-regulator of personal data, taking that power away from the Privacy Commissioner. Oops. The privacy protection being sold to us in Bill C‑34 is already changing hands in Bill C‑36. This is the kind of detail that deserves to be pointed out in the House, but it does not come up in the speeches touting the bill's virtues. These details are never mentioned in the big announcements, but they really change things.

My questions are not meant to be partisan. I am not saying that this is the Conservative perspective. Other people have raised these same questions. Exactly what powers will the new commission have? That is important to know.

When a government asks for more powers in the name of protecting our children, we have every right to read each line of its proposal twice and to ensure the intent really is to protect our children. In this case, I believe the Liberal government has a questionable track record.
Now, to be honest, some things in this bill are good. Because I can see the good, I feel entitled to say that I see other things that are not good at all.
The bill addresses deepfakes, fake intimate images generated by artificial intelligence. This is something we really do need to take action on.
It forces the platforms to identify AI content. Again, that is very good.
It does not touch private messaging. That is good.
It requires chatbots to intervene when a person is in crisis. That is a must.
In her speech, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister said that infinite scroll is a design choice. She was right.
The platforms have the ability to make better choices. I think it is up to us to steer them in that direction. Bill C-34 has that to its credit.

Ultimately, this is not about platforms or commissions. It is about families. People do not need a commissioner to make decisions for them. Our families, our parents, need tools. They need information. Above all, they need to have the final say. Parents must continue to be responsible for their children. The final decision cannot always be made in an office in Ottawa like the Liberals do. On the contrary, the final decision must be made at kitchen tables in the homes of families in Quebec and Canada.

What should we be looking at and working on in committee? I think that is what all parents want to see us do. First, we want to put parents first. We need to work on simple tools and safer default settings. We need to give parents the final say. That is what we should be working on. Second, Parliament is the one that sets the rules. How age is verified and how long the ban lasts are things that should be included in the act, not in regulations that will be voted on later. Third, we need a commission with checks and balances. We want clear limits, transparency and a right of appeal. Fourth, we need to protect our children where they actually are: video games, chatbots and app stores.

Our position can be summed up in a few words. We say “yes” to protecting children. That is obvious. We say “no” to placing blind trust in the government. We say “yes” to platforms that are accountable. We say “no” to a commission that is accountable to no one. We say “yes” to security. We say “no” to mass surveillance. We say “yes” to a government that supports parents. We say “no” to a government that wants to take their place.

It is important that this bill be referred to committee. We need to hear from parents, doctors, police officers and experts. We need to hear from our young people. We need to be able to invite them before the committee and ask them about their experiences, because that is important.
We must get this bill right. Our children deserve a bill that will work for them, and our parents deserve to be trusted.
Mr. Speaker, this is an important topic we are discussing today.
I am a parent myself. I understand that we may sometimes disagree.

In his recommendations, my colleague said that we should look after the parents first. I would say that we need to look after the children first. I have four children. My first was born when I was 20 years old, but the rules were not the same 31 years ago. I look at my son, who is 31 years old today and has three children of his own. When I see social media, I wonder what I would have done 31 years ago. Often, I see that parents need help. My colleague mentioned two polls. One was about parents and the other was about the government. I would argue that they were about both.
Does my colleague not agree that parents need the government's support in setting appropriate rules in order to help them do the best they can?
Mr. Speaker, that is such a good question that I already answered it in my speech.

When I say that children must be the priority in this bill, I mean it. We are doing all this for them. I also pointed out that, according to the Angus Reid poll, 75% of people agree that legislation should be passed to protect our children online, but 72% of people, so roughly the same number, said they want to retain control.

We agree with that. We need to give parents the tools to better understand the reality young people are facing. We cannot ask young people what they want, because they are the ones we are trying to protect. We need to ensure that our young people, who are at the heart of our decisions, are protected and that parents have the tools they need to exercise vigilant, effective and judicious supervision in line with the current situation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying how much I appreciated the remarks made by my colleague from Montmorency—Charlevoix earlier in his speech. He touched on an important social challenge that concerns all of us. I have always said that we enter politics because of our parents and that we serve because of our children. The member captured the issue particularly well when he described teenagers coming home at 10 o'clock at night and heading straight to their rooms. Parents can see the light under the door, but they do not really know what is happening on the other side. I am no longer at the stage of life where I am raising children, but I am the grandfather of two little girls, aged four and six. I can honestly say that, throughout this debate, I have been thinking about them.
What advice would my colleague offer the government on how to better equip parents to deal with the challenges posed by social media in the 21st century?

Mr. Speaker, it is the new reality. Four-, six-, seven- or eight-year-old children are sometimes more adept with electronics than adults. Sometimes parents and grandparents do not know how to help young people. It is not about controlling them. It is about helping them. The child does not know that he or she is going down a road that is going to hurt them in the long run, that will put their mental health at risk. It is up to us to take responsibility for them.

How do we do that? We do it by equipping parents, by having informed parents, by keeping parents in the equation, not taking parents out of the equation by saying that the government will make the decisions. We see that here all the time. The Liberals rise in the House and say how proud they are to intervene in everything and that more and more people need Liberal subsidies to get by.
We want people to be free to make their own choices. It is important for parents to have access to information so they can make the right decisions for their children.

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. I think that we are all here for the right reasons. We are all facing the same challenges. I also agree on the issue of how we can help parents. My colleague mentioned tools earlier. I would like him to elaborate on that.
We have been talking non-stop this evening. Does my colleague have any specific ideas that could be effective and that could really help parents right away?
Mr. Speaker, once again, I do not think that it is up to me, as some great thinker, to start telling people what they should do.

I think that is what committees are for. We can bring in experts and make sure we listen to them. At the end of the day, it is not ideology that is important. It is results and what ordinary people are facing.

What should we do? We can set up a committee, invite experts, listen to what they have to say, present ideas to them and ask what they think about the tools. We can talk to digital platforms, talk to our young people about how they actually use the Internet and work together to develop a law that helps them.

Mr. Speaker, no security system is judged by its strongest lock, but instead by how easily someone gets through its weakest point. The same idea applies to Bill C-34. We need to discuss whether its proposed measures for a safer Internet would actually work when children and platforms test them.

I share the goal of the bill before us. The most important thing is to protect our children. Parents cannot take on some of the largest technology companies in the world by themselves. Parliament has a responsibility to ensure those companies are held accountable for the risks their products create for children and families. However, good intentions alone are not enough. The question before us is whether the mechanisms in the bill would deliver the protections families are expecting.

I have heard from so many parents in Cambridge and North Dumfries who are being asked to protect their children against some of the most sophisticated companies on earth. They want peace of mind. They want to ensure privacy and security for their kids. Most of all, they want them to be safe, but we have to ask: Will the law promising these things actually work when it meets a 14-year-old with a phone or a trillion-dollar, multinational social media giant?

Parliament is being asked to approve the framework today, while many of the important details that would actually protect our children are to be determined later. Under Bill C-34, regulated social media platforms would have to stop children under 16 from holding accounts, but a platform can apply to the new commission for an exemption by showing it has adequate safeguards. What constitutes adequate? Parliament does not know, because that standard has not yet been established. The bill does not name a single platform. Whether it covers TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Roblox or Discord will be decided by cabinet after Parliament has voted. Law professor Michael Geist counted 50 key decisions in the bill left to cabinet and a commission that does not yet exist. That makes careful scrutiny of the bill even more important.

There are other lessons from around the world we could take to inform our conversation here today. For instance, Australia's under-16 ban took effect on December 10, 2025, across 10 major platforms. Four months in, surveys found many Australian children who had accounts before the ban still retained access. Most of those who stayed reported that getting around the restrictions was easy. A larger study found that account use among children fell after the ban took effect, but significant numbers remained on the very platforms the law was written to keep them off. For most of those children, staying on took no effort at all. Many reported that existing accounts were never removed, while others got through age checks, created new accounts or relied on someone else to set one up for them.

The regulator found platforms letting new users simply declare they were 16 or older, and allowing children to retry the same age check until they were eventually let through. One app was reported to allow 24 attempts a day. Some teens beat the face scans by drawing on facial hair. When accounts did close, children moved. Many reported spending more time on gaming platforms and messaging apps, and some said they felt less safe online than before. Apps left outside the ban, like WhatsApp, surged in popularity. One Australian research compared the regulator's job to a game of whack-a-mole, chasing each new app after children had already found it.

Gaming is one of the areas of greatest concern. Roblox and Discord were not among the services covered by Australia's initial ban, yet they offer friend lists, private chats, voice channels, group servers and strangers who can reach a child directly. Roblox now uses age-based controls to limit who can communicate with whom, but neither platform was required to keep a 14-year-old off the service entirely. Indonesia and Malaysia saw the same risk and included Roblox inside their bans.

If gaming and messaging services fall outside the bill's scope, children will simply do their socializing there instead. Platforms usually decide which country's law applies based on the Internet address the phone connects through and a VPN routes that connection through a server somewhere else. A teenager in Cambridge can appear to be in Kentucky, Kenya or Korea, all places where Canadian law does not reach. Many free VPNs make their money by collecting and selling what their users do online, and so a child using one may be handing their browsing history to a company nobody can identify. Australia's regulator now expects platforms to try to stop under-sixteens from using VPNs, but new servers appear faster than old ones can be blocked, which is another game of whack-a-mole.

Here is another weak point. Facial age estimation is quick and inexpensive, but even one of the industry's leading providers reports an average error of approximately one year for teenagers, yet this bill draws a hard line at a single birthday. An error of a year in either direction lets some 15-year-olds through and locks out some 17-year-olds, and children have already shown they will keep trying until the camera says yes.

Government ID is more accurate, but it means handing a child's identity to a private company, and that information is valuable to criminals and hostile foreign actors alike. To its credit, this bill says that information can only be used for age checks and must be destroyed once the check is done, but a rule on paper is not the same as a secure system. Every database containing sensitive information will eventually become a target. Just last month, IDScan.net confirmed a breach involving more than 150 million drivers' licences and identity records. The challenge is only growing as AI accelerates the discovery of software vulnerabilities and the speed at which attackers can exploit them.

Before coming to this House, I worked in systems architecture and database management. One thing this experience taught me is that data scheduled for deletion is still data until the moment it is actually deleted. Every additional database creates another target, another vulnerability and another risk that must be managed. Canadians need to know who will hold that information, where it will be stored, who owns the companies holding it, how long it will be retained and whether Canadians will be notified if a breach occurs.

There is also a gap that no age check closes because the bill restricts holding an account, not viewing content. The government's own charter statement confirms that young people would still be able to browse without an account. A child without an account can often still watch videos and scroll public feeds while logged out, where none of the teen safety settings or parental controls apply.

Parents are still the first line of defence for their children online. The question for Parliament is whether this bill gives parents meaningful tools to help protect their children or whether those tools and safeguards are more effective on paper than in real life.

Many countries are still adjusting their own approaches. France's constitutional council struck down the country's proposed social media ban before it could take effect, citing concerns about privacy safeguards and freedom of expression. All around the world, governments are trying to answer many of the same questions that Parliament is grappling with today.

Australia has also had to go back and strengthen its own law. It doubled the maximum penalty and gave its regulator the power to compel internal company documents. That should give us pause about enforcement here. Australia's regulator is well established, with experienced staff and existing powers, and it still needed months to open investigations into five platforms and has yet to issue a fine.

This bill would create a brand new commission of three to five members that would be starting from nothing while facing the same companies. Officials have said it could take 18 months to set up. However, the minister has said that platforms would have to act as soon as this law comes into effect. Much of what decides whether this law works has been left to regulations that Parliament has not seen. That does not mean the bill is wrong, but it does mean that Parliament is being asked to place considerable trust in decisions that have not yet been made.

Those are not arguments against protecting children online. They are questions Parliament should answer before concluding that this framework will work as intended. How will enforcement work in practice, and will it be based on a user's age or their apparent location? What age verification and safe design regulations will ultimately be adopted, and what opportunity will Parliament have to review them? How will children's age verification data be collected, stored, protected and deleted, and what happens if that information is breached? Will the bill follow children to where they actually spend their time online, including gaming platforms, messaging services and content viewed while logged out? How will Parliament and Canadians know whether the law is achieving its goals and whether circumvention remains widespread? What standards will a platform have to meet in order to be exempt from the age restriction, and how transparent will those decisions be?

I opened by saying that a security system is judged by its weakest point. Here, that weakest point could be a teenager with a VPN, a flawed age verification process, inconsistent and unenforceable rules, unanswered questions from a bureaucratic commission, rival platforms not covered by legislation, data security questions or other unintended consequences that we have not yet identified.

A bill like this, with such important goals and significant consequences, deserves careful study. We need a law that holds up when it is tested. Let us send this bill to committee. Let us find and fix those weak points. Let us get it right to protect our children.

Mr. Speaker, one of the first constituents I met upon getting elected lost their son to sextortion. This bill and our ability to get it right are very important to me and to the many parents out there who are living the nightmare of losing a child to this terrible plague.
I would ask the member across the way if she supports sending this bill to committee, hearing from experts and trying to get it right for all Canadians who are suffering?

Mr. Speaker, I completely sympathize with parents who have gone through things like coercion, extortion, and online harms and scams. We are seeing this happen and it is escalating. It is something that needs to be discussed at committee. We need to find a way to protect not only our children but families. As technology is growing, we need to move in a way that looks at everything.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying earlier, knowing what goes on is important to parents. A lot has changed over the past 30 years. I see it myself as a parent, as I said earlier. My 31-year-old son has three children. What he experiences is entirely different. I feel that parents need help and support.

In her speech, my colleague said that we are not sure whether some platforms will be included or excluded. I would also like to point out that other platforms could be created after the bill passes. We therefore have to make sure to retain some flexibility.

Does my colleague agree that bills like this one should retain some flexibility? Platforms evolve quickly, and new ones are always being created. We therefore have to act quickly and avoid amending bills all the time. The government also needs the flexibility to support parents as they do their job.

Mr. Speaker, parents cannot take on some of the largest technology companies in the world by themselves. Parents can set boundaries, talk with their children and monitor device use, but they cannot control recommendation algorithms, platform design or how harmful content is promoted.

Platforms must be accountable for the risks they create, and government has an important role to play. My concern is simply ensuring that Bill C-34 gives parents meaningful support and meaningful tools, rather than creating systems that are more effective on paper than in practice.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate a number of the comments the member put on the record this evening.

I truly believe that every member of the House of Commons understands that there is harm to children and that the potential there is great. The issue is that as a Parliament, we have a responsibility to take action. Quite frankly, for me, the establishment of the digital safety commission of Canada would be a major step forward.
The member expressed some concerns with respect to it, but I wonder if she could provide her thoughts on the principle of having that commission. Is that something she supports?

Mr. Speaker, I think everyone in this House agrees that online harms are real and that children need better protection. The question is not whether action is needed. The question is whether the specific measures before us would deliver the results that families are expecting. If a law can be bypassed easily, if children can simply migrate to other platforms or if key details are left to future regulations, those are issues Parliament has a responsibility to examine carefully. We can act urgently while still making sure we get this right.
Mr. Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Nipissing—Timiskaming.

I rise in the chamber in support of Bill C-34, the safe social media act. As a mom of two young boys, I think a lot about what it means to help them navigate an increasingly digital and online world. I want them to be able to learn and keep up with the things that delight them, while also keeping them safe from the challenges that the digital environment presents.

I know first-hand that parents are doing their best to help their kids to navigate an online world that is changing faster than any generation has experienced before. I also know that keeping up with fast-paced changing technology is a full-time job. I frequently speak with parents about how difficult it is to understand the apps our children use, as well as the difficulty in managing the content and people they might encounter. By the time many of us feel that we have understood one platform, something new replaces it and the learning curve starts all over again.

Even if we do everything we can, there is still a steady stream of decisions that are being made about our children's online experiences that we do not always have control over. We may not always understand why an algorithm keeps recommending specific videos or how a platform responds to discrimination and harassment. We cannot know everything an AI chatbot might say to a child who stumbles across it on purpose or by accident. Those decisions often belong to companies that build and operate these services. They have responsibilities here too.

In a 2024 survey from Public Safety Canada, only three in 10 youth said they felt safe online. Parents were even less likely to feel their children were safe in these digital spaces. The data is alarming. Young people spend so much of their time learning how to interact with one another and the world online. This is the new place where they explore who they are and find a sense of belonging. We also know that these consequences reach well beyond the screen. Classmates can circulate messages and pictures too quickly for parents, teachers and educators to keep up. All of this has an impact on whether our children can walk into school the next morning.

With artificial intelligence advancing at a rapid pace, we are at a crossroads. As legislators and parliamentarians, we have a responsibility to act now to ensure that these technologies are safe and accountable and that they support, rather than harm, the well-being of our children. That is the future I want for my two young boys and for every child growing up in Canada.

It is in this context that our government is introducing Bill C-34. This legislation would ensure that social media services and AI chatbots are safe by design. The bill includes measures such as a ban on social media for those under the age of 16 until a service can prove it is safe, a new digital safety commission to adjudicate the efficacy of a platform's safety policies and hold them to account, and faster removal processes for harmful or victimizing content. The commission would be responsible for the enforcement of the provisions of the act.

In this era where we are all navigating lives that have a physical and digital presence, there is a real urgency to act and to do this thoughtfully and well for all Canadians. It is an issue that many stakeholders who are concerned with the well-being of children and women have raised the alarm bells on, and on behalf of the residents of Spadina—Harbourfront, I am grateful that we are using our legislative tools to act.

One of the key measures of Bill C-34 is that it would ban children under the age of 16 from having accounts on social media services. AI chatbots would be subject to the duty to protect children and the duty to act responsibly, requiring them to mitigate risks of harmful behaviour by or induced by the chatbot. Everyone has a responsibility to protect our kids.

Bullying 25 years ago often ended when the school day was over. Today, children carry that harassment with them everywhere they go, with direct access through their phones and on social media platforms. They are also more vulnerable to online predators and other harmful actors who can now reach them easily. From online harassment and the spread of misinformation to the proliferation of harmful content such as revenge porn and AI-generated deepfakes, young people are facing challenges that previous generations could never have imagined.

In this new digital era, AI, algorithms and deepfake technologies are also enabling new forms of gender-based harassment and violence toward women and young girls. We must take a whole-of-government approach and consider how these measures, along with the actions we have taken over the past year, connect together. We moved forward on part of this work through Bill C-16, the Protecting Victims Act, whereby our government introduced reforms to protect children in online environments. This has included expanding the child luring offence to better address sextortion, criminalizing non-consensual sexual deepfakes, criminalizing bestiality depictions used to groom children, increasing penalties for child exploitation offences, and requiring online platforms to preserve evidence longer so offenders can be brought to justice. As a woman who stands in public office, it has been incredibly powerful to see our government work alongside other parties in the House to ensure that the sharing of non-consensual sexual deepfakes was criminalized.
No one bill can address every angle of these harms. Our legislation, prevention efforts, stakeholder groups and other supports must work in concert together to keep young people safe.

Last week, I hosted a documentary film screening on the Hill where parliamentarians, staff and community partners gathered together to watch Miss Representation: Rise Up. The documentary, directed by Jennifer Siebel Newsom, explores how social media and AI are fuelling a cultural backlash against women and young girls, affecting their mental health, autonomy and political power. The film is a sequel to the original, which debuted 15 years ago, and this update demonstrates how women's and young girls' experiences with media and technology have intensified quickly over time. The film not only reminds us of the harms the online space can present to young women but also sends a powerful message that technological innovation must be accompanied by accountability.

We need social media platforms to have the framework and regulations in place so that our children are safe online. Bill C-34 is the first piece of national legislation that establishes a regulatory framework for AI chatbots. The bill would require greater transparency from AI chatbots and impose obligations to direct users to intervention services when they express suicidal thoughts, self-harm or an intent to seriously harm others. It would also require operators to provide the new digital safety commission with clear, transparent information on their policies for referring conversations to the RCMP and other emergency services in the case of threats to seriously harm others. The tragedy in Tumbler Ridge is a stark reminder of what is at stake. It reinforces an important principle as we build this legislation and framework.

Canadians expect online platforms to have robust safety protocols and escalation practices in place to protect online safety and ensure that law enforcement is warned about potential violence. We must and can do better for our children and their families. The bill is an important step toward creating a safer digital environment for children across Canada. As the world changes, our legislation must reflect the new terrain we are living in, and the responsibility does not lie with parents and educators alone.

Earlier this month, I had the opportunity to participate in a round table discussion with Pinterest alongside representatives from civil society and academia. The message that came through clearly was that we must get the legislation right. That includes building a system that provides strong protections for children and young people while also recognizing that digital platforms are not all designed or used in the same way. Bill C-34 reflects this approach. The commission can exempt certain companies from the age limit requirement if they demonstrate that they meet adequate safeguards designed to protect children and youth.

Our government was elected on a mandate to protect Canadians, and that responsibility includes our children. Many democracies around the world are already taking action and understanding that the digital age requires new safeguards and standards of accountability. As a middle power with strong democratic values and a tradition of defending human rights, Canada now has the opportunity to help shape the growing global conversation on digital safety. We can work alongside our international partners and establish common standards, best practices and shared expertise.

As we consider what will work best in Canada, we have an opportunity to encourage platforms to design safer spaces from the beginning. That means giving clear responsibilities to put young people's safety at the centre of how their products are built. Blanket bans alone are not enough to support young people navigating the digital world. We must pair this with the right skill sets to recognize harm and set boundaries so everyone can use the technology responsibly. This can act as a model for the rest of us as we all trip through using new technologies together.

We do not have to choose between innovation and safety. Canada can lead with both. Through legislation such as Bill C-34, Canada can help set the standard for a digital future that puts the well-being of young people first.

Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate the hon. member's speech. The difficulty I struggle with is that even as good as the bill is, there is an assumption that these so-called platforms have a right to exist, that they are a part of our world and we cannot do anything about it.

I wonder if the government has given any thought, or whether it would be something the member could take up within the caucus, to how if we did not call them platforms and instead called them publishers, we would have a mountain of common law for what we do when a publisher publishes something damaging. If there is joint and several liability, it is the person who posts something anonymously and the publisher who are responsible. This is a larger question, but I want to pose it now.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague has asked a fantastic and very thoughtful question about where this sits in the ecosystem. We are all asking thoughtful questions about what the right regulatory regimes and tools are, and I think the approach that our government is taking around an independent digital safety commission will help give the guidance that is needed here.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rechie Valdez (Minister of Women and Gender Equality and Secretary of State (Small Business and Tourism), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, one of the things the hon. member mentioned was the documentary Miss Representation: Rise Up, which I had the opportunity of watching. In it, there were a couple of stories of incredible young women, and what they were experiencing online was deeply disturbing. In terms of the new legislation, the digital safety act and the digital safety commission of Canada act, I wonder what the member would like to say on this that would help address some of the concerns of those young women in the documentary.

Madam Speaker, the minister and I really enjoyed watching the film together. At this time when many young women are thinking about what it means to step into and engage in democracy, we have a responsibility to step forward and make sure we get this right. There are real threats to Canadian democracy, and we want to make sure we can all participate safely. What we are doing here sets the groundwork for that.
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for her excellent speech, which I really appreciated.

She has two kids. I have four kids and three grandkids. We will be hearing about kids and grandkids all evening. I talk about this a lot because I am proud of it. I am 51 years old, and I had my first son when I was 20. That kind of thing is life-changing. My son is now 31 and has three children of his own, but things are different these days. The world has changed. When I was 20, we did not have tablets or cell phones. We did our best. When I look at him now with his three boys, I wonder how he handles all this, given everything that is currently happening on digital platforms.
I have a question for my colleague. Does she believe that the government should help parents by supporting them, not by replacing them?

At the end of the day, parents are the ones responsible for taking care of their children and making decisions about them every day. However, a responsible government can certainly support parents in raising their children. I would like to know: Does my colleague think the government should help parents?

Madam Speaker, today I actually received an email from my children's school that said there has been some sharing of deepfakes circulating in grade 7 and grade 8. We have a role, everyone, including the government, and there is a piece of work around education and promotion that is really critical. That is work we are taking on as a government, and we need to do this in partnership with stakeholders to get this right. There is a lot of hard work ahead.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I wanted to reaffirm the targets set out in the bill for harmful content: non-consensual intimate content, child sexual victimization, content inducing a child to self-harm, child bullying, hate, incitement to violence, and terrorism or violent extremism content. It is important that we are establishing that a great deal of hurt is there, and it is the primary reason this legislation is necessary, which would be enforced by having the commission put in place.
Madam Speaker, I agree.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Pauline Rochefort (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Rural Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-34, an act to enact the digital safety act and the digital safety commission of Canada act.

I want residents of Nipissing—Timiskaming to know why I will be voting for this bill, so I will explain. I will start with a question. It will show my age, but the question is simple. Do members remember when keeping a child safe meant knowing where they were and who they were with? Many parents and grandparents will remember those days. The rule was simple: Be home before dark.

Today, a child can be sitting beside a parent in the living room and talking to someone online who the parent knows nothing about. The child is home, and the parent feels reassured, but the risks on the screen may be hidden. The front door may be locked, but the phone is still connected. A cruel message can arrive at any hour, a humiliating image can spread in seconds, and bullying can follow a child home from school.

Childhood has changed. Parenting, as my colleague described previously, has become more complicated. Living in a peaceful northern Ontario community does not shield a child from online harm. We protect children at school and on our roads. They deserve the same protection online.

Parents, schools and governments all have a role to play, and so do the companies behind TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, YouTube, others that may be out there and others that will come. I think it is very important to note that all these companies provide so many benefits. They bring benefits to our lives. In northern Ontario, where distances are part of our daily life, online platforms help young people stay close to friends and family, including their grandparents. They help them learn, create and connect. Those connections matter, and there are many more benefits we could talk about. Our task is to preserve those benefits while reducing the risks.

The evidence shows that action is needed. According to Statistics Canada, one in four young Canadians aged 12 to 17 reported experiencing cyber-bullying in the previous year. Among young people who have a hard time making friends, that number is even higher, at one in three. Let us think about that. These are young people who struggle to make connections, who go online and are subjected to cyber-bullying. Behind these figures lie children, families and very real suffering.
What would Bill C-34 do? I will highlight the three major changes.

First, it would provide stronger protection for children under 16. The bill would prevent children under 16 from having accounts on social media services. However, a platform could receive an exemption if it demonstrated adequate safeguards for children. That gives companies an incentive to act and an incentive to make their services safer.

Second, the bill would create a digital safety commission. It would review companies' safety plans and oversee whether they are meeting their duties. If a company is earning money supplying services to Canadians, it only makes sense that it should explain how it is managing those risks. Someone should be there to check whether its measures are adequate. That would be the role of the digital safety commission.

Third, the bill would require action on some of the most harmful material online. This includes content that sexually victimizes a child and intimate images shared without consent. The proposed framework would require these types of content to be made inaccessible within hours of being either identified by the service provider or flagged by a user. Members can imagine a young person discovering that an intimate image of them is being shared. We can imagine their fear and a parent trying to find a way to deal with the issue. In those moments, time matters.

The bill would also address risks from artificial intelligence and, specifically, chatbots. Regulated chatbot services would have to take steps to reduce harmful behaviour and direct users toward crisis support in certain serious situations.

Now, some parents will say, “I know my child. I know what's best. I should decide.” I respect that view. Parents know their children in ways that governments never will, but parents do not design the systems that decide which video appears next to a video that they approved. They cannot control how quickly an image can spread or check every account that comes into contact with their child. In this environment, how much can a family truly manage? We can think of a parent who is working shift work, a caregiver who has several children, a grandparent who knows little about the app. Online safety should not depend entirely on a family's spare time or technical knowledge.

We already accept that children need different rules as they grow. We set minimum driving ages, require safety features in vehicles and teach young drivers how to use the road. While social media certainly is different from driving, the principle is useful. Education, family guidance and safety standards can work together.

Just as there are underage drivers, there will also be some who will try to get around the rules. That is why the bill would require covered platforms to use effective age checks with oversight from the digital safety commission. Companies that fail to meet their duties could face corrective orders and substantial financial penalties. A measure does not have to prevent every incident to serve a purpose. Seat belts are an excellent example of that. They do not, unfortunately, prevent every injury. We still require them because reducing harm matters.
The test should be clear. Do these measures work, and are they proportionate to the risks?

Some key questions also need to be answered. How can age be verified without compromising privacy? Who will have access to the information collected? How long will it be kept? Those are all great questions. The bill provides for safeguards regarding the information used during the age verification process, including its protection and destruction once the verification is complete. It also restricts the collection and use for the purposes of the verification. Protecting children also means protecting their personal information. The two go hand in hand.

It is important to note that Canadians want us to act. In a March 2026 Angus Reid poll of 4,000 people, 75% of respondents supported a ban on social media for those under the age of 16. People in Nipissing—Timiskaming are also calling on us to better protect children online.
There are certainly things that should give us pause. Certain details will be difficult to sort out, but doing nothing also has consequences.

For a child being bullied tonight, the harm is already happening. For a family trying to stop an intimate image from spreading, the need is immediate. We cannot promise a world without risk, but we can take reasonable steps to make it safer. As Parliament studies this bill, young people themselves must have a voice. I encourage young people from Nipissing—Timiskaming to contact my office and tell us what helps them online, what concerns them and what would make their experience safer. We need to hear from them.

I conclude by saying that, ultimately, whether we are young, old, parents or young people, we all share a responsibility to help ensure that all children are prepared for the world they are entering. We have a responsibility to ensure that it is a world that is safe for them. Children deserve a safe world.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, my colleague opposite mentioned rural and remote communities. We know we need these safeguards to keep kids safe online, but there has actually been comprehensive research that shows that with the right and appropriate safeguards, particularly for teens who are more in the 15 to 16 years old age range, some forms of social media might actually provide benefits, particularly in rural communities and particularly for young sexual minority groups. These young adults may depend on online platforms for peer support, cultural connection and access to resources unavailable in their off-line environments. Systemic academic reviews confirm these facts.

I am not saying there should not be online safeguards for kids, because there have to be, but if the government is going to apply these safeguards, there is also a risk that these resources could be removed.
What is she doing to replace them?

Madam Speaker, yes, certainly I am from what we would define as a northern rural community. Actually, in the past month or so, we have been making many calls to residents in our riding. There is very strong support for this particular bill, and there is concern around social media exposure for kids 16 and under. I do recognize all the benefits she pointed out, and I do not disagree with what she said. At the same time, there is a world out there that is also in need of some regulation, and that is what this bill is proposing.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rechie Valdez (Minister of Women and Gender Equality and Secretary of State (Small Business and Tourism), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, Miriam from my riding has said that becoming a new parent recently has made her so scared of how quickly social media is changing. She hopes her son grows in a world with a safer Internet space. She can only protect him so much. Every other product a child uses had to meet a safety standard before it reaches them. There are car seats. There are medicines and there are toys. When he grows older and would like a phone, she is scared of how much access he will get to an unregulated online world. When it comes to kids' safety, the apps on phones are the one exception not required to meet a safety standard.
I just wanted to ask the member for her thoughts on what Miriam said.

Madam Speaker, I would simply like to respond by saying that there is a reason democracies around the world, from Australia to the United Kingdom, are taking action on this issue. It is exactly for the reason the member described, and this is why it is timely for us to take action as a country.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, again, I just want to point out that my colleague opposite actually did not answer the question. She did not talk about what resources would be available to young sexual minorities in rural communities who might use, with appropriate safeguards, certain types of social media to find resources and find community. She did not answer that question and that is a concern in her riding that she failed to be accountable for.

We know from Australia what has happened with its very similar legislation is that this has actually pushed kids off safe spaces and into the dark web. The bill is silent on how the government would handle that. In fact, it is asking Parliament to devolve a lot of power into regulation without answering some of these key questions. Also, the bill does not include some of the most pernicious places that have a lack of online safety, like gaming platforms.

Why would my colleague be silent on the types of resources that would be removed from young sexual minorities in her riding? Why would she be silent and not provide more details or scrutiny on the fact that certain types of platforms where we know this type of abuse happens, like gaming platforms, are not included in this bill?

Madam Speaker, that is a fairly long question that has been posed and that is why I am proposing that this bill go to committee. It should be studied and discussed. I think that is exactly the type of question that is very valid and should be brought up at the committee level.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I will be sharing my time with my colleague from Brampton West.

Our need to provide better safeguards to protect children online is real. In fact, just to illustrate this point, one in four Canadian youth aged 12 to 17 has experienced some sort of online harm. Police reported online sexual exploitation reached 16,905 incidents in 2024, and this rate has risen under the Liberal government 347% in the last decade. Parents are trying to provide some safeguards for their kids online, but they are also asking for our help. Any approach that we take to provide these safeguards should support parents while also protecting both their rights and their children's rights, and parents' right to determine how their child becomes a digital citizen while ensuring that environment is safe and also looking at the privacy and speech rights for Canadians.

The question that we should be looking at in this House is not whether we should act, but how and whether this bill is sufficient or if it is asking us to undertake measures that devolve powers that we as parliamentarians have, for vague assurances that really deserve answers from the government.

I have a lot of questions with this bill, and I am going to start with the matter that we were just debating in the previous section, which is the ban on social media accounts. My first question relates to the best practice that we have already seen as Australia has rolled out similar provisions. We have seen that most kids at the age of 16 still had accounts months later. Harm complaints did not meaningfully decline. In fact, teens turned to VPNs, shared family log-ins or simply lied about their age. The ban did not actually do anything.

With regard to this aspect of Bill C-34, the questions I would have are the following. If a teenager is pushed off a large platform that has a well-established trust, safety team and system, where do they go, because they are going to go somewhere, and has the government been seized with this question, particularly knowing that other jurisdictions have already had this experience? Are they going to smaller, unmoderated corners of the Internet where their parents cannot see them and has the government thought about whether this measure may push vulnerable kids somewhere darker on the Internet? How will the government measure to know whether this is working? The government has been silent on these issues.

This deserves much more scrutiny because of how the bill proposes that the ban would work. A platform could apply to the new commission that is proposed in the bill for an “exemption” if it shows “adequate safeguards”. Adequate by what standard, set by whom and when? The bill is silent on these things. If the largest platforms could win exemptions, is this a ban or is it a negotiation between a regulator, not elected officials, and big tech held outside of this chamber? I have a problem with that. If safeguards exist that are good enough to earn an exemption, why not write them in law for every platform today? These are questions the government has not answered, and I suspect that it is facing internal questions within its caucus on this issue as well.

Bill C-34 sets out the general types of services it would cover, social media, livestreaming, adult content platforms and AI chatbots, but the exact test for which specific services count as a regulated social media service is left to regulations to be written later. Parliament is being asked to pass a bill before knowing where that line falls. That decision would be made by cabinet, not by this House, so we are being asked to devolve that power. In fact, the ban itself would not be automatic through this law. It would only apply to the platforms that cabinet later chooses to name in regulation. We should probably be having that debate in Parliament.

Additionally, many types of the severe dangers children face online, like grooming and sextortion, happen on gaming platforms and chat services. Would those be covered under this bill? It does not seem like it. The government may say that cabinet can add new categories of services, but why is that being left to regulation? Why are we not having that debate now? I would like to know why the government is silent on this and if it is being silent for a reason. Is it because of lobbying or is it because existing safeguards are good enough or it does not think that it can make privacy work or because the bill is not technology agnostic? Those are all questions that the government should be able to answer.
