As we continue to debate on this important legislation, I urge my fellow members to consider the public safety concerns I have presented today and remember the full range of regulations that exist within this piece of legislation that would not only protect our children but also provide sufficient opportunities for social media platforms to implement necessary safeguards, because the safety of our children must be our top priority and should not and cannot be a responsibility left to parents alone.

The digital environment is not safe for children. Leading health authorities now warn we cannot say that social media is sufficiently safe for young people and that governments must act decisively to reduce these risks. We are proposing this legislation because it is our responsibility to act, to act now and to act with urgency.
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend clearly put a lot of time, research and thought into sharing her ideas.

I want to ask about one aspect of the concept of the age restriction. When this bill was initially tabled, I think the general impression of the bill had been that it would establish a required minimum age for access to social media, but upon subsequent review, it seems that the bill would not actually do that. It would require social media companies to incorporate certain design features in order to be able to offer youth accounts. Effectively, it would not really be an age ban. Rather, it would require certain design features before companies can offer youth accounts.
I wonder, in the interest of clarity for members of the House and the public, if the member can clarify whether she considers that the bill would be an age ban or not.
Madam Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member on his upcoming additional child, number seven. It is fantastic news.

My understanding is that we are looking at age 16 and over as the appropriate age for being responsible and mature enough to navigate social media. The more important thing would be requiring the platforms profiting off our youth to do the work to make sure they are protected. In whatever ways that needs to happen, we need to make sure we are providing a safe online environment for our children, whether they be 10 years, 16 years or five years old. It is is really important and worth investigation.

Madam Speaker, I thought the analogy to seat belt legislation was particularly useful. We are talking about an inherently dangerous product in what is available online and the threat it poses to our children. This is really not unlike consumer protection legislation. It is not unlike what we do with other dangerous products in terms of regulation. We really want to be able to lower the boom on a corporation, just as we did, for instance, on ones that made cars at the time but did not put in seat belts once that was regulated and required.

Would the hon. member be interested, as I am, in figuring out how we could amend this legislation to create the maximum incentive on the corporate tech billionaires and trillionaires to make them see that Canada is not a good place to do business if they are going to harm children, and that the penalties would scare the hell out of them?

Madam Speaker, I agree wholeheartedly that a lot of what we are aiming to do is put the responsibility properly on those who are profiting from these online platforms and to put guardrails in place so we do not have the terrible incidents we have seen in the past in this country and across the world. That is exactly what we are aiming to do.

Madam Speaker, legislation is of course important, but there are many roles that society can play. When it comes to parents, guardians, next door neighbours, faith groups, educators and community-based organizations, many people can play a role in making sure we provide young people with the skills and tools they need.

I would like to know from the member if she has put some thought into different ways in which parents and other members of society can play a role to really help tackle this huge challenge we have in front of us.

Madam Speaker, a big thing I think about often is getting our children outside, getting them out of doors and connected to real people in three dimensions, in real time and in nature. I have seen, even with my children, that if they have too much screen time, the behaviour starts to get a little wonky. They start to fight with me, my other kids and my husband. When we all get out of the house and go for a walk, we reset. It is really important for kids to have, as they are growing up, a sense of community, whether that is a religious community, a neighbourhood community or an activity community. We gravitate to those supports, and the more we can do to get our kids and youth off screens and actually engaged in the world around us, the better we will be.
Madam Speaker, today I rise to speak to Bill C-34, the safe social media act.

We have been hearing a lot about the duty to act responsibly, the duty to protect children, and the duty to make certain content inaccessible. When we talk about protecting our next generation, we have to talk about the digital world they are growing up in. Even as one of the youngest MPs of the House, and the youngest member of Parliament for British Columbia, I belong to a generation that experienced a full childhood before social media became part of our everyday lives. I remember a time when, after school, I would catch up with friends meeting them in person. If we wanted to talk to somebody, we picked up the land line and hoped they were home. I spent time outdoors biking with my friends to the corner store, skateboarding, playing tag and making memories away from a screen.

Today is a bit of a different world, of course. Children are growing up in an environment where social media is always within reach. Endless scrolling really is endless. Instead of simply catching up with friends, they can find themselves spending hours online, caught in addictive algorithms designed to keep them scrolling for many hours. There are concerns about what they are exposed to, how online platforms influence their behaviour, and what happens to their mental health as they grow up spending more time on their phone.

There are ways to mitigate this, of course. Consider YouTube, for example, which has been a bit of a leader in this space. It allows users and parents to turn off endless scrolling in the settings, to limit the addictive nature and the endless scrolling that many kids are growing up with these days. This is an example of the options we want our social media platforms to allow as settings.

We cannot expect our children to navigate these challenges on their own. Protecting young people means taking a serious look at how these platforms are operating and the responsibility they have to the children who use them. Social media does create opportunities for people to connect, to explore, to learn and to express themselves, but we cannot ignore the risks that come with it, especially when it comes to their mental health and personal safety.

Algorithms can amplify harmful content and expose young people to unrealistic standards, which they see day in and day out. For some people, this can contribute to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem and feelings of isolation. All these have been on the rise, as reported by psychologists, especially in younger age groups, which are using these technologies on a very frequent basis. At the same time, online platforms can also expose users to cyber-bullying, harassment, exploitation and other harmful content that can have very serious real-world consequences.

In 2025, 23% of Canadian youth aged 16 to 24 reported spending almost one-third of their day on social media. Research has associated longer screen times with poorer mental health indicators, including higher levels of anxiety, depression, and psychological distress, as well as reports of suicidal ideation. This matters because protecting young Canadians is about making sure the digital world does not come at the expense of their well-being or their relationships with others. Young people need supportive environments where they can build meaningful connections and access help when they need it.

We also have to recognize the role that social media platforms play in shaping what young people see online. Algorithms influence the content they are exposed to, and recommendation systems can repeatedly push harmful material onto someone's screen. For a young person already struggling with their mental health, repeated exposure to harmful content can create additional risks. Over time, this can normalize very dangerous behaviours and make it harder for young people to seek help.

It is crucial that online platforms take greater responsibility to ensure that their algorithms prioritize safety and well-being, especially for vulnerable users. It is also very important that the social media giants that are monetizing the attention span of our next generation be held accountable for the harms they are causing, and that our legislation have teeth to enforce consequences for the social media companies that are providing these harms to our youth.

I will soon be introducing my own private member's bill, which is a national strategy for suicide prevention. Of course, one of the main things it is also looking at is what some of the risk factors are for suicide, which is unfortunately all too common in our modern day and age.

It is an unfortunate reality that there is content on social media that can sometimes propagate tendencies toward self-harm and toward suicidal ideation. It is very important that it is not just up to parents to regulate the things their kids are seeing and to be the police of the content their kids are taking in. That is why it is up to us as government to do that.

We need to ask ourselves this: Is it fair to expect parents to manage these risks on their own while the companies designing these platforms face limited accountability? Parents are already balancing the pressures of everyday life. We cannot expect them to monitor everything that their children do 24 hours a day, particularly when kids have their own screens. We cannot constantly see everything that our kids are seeing. It is, frankly, impossible. Parents have an important role to play, of course, by setting up certain settings on devices, but protecting children cannot fall on their shoulders alone.

Social media companies design these platforms. They design how content is recommended and how users interact with these services. That is why we need clear expectations for these companies. They must take meaningful steps to identify risks and reduce harm. Just as importantly, they must be transparent about what they are doing and demonstrate that their efforts are making a difference. Canadians should not have to simply take a company's word that a platform is safe.

Technology has moved faster than the rules to protect our people are keeping up. We have been slow to respond to these changing online environments, and we need to take action. As a result, harmful content can spread unchecked, and dangerous behaviours can be amplified. Vulnerable users can repeatedly be exposed to materials that put their well-being at risk.

Bill C-34 takes an important step toward closing that gap by recognizing that those who design and profit from these platforms also have a responsibility to prevent foreseeable harms, the harms that they know they are causing. We should not wait for a young person to experience harm before expecting action from the companies that operate these services.

The legislation would establish clear expectations from social media platforms. Companies would be required to assess the risks associated with harmful content on their services and take proactive steps to reduce those risks. Users would have access to a clear reporting and complaint mechanism so they know where to turn when they encounter harmful content or have concerns for their own safety. It is important that we make sure this happens with a very quick process, because throughout this, we do not want to see young people turn away from platforms that we are familiar with and go toward corners of the Internet that might be less regulated. That is why it is important that the legislation move quickly. If we stand these things up, we can prevent people from going to less safe corners of the Internet.

Another factor here is, of course, the new challenges emerging with artificial intelligence. AI has made it easier to create fake or manipulated images that damage someone's reputation. Some content can go viral within minutes. It can also make it much harder for people to distinguish between authentic content and material designed to mislead them. We have now entered an age where when we see a photo, it is virtually impossible to tell if that photo is real or if it has been generated in a matter of seconds by somebody on a keyboard anywhere on the planet.

AI chatbots raise additional concerns, particularly when they interact with young people who are experiencing emotional distress. These interactions feel very personal, and young users may not always understand the limitations of these systems. We need appropriate safeguards to reduce the risk of harmful responses and ensure that vulnerable young people are not left without proper support.

Take the example of somebody using an AI chatbot as a counsellor, for example. These chatbots are not registered counsellors and can sometimes give very misleading and harmful advice to the young people who are using them. Some government oversight is very needed here. We cannot wait until harm has already occurred before asking how these technologies should be used responsibly. Platforms must take responsibility for the risks associated with the services they provide, including the AI tools that they make available to their users.

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend spent a lot of time talking about the problem, and I completely agree with his description of the problem. There is going to be no disagreement in the House that we have a serious problem with what happens online and the effects it has on young people, that we need action and that this action has to include real accountability for platforms and actors for the things they are responsible for. The work we will do at committee on this bill specifically will be to study the government's proposed solution to see whether it is fit for purpose.

One of the questions I have, I asked earlier, and I wonder if the member has thoughts on it. The bill does not appear to be an age ban, which was initially proposed. I think it proposes to require certain adaptations or changes to design features, ultimately with the idea that the social media platforms that exist could continue to offer youth accounts. There would not be a requirement, for instance, for parental consent for those youth accounts.
Can the member tell me whether my reading of the legislation is correct, or does he see the bill as being an age ban, as some have proposed?

Madam Speaker, it is very important that in this process, we make sure that these platforms are fit for young people to be on them. If they are deemed fit for use, then of course that is great and youth will be allowed to continue to use them. However, if there are platforms that are deemed to not be taking these measures, then there will be a ban until they are. It is an age ban particularly for the platforms that have the most severe consequences.

Madam Speaker, there is something of a lovely age gap between the member for New Westminster—Burnaby—Maillardville and I, and it is with a sense of generational continuity that I address him. Our first conversation was about how his best friend was the grandson of one of my very best friends. This is one of those things where some of us have more familiarity with social media than others.
I want to ask a question following up on the question from my friend from Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan.

We do not really have an age ban in the bill. I think all of us are united in wanting to protect children from online harms, but my current fixation is what we could fix through amendments to this bill. We could create incentives for corporations to protect children in Canada, saying that otherwise, they would suffer significant and crushing financial or personal punishment. They would then be highly incentivized to make sure their platforms do not harm our children. Does the member have any thoughts on that?
Madam Speaker, I would like to first off thank my hon. colleague for the question. I would also like to say hi to Walker and Pam Jennings, with whom we share a mutual friendship.

I agree with my hon. colleague that this legislation needs to have teeth. We, of course, are talking about very large social media giants, and a slap on the wrist would not be enough for enforcement. We need to make sure we have penalties, particularly for the worst cases and worst offences. These are things too horrible to even talk about, but when we talk about about sexualized deepfakes of children, for example, they must be removed in a very swift manner, and if not, there need to be consequences for the social media giants.

Madam Speaker, the government has an essential role to play in protecting children and keeping them safe while respecting parental authority. The goal is to strike a balance between protecting children and respecting parents' responsibilities.
Can my colleague explain how this bill would help speed up the removal of intimate content distributed without consent and content that sexually victimizes children, in order to better protect them?
Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for his excellent question. It is important for social networks to ensure that this type of content, which is harmful, is removed within an acceptable time period.

Madam Speaker, it is a real honour for me tonight to join what is a very important and substantial conversation about how we protect our kids in the age of the Internet. Obviously, as members know, this is a deeply important and personal conversation for me, as I am the father of six children I have met so far and one who will be born in April.

If the House will indulge me briefly, I just want to say that I am so proud of and grateful to my kids. I love them. I care about them. I am proud of what they do, and I feel so supported by them in the work that I do in this place. The way my kids take care of chores and responsibilities around the house, which maybe I would do if I was home more, is really heartwarming and something I am very grateful for. I am grateful that my kids can come with me to Ottawa from time to time to learn about the work I do here. Even when they are not physically with me, I always have them on my mind and in my heart as I think about the work we are doing and the country we are trying to build for them. That is especially the case, of course, as we deal with these weighty questions of child safety online.

It is interesting the way, coincidentally maybe, the parliamentary calendar has lined up tonight. We are having a debate on Bill C-34, and during private members' hour, we were debating Bill S-209, another important piece of legislation that deals with the question of the safety of children online. It is interesting to look at what these two bills would do, and at some of the similarities and differences. During my speech, I will make reference to some extent to both of those pieces of legislation.

Because I did not have a chance to speak to Bill S-209, I want to recognize and express my appreciation to the whole House for the passage of it at second reading. I think it is excellent legislation. I look forward to the study that is going to happen at committee. I salute the hard work of Senator Miville-Dechêne, as well as my friend and colleague from Battlefords—Lloydminster—Meadow Lake, who sponsored the bill in the House, and my friend and colleague from Peace River—Westlock, who has done so much work on the protection of children online for the entirety of his time as a member of Parliament.

In Bill S-209 in particular, but also included in the provisions of Bill C-34, is the issue of trying to address the scourge of early exposure to pornography on the Internet by young people. This is a massive problem, and I think we should correctly identify it as a form of Internet-based child abuse. Exposing children to sexual imagery is child abuse.

So many children are exposed very early on in life to sexual and often violent sexual images that they stumble upon when on the Internet. Some statistics suggest that the average age of first exposure to pornography is 11, so many children, boys and girls of nine, 10, 11 and 12, are seeing sexual scenes and violent sexual scenes at a time when they are obviously not making choices. They are not knowingly and wilfully doing this. They are stumbling into things they do not understand, and it is shaping their beliefs and expectations in ways that have lifelong effects that lead to increased sexual violence, all kinds of other harms and wildly dangerous expectations of what is expected in the context of intimate relationships.

It is incumbent upon all of us to try to address and confront this epidemic of early exposure to pornographic material by children. This is something we have been talking about in the House and has been talked about repeatedly in the Senate for many years, yet there has been a failure to complete the required legislative action.

We almost got there in the last Parliament, and now we have the continuation of these efforts. There was a similar bill to Bill S-209 in the previous Parliament that the government was not supportive of, so I am very pleased to see the adoption at second reading and look forward to the continuing work as we go forward. I know that Bill S-209 has certain new features that are different from a similar bill in a previous Parliament. It is now the absolute gold standard in terms of privacy protection. The way Bill S-209 has been written, it has been endorsed by the Privacy Commissioner. It has been worked over so extensively across multiple Parliaments to be airtight in terms of the provisions to protect privacy. Again, I want to recognize Senator Miville-Dechêne for her extensive work on that, as well as the colleagues I already highlighted in this House.

Bill S-209 and other bills aimed at protecting children online obviously have to include requirements around age verification or age estimation tools. This is inevitable. If we want to take the position that, on the Internet, some material should never be accessed by children and the same material should be available to adults, the only way to make that distinction is to have credible tools for age verification or estimation. The only alternative to that is you make it available to everybody or you make it available to nobody. Assuming that we agree that a distinction has to be made, we need age verification or estimation tools. That is the only way to do it.

The legislation that has moved forward to committee today would require age verification or estimation. It does not prescribe the specific mechanics of that method, and I think that is appropriate because technology will develop and we will find more and more credible and effective ways of doing this over time. In an area where technology is constantly developing, even over the time the bill is being discussed, we should not prescribe the specific method. The legislation would require that age verification or estimation occur in such a way that children are not being exposed to these materials. Further, it provides an opportunity for the government to prescribe age verification methods that could be used and also establishes criteria for those methods that include the use of third parties and the protection of privacy.

The use of a third party for age verification means that an individual would go to a third party to verify their age or have age estimation in some way with that third party and then receive a kind of digital key. I am not a real technology person, I will admit, so I am sharing terms that may not be the precise technical terms, but this is how the design of the legislation works. It is that people can go to a third party, get what is effectively a digital key and bring it back to whatever site they are trying to access, and the site they are accessing is not the one that did the age verification. The age verification was done externally. It is what I know Senator Miville-Dechêne has called double anonymity. People's privacy is protected because of the use of the third party verification method.

There are these various requirements in Bill S-209 that really make it the gold standard in terms of privacy protection, but we need to have age verification or estimation if we are going to say there is going to be an age cut-off required for access to these kinds of materials. This is very important. We know the problem. The early exposure to pornography is something that desperately must be addressed. We finally seem to have an emerging consensus in this House to be able to move toward the realization of that objective.

As I understand it, Bill C-34 would address the issue of exposure of minors to pornography. However, it would only address it in the context of social media. Bill C-34 would not deal with age verification or estimation for dedicated pornographic websites; that is in Bill S-209. Bill C-34 would deal with pornographic content on social media and the presentation of it on those platforms. Those provisions are certainly important, and action is required on the social media side, but it is important to be clear that Bill C-34's provisions would not address the full range of places where this material is available. This is why Bill S-209 is very much required. Bill S-209 would address everything. It would address all of the places that kind of content is available.

I spoke about being a parent, and I want to just reflect a bit on some of the discussion about the relationship between parents and the state in terms of protection of children online. I believe very much in the paramount importance of parental involvement and parental decision-making. I think the job of the state is to act as an ally to parents, to support parents in the protection of their children by helping parents and maybe by performing tasks parents are not able to perform. The state should prevent bad actors from trying to interfere in the lives of my children. It should try to prevent bad actors from targeting my children with dangerous or abusive material. It should try to protect my children from being exposed to things out and about outside of my home.

People have rightly pointed out that parents can, in the context of their own homes, establish rules around what material their kids can access online. This is true, but many of our kids have access to screens and to the Internet in other places, maybe when they are at school or with friends. We can do our best as parents to provide protections elsewhere, but we cannot be everywhere. We cannot be in those places all the time, so I think it is right and legitimate for the state to seek to protect children in ways that are allied with the efforts of parents. Parents want to protect their kids, and I think they are looking for state action in those other spaces, which is why it is right and legitimate for the state to seek to prevent minors from being exposed to, for instance, sexual material online, but also to other types of dangerous material, insofar as they are doing so in a way allied with their parents.

If we are talking about sexual material, exposing children to that material is a form of child abuse. It should never be allowed, ever, under any circumstances, and the state obviously has a compelling interest in preventing child abuse. I really see the importance of allied action between parents and the state, the paramount importance of the role of parents in the lives of their children, and state action that supports child protection in ways that are allied with the actions of parents.

There is obviously a lot in this bill. I am going to try to cover as much as I can here. On the issue of social media, I agree with what members have said. They have grave concerns about early exposure to social media and some of the design features of social media, aspects of the algorithm, etc. They have an addictive quality. They tend to create anxiety. It is important for us to discuss and look for ways to respond to that. I am quite sympathetic to arguments in favour of establishing that, under a certain age, kids should not have access to social media. I share many of the concerns members have articulated.

I also think it is important to identify that Bill C-34, as it relates to social media, would not impose an age ban as many people understand it would. I was just chatting informally with a colleague about what we mean by an age ban.

What Bill C-34 says is that someone cannot access social media if they are under 16, unless this social media company makes certain adjustments in terms of design features and it complies with certain directives established by regulation. The member said that I have that right. If the social media companies comply with those directives of government, then they will be able to issue youth accounts. In fact, the Liberal member who spoke before me said that they want the existing mainstream platforms to be able to act in ways that will allow them to offer youth accounts so that young people do not end up accessing other dark corners of the web that are less regulated, etc.

The point is, I think it is important for parents at home to know, this bill is not about saying people under 16 should never be on social media. It is about the government saying that it will allow young people to be on certain social media platforms that comply with certain things that the commissioner has established, but it will retain the ability to prevent young people from being on other social media platforms if certain other requirements are not met.

I do not think that constitutes an age ban, as maybe it has been sold, or as most parents understand an age ban to be. I think parents would understand the communications around an age ban to be that young people are not going to be on social media anymore, period. That is not what Liberal members are talking about. Liberal members are talking about a world in which young people would be on social media, on the same social media platforms, and those social media platforms would be required to comply with certain design features. I say that not to affirm or criticize that approach, but simply to say it is important for people to know what that approach is, so that people are not expecting this legislation to be something that it is not. We can have an argument about the idea of an age ban, but we should also kind of debate what is in this bill and whether this is the right approach as opposed to other kinds of architecture.

I think the other concern worth raising and reflecting on, and I know this is going to go to committee and it will be studied there, is how much, in terms of those design features, is being left to regulation. At what point is this going to be through regulation, through the action of a commissioner saying, okay, we kind of like what is going on on this platform and we do not like what is going on on that platform? Of course, we have different kinds of social media platforms that are doing different kinds of things. Some skew a little one way politically, some skew another way politically. There are different things going on, on different platforms.

If we were saying, always and ever, our young people should not be on social media, that would be one kind of architecture, but this sort of involves the government saying, in any case, we are going to have some platforms where people are on them and some platforms where people are not on them, or they can be on those platforms if they comply with certain things the government says. That just raises some potential questions about how regulatory intervention could shape what digital platforms are doing in a world where young people are ultimately still on the platforms. If someone's concern is the anxiety induced by a presence on these platforms, it seems like the world envisioned by the government on Bill C-34 is still one in which minors, people under 16, are accessing social media. It is just subject to some of these limitations.

I do think another thing to just point out is that there is always concern when we have government legislation, with the Liberal government in particular, about the implications for censorship. I am very concerned about genuinely harmful content online and its impact on young people. I also know that sometimes, informally in debate, government members will call things misinformation or disinformation simply because they disagree with it. They will accuse someone else's argument as being disinformation, simply because they disagree with it. I think there is sometimes a lack of trust, legitimately, in the government around actions that it takes online.

We are eager to engage in the discussion around this bill in good faith, because we think there are many important issues that are raised in it. Certainly, we need to act and look for opportunities to act together to protect our children, but there is a lack of trust in the actions by the Liberal government in the online space in general. I think there are good reasons for that if we look at some of the legislation it has brought forward in the past.
Twenty minutes flies by. I could talk for another 20, if this House would allow, but we will have questions and comments soon, so maybe I will be able to add to it at that point.

Madam Speaker, after listening to my colleague, I realize that we both care about protecting our children online. I think that if we did not care about this issue, we would not be here tonight at this late hour.
Bill C‑34 proposes several improvements to better regulate social media platforms in order to protect young people from harmful online content that could have an impact on their mental health.
If my colleague supports the bill's guiding principles and the broad objectives it seeks to achieve, will he vote to send it to committee so that it can be studied in depth?

Madam Speaker, genuinely, it is always a challenge when we are asked to rule on the objectives of a bill. I agree with the stated objectives. If a stated objective is to protect children, I agree with protecting children. I have a lot of questions about the architecture of the bill and whether it achieves its objectives.

I look forward to the study that is going to happen at committee. I hope we have a detailed and robust study. I hope we are able to see amendments to address some of the issues around the architecture. I think action is required to protect kids online. The status quo is not acceptable. We need new robust responses by government to this challenge.

I hope that through the process of debate, refinement and amendment, we can get to a piece of legislation that answers all the questions that I and other members have and achieves the objective that we are all saying we want.
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member from Edmonton for his thoughtful reply.

I am genuinely interested in getting to the gist of the matter. I would like to give him the opportunity to expand a bit more on the architecture that he thinks would be acceptable to gain his support for the bill. The architecture could be presented either here in the House or at committee.

Madam Speaker, I was getting to it toward the end of my comments. I think the concerns about misinformation, disinformation and hateful content are real and legitimate concerns. I also think that sometimes that language can be used to silence different opinions.

Often in debates in this House, I have heard a person make a good-faith, well-reasoned and perhaps true argument, and someone else says it is disinformation or misinformation. There may have been times when those accusations have been levied in lots of different directions.

We have to be very careful with the creation of a new agency that would establish standards for regulating harmful content and ensure that it is not being used to limit legitimate speech and debate. At the same time, there is real, genuine harmful content that we obviously want to put a stop to. That is the work that has to be done in striking the right structure to get the work done.

Madam Speaker, I am surprised that we are discussing the difference between misinformation and disinformation. I think my friend from Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan would agree that if we look at any dictionary definition, “misinformation” can be understood to be an error or mistake, and “disinformation” is defined universally as being deliberately deceptive. Spreading something with the intent to deceive is usually what we find in the dictionary there. I think it is important in this place that we not suggest they are the same term or that they can be confused.

In terms of this legislation, I know there is a lot to be determined later in regulations. For that terminology, can we assume that any commissioner will rely on commonly understood Oxford English Dictionary sorts of definitions for the difference, with “disinformation” meaning deliberately deceitful?

Madam Speaker, of course I agree there is a difference between those two words. My point was simply that those words get thrown around casually, often interchangeably, and admittedly in a way that is disconnected from the true meanings of them. Because it is against parliamentary rules for someone to accuse someone else of lying in this place, I think often people just say that something is misinformation, which is their way of trying to get underneath the rules of not being able to say someone is lying.

The point, though, is that when we have the casual use of the terms “misinformation” and “disinformation” thrown against political critics at the same time as there is legislation aiming to, through legal intervention and online regulation, prevent misinformation and disinformation, there is a bit of a problem: How do we prevent the misuse of terms that we see in political discourse from creeping into the misuse of terms in other places?

I will pick up on what the member said as well. She highlighted the number of decisions that are left to regulation. That is a concern we have in general. The number of decisions in this framework that are ultimately left to regulation rather than established in legislation increases the risk and potential concern of abusive decisions later.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, put very simply, this legislation is all about protecting our children. I think everyone in the House recognizes the value of that. Putting in regulations that would ultimately deal with social media services, AI, chatbots and so forth is a good thing. I believe the member would concur with that.

There has been some misinformation. If we take a look at pornography, it is being dealt with in a very limiting way to protect the interests of children. There are also age verification issues within that.

Would the member not recognize that the principle of the legislation is sound and that we need to get it to committee stage, where a lot of the details could be fleshed out? In particular, I am a big advocate of the commission. I think the commission is one of the ways in which we could see an enforcement of the regulations to hold these services and programmers to account. I would like his thoughts on that specifically.

Madam Speaker, I do not doubt the sincerity of every member who is talking about their aspirations to protect kids. I think that aspiration is widely shared. It is also important to underline that good intentions are not enough in legislation. What becomes law is not the good intentions of legislators. What becomes law is the text of the bill. That is the work we are doing now and that we will do at the committee. It is to discuss, as I did in my speech, the alignment between the intentions and the results as they would be created by the legislation.

There are good things in this bill. It is important to acknowledge that there may have been some dissonance in the communication that there would not be an age ban. It would not actually prevent people under 16 from accessing social media. While there are important and positive provisions around pornographic content, it would not cover pornography websites; it would only covers social media. That is why Bill S-209 is important.

The work that is going to happen at committee, the study, is very important. It is important to acknowledge what the bill would do and what it would not do. Again, it would not create an age ban. It does not address all issues of pornography. It only deals with pornography on some kinds of websites. However, there are important and positive aspirations that are expressed through it, and it is worthy of serious and thoughtful study.

Madam Speaker, I have heard my hon. colleagues mention several times, with a bit of fence-sitting, the question of whether the bill constitutes an age ban for young Canadians under 16. I am curious if the member is able to clarify that. In his view, would it be preferable to have a universal ban for Canadians under 16 on social media platforms, or would it be preferable to have social media platforms fix their systems such that there would be limitations on age-inappropriate content and young Canadians could safely use those platforms, given some of the benefits that we know exist? Which of those two options would the member prefer? I cannot tell based on his remarks this evening.
Madam Speaker, in the point I made, admittedly, I did not comment on that either way. I simply pointed out that the bill is not an age ban.
What would the ideal architecture be? I think there will be lots of time to study that question at committee. I am open to the argument—
We are resuming debate.
The hon. member for Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie.

Madam Speaker, the digital world now occupies an essential place in the lives of Canadians. It allows us to communicate, stay informed, learn and stay in touch with the people close to us. However, those opportunities also come with risks that we can no longer ignore. Today, children are accessing social media at increasingly younger ages, sometimes without their parents being fully aware. In a few clicks, a child can create an account, start using a platform and become exposed to harmful content while leaving his or her personal data behind.

In this environment, we have to wonder whether we are doing enough to protect our young people. I had a chance to consult with the people of Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie to better understand their concerns about these bills. During our conversations, child protection was front and centre, especially in terms of the negative effects of social media. These discussions reminded me that this issue extends far beyond technology. It concerns our families, our schools, our communities and the health of the next generation.

Parents want their children to reap the benefits of the digital world without being exposed to risks they are not yet able to recognize or manage on their own. As parliamentarians, we have a duty to listen and respond to their concerns.

The data presented in connection with this bill are concerning. According to the available data, over the past decade, depression has doubled and anxiety has quadrupled among young Canadians aged 15 to 24. Research also shows that young people who have been victimized online report three times more suicidal thoughts. These numbers should make us think long and hard about the environment in which our young people are growing up. It is important to recognize that mental health is influenced by many factors.

Social media cannot be held responsible for all the problems young people face. However, when the risks associated with digital spaces compound the challenges that teenagers already face, we cannot afford to look the other way.

According to the data, Canadian police recorded 19,516 incidents of online child sexual exploitation in 2023. That is 59% higher than in 2022. Behind these numbers are victims, families and lives that have been profoundly disrupted. These numbers illustrate the scale of the challenge before us. They demonstrate why digital safety must be regarded as a collective responsibility and why our responses must keep pace with evolving risks.

That is precisely why this bill represents a significant step forward. It proposes a shift from a primarily reactive approach to a more preventive one, in which platforms must assess the risks associated with their services and take measures to mitigate them.

First, tech companies must be held accountable. This bill therefore requires the services in question to regularly assess certain risks associated with their operations, make changes to their design to minimize harm and implement clear reporting mechanisms. It also provides for the publication of digital safety plans to help Canadians better understand the risks inherent to these platforms and the measures taken to address them. This transparency is essential.

Second, the bill proposes to strengthen the protection of children. It prohibits anyone under the age of 16 from owning a social media account, subject to exemptions for platforms that can demonstrate that their services are sufficiently safe for our young people. This approach is based on an important principle, specifically that protection must be built into the design of the services rather than simply added once a problem has emerged.

At that age, young people are going through a critical stage of their development. Their identity is taking shape, their social relationships are becoming increasingly important, and their ability to cope with certain pressures continues to evolve. Repeated exposure to bullying, harmful content and mechanisms that encourage excessive use can pose an additional risk.

Protecting young people does not mean denying their ability to think or make decisions. It means recognizing that the environment they grow in has to take their age and developmental stage into account. It is not just a matter of setting an age limit. It is also about encouraging companies to do more to create safer digital spaces.

The bill provides for expedited procedures to make certain content inaccessible, particularly content that sexually victimizes children or survivors, as well as intimate images shared without consent. When such content circulates online, every share can prolong a victim's suffering. Swift action can help limit its spread and prevent the affected person from being victimized again.

Our policies must be able to respond to today's risks while taking into account that technologies will continue to evolve. Some people may wonder whether these measures might infringe on freedom of expression or privacy. The answer is no. These concerns deserve a serious response. Freedom of expression is essential to our democracy. Canadians must be able to express their opinions, criticize the government, debate social issues and freely participate in public life.

The bill is not intended to suppress legitimate debate or ordinary conversations. It targets specific categories of harmful content, particularly the sexual exploitation of children, the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, the bullying of children and any content that incites violence.

Protecting young people and preserving freedom of expression should not be seen as opposing objectives. We can preserve the right to debate while requiring that businesses take action against serious harm. Privacy protections are just as essential. Age verification mechanisms must be implemented responsibly, with guarantees regarding the collection, use and destruction of personal data. The goal must be to protect young people, not create new risks to their privacy.

To ensure obligations are met, the bill also establishes an independent digital safety commission. Among its responsibilities, the commission would review platforms' safety plans, assess their age-verification mechanisms, support victims and ensure that platforms meet their obligations. It would also have the authority to impose financial penalties on platforms that fail to comply with the law. Under the proposed framework, these penalties could amount to up to 3% of a platform's global revenue. This is important because obligations must be backed by credible enforcement mechanisms.

I would now like to return to the consultations I had the opportunity to conduct with the people of Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie. The concerns raised by constituents remind us that the decisions we make here in the House of Commons have real consequences for families across the country. We must show them that we are prepared to act, not only when harm occurs, but also before it happens. We must ensure that platforms take responsibility, that victims have access to support and that parents are not left to navigate systems over which they have little or no control.

Prevention, digital education, support for families and work with specialized organizations will remain vital, but we cannot use the fact that we are doing those things as an excuse not to take action. Maintaining the status quo is not enough when risks are increasing, technology is changing and children continue to be exposed to preventable harm. We therefore have the responsibility to adapt our laws to address these challenges. We have the responsibility to ensure that platforms that profit from these young people also help keep them safe. Above all, we have the responsibility to place the well-being of our young people at the heart of our decisions.

This bill gives us an opportunity to recognize that just because our children are at home or at school does not necessarily mean that they are safe. We also need to make sure that they are safe in the digital world. By enhancing prevention, demanding greater transparency and accountability from platforms, expediting the removal of some particularly harmful content and establishing independent oversight, we can help create a safer digital environment. We must act with determination but also with discernment by protecting freedom of expression and privacy, which are at the heart of our democracy. Young people deserve to be able to learn, communicate and grow without being left alone to navigate risks that businesses have the means to prevent. That is our responsibility to our families, communities and future generations.

I want to thank the people of Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie for speaking with me and sharing their concerns. They remind why this work is necessary. As young parents, we have a responsibility to keep our children, youth and communities safe. This bill is an important milestone for the community that we represent here in the House. We may not be able to overcome every challenge that the digital world creates, but we can choose to protect the most vulnerable among us more effectively. When it comes to our children's safety, we have a duty to act.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague gave an excellent speech. He touched on a number of the key points in this bill. The reason we are still here tonight at this late hour is that we care deeply about protecting our children online.

I would like to know his opinion of the bill's architecture. Rather than imposing an outright ban, the bill allows platforms to be exempted if they can demonstrate that they have a rigorous safety plan, which would be assessed by an independent commission. That safety plan must show how children will be prevented from being exposed to harmful content. I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on that approach. In my opinion, it was the right approach to take.

Mr. Speaker, that is a good question. I do agree with my colleague's comment. This bill is intended to prevent harm. It also enables online companies to structure their operations to comply with the Government of Canada's framework. Once this bill is passed, young people who go online will be exposed to a much safer digital environment with stronger safeguards. Young people will be in a safer environment, and parents will have greater confidence that their government is acting responsibly.
Mr. Speaker, I thought my colleague's intervention was very detailed and a really good analysis of Bill C-34.

He mentioned he had the opportunity to talk to people in his community and I want to know if he had the opportunity to speak to any families or young people about the implications of this proposed legislation.
Mr. Speaker, that question is very much like one that a parent asked me recently when I was at the first meeting about this bill in Saint‑Basile‑le‑Grand.

The parents were very pleased that we were able to meet with them. They made it clear that it was time for Canada to act and that we had made the right decision. Parents shared their concerns with us. In no uncertain terms, they called for regulation. They feel this bill will address mental health concerns by providing much more robust protection against unauthorized images and the proliferation of intimate videos.
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague, as well as the people of Mont‑Saint‑Bruno—L'Acadie on having him as their member of Parliament.
Can my colleague explain to the House how this bill will require the platforms to take responsibility for digital security rather than leaving it up to users to protect themselves?

Mr. Speaker, this bill is not going to impose bans without consequences. These companies know that. We have included penalties of 3% if they fail to reliably implement everything contained in this bill. There will be 3% penalties. This bill requires accountability.
We take comfort in the fact that if companies fail to comply with or respect this bill, they will be penalized by the commission that will be established.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague explained, parents cannot monitor their children 24-7. In various settings in real life, we have certain expectations regarding the protection of children, whether at school, in community organizations or in different institutions. When we leave our children in these settings, we expect them to be safe.

Today, the virtual world is playing an increasingly important role in our everyday lives. It is a fact that children spend time in these virtual spaces. That is why I think it is important to put certain regulations in place to ensure the safety of our children when they use platforms like social media.
I would like my colleague to talk a bit more about that.
Mr. Speaker, as I said very clearly in my speech, through this bill, we must show them that we are prepared to take action not only when harm occurs, but also before it occurs.
This bill is not only preventative. It is also coupled with corporate accountability.

As I said in my speech, children are not safe only at home and at school. When they leave those settings, they are exposed to the digital world. We need to make sure that our children are protected and safe in that world. If they are not, companies will be held accountable, and their fees could amount to 3% of global revenues under the provisions of the bill.
Mr. Speaker, quickly, why is it important to establish an independent digital safety commission?
Why is this a step forward, according to my colleague?

Mr. Speaker, one of the things I like in this bill is that the commission will ensure that the provisions are applied and enforced. This is an independent commission that will closely monitor identity verification and ensure that the law is enforced. If the law is not obeyed, companies will be held liable and subject to a 3% penalty.
Mr. Speaker, I again commend my colleague.
Can he explain how the new digital safety commission of Canada will enable us to better monitor platforms, ensure that they meet their obligations and hold them accountable if they fail to do so?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his great question.

The commission bolsters the credibility of this bill or the future act. It will prevent any interference from the Government of Canada when it comes to decisions related to the applicability of the bill. The commission will have free rein to monitor these digital companies and take action if they fail to comply with the provisions set out in this bill.
As I said earlier, non-compliant companies will be subject to the measures set out in this bill's accountability framework.

Mr. Speaker, we all have a role to play, as members of society and of organizations, faith groups, not-for-profits and community-based groups, in making sure that we protect our children. Outside of this legislation, I know that my hon. colleague is a father. I am a father. Does he have any advice for people within his constituency, but also for Canadians, on how to best prepare young people for the evolution of technology?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his great question.

As I said in my speech, it is important to recognize that mental health is influenced by many factors. Social media cannot be held responsible for all the problems young people face. As parents, as elected officials, we must assess all of the risks associated with digital spaces and ensure that the challenges that young people are already facing are dealt with on a daily basis.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague said that he spoke with constituents in his riding. Can he tell us more about the response from parents? What feedback did he receive in those discussions?
Mr. Speaker, that was the first event I held in my riding this year in relation to the two bills. I am talking about Bill C‑36 and Bill C‑34.

I was surprised by the response I received from my constituents when I launched the call to consult the people of Mont-Saint-Bruno—L'Acadie. The response from parents was overwhelming. I even had some other local elected officials show up to share their point of view and explain why it is important to quickly implement these bills.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising, of course, to say that in relation to Bill C-34, which would enact the digital safety act, I want to vote for it, I want it to get through second reading and I want it to get to committee, but I am not wildly enthusiastic about the bill.

I am desperately upset and nervous. I hear from all my constituents. I have to say, I hold a lot of community meetings in my riding of Saanich—Gulf Islands. In nine different locations, in a compressed period of time, I saw hundreds of people between Labour Day and when Parliament resumed. At every single one of those meetings, constituents expressed concern about amounts of screen time, about how to protect kids and particularly about artificial intelligence.

From the time we first started looking at this kind of legislation with Bill C-63 to now, looking at Bill C-34, the inclusion of chatbots in this legislation reflects the degree to which the government recognizes that it is not just that kids are being exposed to horrible images. Kids, and seniors for that matter, are tricked by fraudsters who may not be real people at all.

A real live human being, whether they are a troubled adolescent or a senior, can be drawn into deep harm by things that are accessible on websites and on platforms, or whatever we want to call them, and damage is done on gaming sites across the spectrum of what is available on the Internet. With what young people see, and the ways that it affects mental health, the harms that are done have outraged Canadians from coast to coast to coast and people around the world. We have already had many members reflect on the experiences in Australia, the U.K. and New Zealand, and other efforts by other jurisdictions around the world, other democracies, where there is outrage.

I think of the tech giants and the “tech bros”, as they are referred to, whether it is a Zuckerberg or a Sam Altman, as almost, in a historical sense of the growth of human civilization, a cancerous growth that is nothing but harmful. They do well for themselves, but they harm everything all around our society. The reality of their business model is that they harvest private information. They dive deep into our lives. They have damaged Canadian democracy. We should never have given up the digital services tax. We must find a way to try to extract back for Canadian society some of the damage they have caused, but in the meantime, the damage gallops ahead, and now we are looking very seriously, and heartbroken, at the loss of life of our children and the mental health crisis in a number of kids.

I would refer to speeches I have heard in this place, which were excellent, from people across the spectrum, like the hon. member for Lethbridge, who was one of the first speakers on Bill C-34; the member for Outremont, the parliamentary secretary; and just recently tonight, the member for University—Rosedale. Many of us speak not just as parliamentarians but as mothers and, in my case, as grandmothers.

I am, as I mentioned earlier tonight, enraged by what these corporate pirates have been able to get away with. Bill C-34 is a good-faith effort. I have met with parent groups that have self-organized, groups like Unplugged Canada, who say that if Australia can do it, we should too. It is true that Australia's ban for kids under 16 has not worked entirely; 70% of young kids under 16 in Australia are still accessing social media. Frankly, though, if 30% of kids who were on social media in Australia are off, that is better than nothing.

These places are dangerous. I would prefer not to call them “platforms”. Members may have heard me mention this before. We let them call themselves something novel, and in doing so, we allowed them to escape responsibility for what they do. We should have, as a society and across many countries, said, “Hey, you guys. You made up this name, 'platform'. What does it mean? You're a publisher, aren't you?”

If we called them publishers, there is abundant jurisprudence in common law for what to do with a publisher who publishes scurrilous and libellous content. The publisher and the originator of that content are jointly and severally liable, and that has been very effective in making sure that newspapers do not publish anonymous attacks that amount to libel. Instead, we have this sort of neutral term, “platform”, like it is friendly. That is what we thought at first, right? Facebook is friendly. We can make friends on Facebook.

Facebook has managed to evade a lot of basic legal principles. Getting past my outrage as a mom and a grandmother, I look back to my law school background and when I practised law. Where are the principles here from which we can draw some background knowledge, some tools that work? We are here as parliamentarians making laws, so I would like to rely on some solid background jurisprudence that works here.

Obviously, we know there are flaws in Bill C-34. I want to get it to committee. I think the largest flaw is the degree of unknowns in passing the piece of legislation. We do not know what the regulations will look like. We are giving a lot of power to an idea of a commission. It may be the best idea since sliced bread, but there is the digital safety commission and the notion that there will be digital safety plans and that they will be able to evolve things in a magical way that is not yet entirely described. It does not mean I am not going to vote for this at second reading, but it means I would like to see some buttressing.

I thank the Minister of Canadian Identity, who has been consistent since the bill was tabled in June in saying we are going to take time to study it. There are competing interests. Where are we on the civil liberties side? Where are we on groups like OpenMedia? Where are we with enraged parents, with Unplugged Canada? Can we not find some way to improve the legislation in committee to such an extent that we have societal consensus that this will work?

To do that, I started, again, looking at it like a lawyer, as I tend to do, and wondering why on earth we would decide to say, as the bill says at clause 85, “The purpose of a penalty is to promote compliance with this Act and not to punish.”

Why would we not want to punish a corporate actor, a private sector profit-making pirate? Why would we not want to punish them if their negligence leads to a child's death? I would like to punish them. Do we think these penalties are going to encourage compliance with the act? The maximum penalty is found at clause 88, at $10 million. To these guys, it is a slap on the wrist. It is the cost of doing business. I would like to make the legislation have some teeth that would guarantee that whatever platform or gaming or new device they dream up, whatever it is they put out there, they will think, “Uh-oh, we're in Canada. We'd better be careful. We can't allow a child to be harmed. If we allow a child to be harmed, that's catastrophic for our bottom line.”

There are ways to do that. I think one of them is to not say that the purpose of penalties is to encourage compliance. Let us say that the purpose is to punish the hell out of them, and if they, as corporations, think they are going to come into Canada and not understand the duty to protect children, again, let us look at our precedents.

We have a lot of laws on consumer protection. The member for Halifax earlier said it was like passing a law that said we had to wear seat belts. Well, guess what. It was illegal to sell a car that did not have seat belts. It was not just a slap on the wrist. One could not do business. If we are regulating a product that is inherently dangerous, and these social media platforms are inherently dangerous, we had better make sure we have teeth behind our regulation.

Here is a well-worn principle: strict liability. Let us attach strict liability to making sure that children are protected. Let us not just say “an operator” has a duty to protect children, but the directors of a corporation. Personal liability attaches to directors. At that point, we have their attention because maybe they are going to jail. Criminal negligence and strict liability are principles I would like to see added into the act when it goes to committee, as amendments.

We need to get this right. We need to move ahead. We cannot afford to wait. These companies will come up with new tools and new toys and new tricks. We cannot outsmart them, we cannot outrun them, but we can hold them to account.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that there are parents and grandparents in the House this evening.
I listened carefully to my colleague. She said that some improvements are needed.
Can my colleague clarify what changes she would like to see to improve Bill C‑34?
Mr. Speaker, yes, I have a lot of ideas and I hope to be able to propose amendments in committee, especially when it comes to punishing social media platforms. Furthermore, there are precedents.

I want to mention quickly that if we look at what we do with anti-spam legislation in Canada, that is attaching to directors their behaviour. If they are aware of this conduct and they direct it, they are personally liable. That is the kind of thing that really gets their attention.

Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to my colleague's speech. She talked about young people's mental health. I think that all of us parliamentarians share this concern, or else we would not be here at this late hour debating Bill C-34. We know that excessive use of social media, the bullying that young people can suffer online and the risk that young people may be exposed to harmful content online are all factors that can affect mental health. I also believe that we must all work together to find ways to address this issue as much as possible.

I heard my colleague mention the importance of this bill. However, she has some concerns and questions that she would like to see explored further. I gather that she is prepared to vote in favour of advancing the bill to the next stage.
I would like her to talk about the importance of committee work for a bill like this. Why is it important to conduct a thorough study of the bill in committee?

Mr. Speaker, it is very important for the committee to have time to really study the bill, without closure or time limits. First, the committee needs to listen carefully to the witnesses and take the time to draft the best possible bill. That is why it is so important not to rush things. It is important to take the time to reflect carefully and draft the best possible bill.

Mr. Speaker, one important aspect of the bill is establishing an independent commission on online safety. This commission will be tasked with reviewing the platforms' safety plans free from any political interference. It will therefore fulfill various roles to ensure that our young people are protected online.
I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on that. What does she think of the commission proposed in the bill? Does she see that as a step forward?
Mr. Speaker, the idea of the commission is not a bad one, but it is still very vague.

There is also the issue of independence. The commissioner will be chosen by the government or the minister of the day, draw a government salary and implement the government's policies. It is therefore not entirely clear that the commissioner will remain fully independent.
However, that is not the main problem. In my view, the problem is that we have an extremely important duty to protect Canada's children and youth.

It should be with the possibility that if they violate that duty to protect our children, they are going to suffer consequences so severe that they are highly motivated to ensure that their conduct avoids harm to children.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise today in the House of Commons to speak on Bill C-34 on behalf of the good people of Scarborough—Woburn.
I want to acknowledge that we are having a consultation process on Bill C-34 on Friday and I want to thank all the participants in advance for agreeing to join that discussion.

The times are changing. We have seen, and I have seen, much change over the last few decades here in Canada. It did not seem so long ago when we would spend half a day in a music store going through CDs, identifying a couple of CDs, picking them up, going home and listening to them, or going off to Blockbuster on a Saturday afternoon, finding a few DVDs, picking up some popcorn and going home and making a complete night out of it. Times have changed. Back then, there was technology. We had cellphones. We were lucky if we had a flip phone that could maybe send a text message. The most advanced technology on that was maybe playing the snake game on it. That was pretty advanced technology.

However, we are in a world today where everything seems to be instant. There is such an abundance of content and unlimited choice. We are in a world of constant creation. So much has changed over the last few decades. Now most people have cellphones, tablets, some have virtual reality, smart watches, notebooks. These things are mobile. We can go out there and use them anytime. AI and processing power have increased so drastically and with that we have seen some incredible changes in society, and some of those have become incredible challenges.

Everyone is impacted by these challenges, but I want to talk a bit more about and focus on gen Z. It is the age group that seems to be highly impacted, of course, not only with respect to this legislation, but also the advancements in technology.

Bill C-34 is designed to protect young Canadians in online spaces, and to ensure that social media services and AI chatbots are safe by design. More specifically, it would ban social media for youth and children under 16, unless the service can demonstrate that it is safe. Platforms would be able to submit applications to the new digital safety commission to become exempt from the ban if they can demonstrate their product is safe for children. It would establish a new safety commission to ensure that platforms have safe policies and hold them accountable. There would be age verification, safeguards, a faster removal process for harmful victimization content and, of course, financial penalties.

This is a different type of legislation than we have seen in other jurisdictions. Some members have mentioned Australia. I want to thank the members on all sides of the House, because this has been a really incredible debate to talk about the future of Canada, especially when it comes to our children. Australia introduced legislation, but this is very different, because it attempts to work with platforms to ensure their product is safe. If they can prove that, young people would be allowed to use it. If they cannot, it would not be available to them.

We know there has been a constant increase in screen time for young people over the last few decades. Adolescents are spending literally thousands of hours a year online. The Canadian Paediatric Society and the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines recommend a maximum of two hours per day of screen time for young people between the ages of five and 17, one hour per day for young people between three and four, and no screen time under the age of two. However, according to recent data from StatsCan, more than half of Canadian children and youth exceed those daily recommended limits, and the average hours of usage are between five and seven hours today. We know there is a direct correlation between the amount of time a young person is online and things like mental health and the stress levels young people feel. Many colleagues have talked about this today. The more screen time, the more stress young people have. Sleep patterns and regulation get altered with increased screen time. We also know that platforms are using very sophisticated algorithms and AI chat boxes that can cause significant harm to young people.

We all have a role to play. As lawmakers, we have a role and there are many things we can do, in addition to Bill C-34, to better position our young people for success. We know that Bill C-34 would, if it passes in the House, be put in place to protect young people online. The spaces we are talking about are online spaces. This is no different, if we really think about it, than how we protect young people at playgrounds. We make sure that playgrounds are safe. They are designed to be safe so young people, when they are using the equipment, are safe from harm. We have to design our online spaces the same way. We need to protect our children by making sure that those online spaces are designed so young people can find success.

Parents have a role to play. We need to make sure that parents are restricting and monitoring how much screen time a young person has. I asked my youngest daughter before I left to come to Ottawa if she could show me how much screen time she had this week. I am not going to mention it because that is her personal business. It was interesting to reflect on those numbers.

In addition to that, we can rely on our educational systems, the curriculum and pedagogy that is out there that goes to protect young people through digital literacy. This is an important piece as well. We need to make sure that digital literacy is at the forefront of this and that we put in place the best types of tools to protect young people.

We know that if we jump online, any of us in this room, and we start going down a rabbit hole based on one or two choices, 30 minutes later we can be in a world that we did not want to be part of and we wonder how we got there. It has happened to every single person. In addition to what we can do as society members, as not-for-profit faith groups and as educators, the government is really looking for ways to better position Canadians for success.

Bill C-34 is just part of a larger group of pieces of legislation that the government has come forward with to help better protect Canadians. Bill C-36 would protect privacy. It relates to deepfakes and AI. Bill C-16, which I believe we passed in June, is the Protecting Victims Act. It protects us, at the end of the day, from the non-consensual sharing of intimate AI-generated deepfakes. Bill C-25 has to do with our democracy: the Strong and Free Elections Act focuses on federal election rules and the use of AI.

In addition to those bills, I introduced a private member's bill in May of this year, Bill C-277. I believe this bill can play an important role in the challenges we have when it comes to artificial intelligence, chatbots and the use of deepfakes. The bill would regulate the online use and dissemination of deepfakes. It would increase transparency and better protect Canadians from serious harm in the digital age. The bill responds to a growing risk posed by artificial intelligence and emerging technology manipulation.

At the core of this bill, Bill C-277, it acknowledges that we, as Canadians, as humans, have the right to our own image, our voice, our face and our likeness, and it puts the onus on technology companies to identify artificially created deepfakes that are online. We own our own images. Labelling can be used to ensure that people, when they see a label, know something is fake, but there is also the ability for us to have that information removed.

In conclusion, Bill C-34 would move our society forward when it comes to placing well-thought protections in place to support the health and well-being of young people. We must remind ourselves that we all have a role to play. We must ensure that young people can benefit from technology without being exposed to its most harmful consequences. This means establishing the appropriate safeguards, which Bill C-34 would do.

Technology will continue to evolve, artificial intelligence will become more powerful and the digital world will become even more deeply integrated into our lives. It is our responsibility to ensure that our laws, institutions and communities evolve with it.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Karim Bardeesy (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I really appreciated my colleague's speech.

In our riding of Taiaiako'n—Parkdale—High Park, we held a round table, as well as a round table with the member for University—Rosedale. The member mentioned a gathering he is hosting in Scarborough—Woburn on Friday. I wonder if he could share more details about why he has chosen to engage parents in this way and what he expects to hear.

Mr. Speaker, I have the best constituency team in the country. There are incredible people working in my office, and they have engaged with psychologists, doctors, educators, superintendents, youth workers and folks from faith groups. We are asking them to come and meet with us to go over pieces of this legislation and to get feedback. We will collect a bunch of data points, put them together and present it to the minister on behalf of the people in Scarborough—Woburn.
