It is a simple model that we have been using more and more. We just did one on the fresh water review. It seems to be a model we can use to make sure that the voices in our community are collected and presented back to the government.
Mr. Speaker, the member talked about the number of hours we are online, and I, too, would be afraid to look at my hours online.

Can the member expand on what he thinks would help to avoid some of the problems they had in Australia, where a lot of the youth are just going around this? How would Bill C-34 address any of the problems they had in Australia?

Mr. Speaker, this bill is different from what took place in Australia. In Australia, there was a complete ban. I think this bill is a realistic approach. We are not going to be able to just ban social media. It is not going to work. We are attempting to work with platforms to ensure that they put in place the right type of safeguards, and the onus is going to be on them to prove they are safe. If they are approved, then they will be open for young people to use. If they cannot reach those specific guidelines or safeguards, they will not be able to present their social media for use with young people in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we know that all parents sometimes experience unbearable stress because of the dangers that our children may be exposed to online. As a parent, I know that feeling.

To what extent can Bill C‑34 provide meaningful protection and a genuine sense of security for parents? Can my colleague provide parents with some reassurance and ensure that they are not misled by the opposition's use of this bill for political purposes?

Mr. Speaker, it is important for all members of the House to recognize that legislation is important. There is no question that legislation and law set the foundation of the tone and expectation of Canadians, reflected through the members they voted for in the House. This is an important element of our society.

When it comes to young people and the home, there is nothing that replaces guardians, parents, siblings, aunts, uncles, community members and neighbours when it comes to making sure that young people have what they need for success. The simple fact is that, if a young person is spending hours and hours each day online without the ability to go outside to play, interact and work with siblings to figure out problems in real time, it will pose a challenge for that young person. It is important that parents set children up for success by making sure that screen time is limited, and that algorithms and platforms are used in a responsible way, which is what this bill attempts to do.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Karim Bardeesy (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have the biggest companies on earth with the most sophisticated attention-holding technologies known to humanity, and we have a kid with a phone. There are the most dazzling, seductive, funny, curiosity-inducing images, texts and videos, and there is a family at the dinner table, hunched and shrouded in a blue glow, or there is a classroom of semibored learners. There is a predator, and there is a child on the other side of the world.

It is time to act for these families, kids and learners, and to start to rebalance the playing field just a little. It is time to do what one parent said at the round table the member for University—Rosedale and I co-hosted with SickKids and other stakeholders. She said she wanted her kids to discover who they are, who they were, before their algorithms told them.
This is the opportunity in front of us. This is why we are acting today. This is why we are acting now. This is why we are acting to get it right.

Many of us have had different journeys to this piece of legislation. Many of us have had different journeys to the House. It was the prospect of bringing this bill, and this measure, over the finish line that helped inspire me to run for office. As a parent and a new educator at what was then Ryerson University, in the late 2010s we started to see the kinds of things that are causing such concern today, and that have resulted in the bill before us.

I started a think tank that was then called the Ryerson leadership lab with colleagues Shoaib Ahmed and Sam Andrey. We decided to test what was happening in the world, what Canadians were thinking about the power of this technology and whether they wanted intervention on this. We did a survey. We put it out in 2019 in “Rebuilding Canada's Public Square”. This is seven years ago now, and already the appetite was there. In that survey, it was found that 60% of Canadians believed that government should intervene with social media companies to require that they fix the problems they created in our political system.

At that time, in 2019, social media companies were already amongst the least trusted companies in Canada when it came to doing what was in the best interest of the public. Seven years ago, 52% of Canadians already felt that they had little or no control over what they saw in their social media feeds. This was at a time when the social feed still had at least a bit of a chance compared to the algorithmic feed that has become so dominant in our feeds. I mentioned that 60% requested government intervention.

Just two years later, the number of Canadians went up 11 percentage points, with 71% of Canadians supporting government intervention with social media companies. Canadians were already seeing the hateful content, the harmful content, seven years ago and five years ago. Racialized Canadians were 33% more likely to encounter hate speech and 52% more likely to encounter racist content online than non-racialized Canadians.

Already, years and years ago, Canadians were telling us, Canadians were telling each other, young people were telling their parents and educators were telling parents that there was a problem, that these technologies were too powerful, that the machines guiding these technologies were too powerful and that we needed to act. Governments slowly attempted to do so.

In the meantime, in that period of time, the information, the technologies and the research became even more convincing. From the social scroll to the infinite scroll, there is perhaps no more powerful tool in the world to monetize our attention, that most scarce resource, that most precious resource. New features were being added to social media platforms such as streaks, which was fun. I am going to click on this today, and I am going to click on it again tomorrow. I am going to click again, and someone will see that I saw them and I saw that they saw me. That is great.
There were GPS connections within social media feeds. Great, now someone can find me wherever I happen to be, even if I do not know who they are.

On the corporate side, what was happening? Trust and safety divisions were gutted. Content moderation was being rejected. The investment in the very AI tools that can be misused to make the existing tools even more dangerous was embraced by these companies. Companies were suppressing research, litigating or budgeting for the fines they would incur by failing in litigation. It was just a cost of business, as was attacking whistle-blowers.

This adoption of the AI technologies that are being used to supercharge what was already a dangerous platform is kind of like owning the drugstore, buying the cigarette company, and then putting those cigarettes back at the front of the store, but then spiking those cigarettes with crack cocaine made in the pharmacy.

The combination of social media and AI technologies was used in a potent way to monetize the worst forms of attention-seeking and of attention-grabbing content. This was the fundamental objective and the fundamental economics of the platform. The discovery pieces from the lawsuits coming in from the United States thankfully revealed that this was being used in a systematic way by platforms and continues to be used, in the case of X, or Twitter, to monetize our attention and to cause many of the harms we see in front of us.

Meanwhile, what was the research telling us about about the kids, and what were kids and teenagers telling us? Very importantly, we were learning that the time of greatest vulnerability coincided with important life stages and that these differed by sex. For girls, the time of greatest correlation between social media use and lower life satisfaction was between the ages of 12 and 14, during those very key puberty adolescent years, and again at age 19, which is often the age when they take on higher education. For boys, the association between lower life satisfaction and increased social media use was highest between the ages of 15 and 17. Again, this correlates with their journeys through pubescence and adolescence, and into adulthood.

The platforms knew this, and they took advantage of this to feed teens the very content that got them further hooked to these platforms, to their business models. Parents were at a loss. Parents were around dinner tables. Students, including the university students I was teaching at that time, were telling us that they were addicted and hooked to this content. They wanted alternatives they could not find. Policy-makers started to act. We started to act. Just in this Parliament in the last 12 months, as new MPs, we started to act.

At the gathering the member for University—Rosedale and I co-hosted, we heard from Coleen Dudley from The Neighbourhood Group, a peer educator who was telling us about the solutions we needed to find. We heard from Jessica Besser-Rosenberg from Unplugged Canada. We heard from Dana Cramer from the Young Digital Leaders of Canada. We heard from the leaders who are on the front lines of these issues saying that it is time to act, that there are solutions available and that we must act.

Recently, at the Attention conference at McGill, we heard Alex Munter of the Canadian Medical Association compellingly say that a parent's no has no power because of the power of the biggest social media companies in the world and their biggest technologies. We heard from Ravi Iyer that AI-empowered chat bots are doing such a good job of easing the way into a false sense of socialization for kids, that kids are losing the ability to have the frictions that are required to develop social learning. Recently, we heard from Suki Huang, a youth champion at The Dais, who told us that the youth did not choose this system, but they feel that they need to be on social media.

What alternatives are available to those kids? I think a complementary piece of work that we and the government have to be doing around news literacy is figuring out, if kids are not present on social media platforms, how they can get that news from other places. We need to put forward efforts to help them touch grass, enjoy the off-line world and be able to gather all those pieces.

This bill, Bill C-34, is a culmination of the work that is a response to all those things I mentioned. I want to salute the former occupant of this seat, the hon. Arif Virani, former Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada, who brought a bill forward beforehand. There are so many aspects of this bill that are important, such as the requirement to file digital safety plans, the requirement to publish those plans and the requirement for the commission to review them. This would not just protect kids; this would protect all of us, because if the digital safety plans and the design features that need to be improved would be improved with a push from this bill and from the commission, which would need the crucial flexibility to adapt to changing technologies, then we would have a safer online space, not just for teens, but for everyone. There would be the requirement of a resource person to address user concerns. How nice that would be. Who has tried to reach out to a social media company and been deterred?

We have learned so much over the last six to seven years. We have been able to experience and expose the harms that have been created. It is time to take our agency back. It is time to reclaim a greater share of digital sovereignty for Canada. It is time to claim a share of our humanity back. It is time to act now, and protect not just the kids, but everyone in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the member raised how racism and hate speech are definitely deplorable and should be prevented and punished. That said, how does the member opposite see Bill C-34 determining what qualifies as free speech and hate speech? Who would be qualified to make those determinations going forward with Bill C-34?
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate and identify with many of the desires of the freedom of speech and the fundamental protections that exist in the charter.

We have provisions in our hate crimes legislation that are very clear about the difference between, for instance, speech that seeks to vilify or dehumanize and other forms of speech. I believe the existing pieces of legislation we have will be looked at closely by the digital safety commission, just as they are looked at by any police service that has to enforce them.

Mr. Speaker, I do not have any children of my own, but I am an uncle and a godfather. These children will grow up facing risks that we never had to confront as children. As legislators, we must understand that and implement a regulatory framework that ensures our children's online safety.
Could my colleague explain why it is important to act now and how Bill C-34 represents a significant step forward in protecting children in the digital world?
Mr. Speaker, as it stands, parents and teenagers themselves lack the necessary tools.

Two or three years ago, my family met with other parents in our neighbourhood to share advice on how our four families could work together to help our children deal with these issues, while also helping us as parents navigate them.
Teenagers and children are not the only ones affected by social media and its ability to connect us with others and share information.
In my view, the commission will be responsible for providing guidance to parents and families, and the bill itself does a great deal to help parents.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for his remarks. I know they come from a place of really wanting to do right by our youth, and I know that is a goal we all share.
I am wondering if the member can define what an adequate safeguard is.

Mr. Speaker, there are going to be lots of places that do that, like through the commission and through the regulations that may come out of the act. I think it is important to have transparency. We do not have transparency at the moment. In fact, we have had the opposite of transparency. We have had the intentional obfuscation or intentional suppression of what some of these platforms are doing.
I believe that this legislation and the commission's actions, in particular the filing of digital safety plans, will force a levelling up that will bring more transparency to these things.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to my question, my colleague began talking about the new digital safety commission of Canada that this bill will establish. I would like to give him the opportunity to elaborate on why he thinks setting up this commission is a positive step forward.

Mr. Speaker, anything we can do to reduce people's dependence on social media will be helpful. The commission's role is to publish research and review social media platforms' plans. In my opinion, the commission will enable us to help social media platforms be more positive and earn people's trust.

Mr. Speaker, I start my speech, as many members have, with thoughts of my children. I have a 10-year-old son and an eight-year-old daughter, who are hopefully asleep by this point in the debate. I am living in this wonderful spot where they still like hanging out with their dad and do not have the device that many of us have in our pockets, with constant unfiltered access to the Internet. Having seen this debate before and having many colleagues and friends who have children who are older, I am afraid, like many Canadians. I am afraid of what will happen in a few years with the conversation when they ask, “Can I have a phone?”

That conversation is coming. It is coming for all of us as parents. It is worrisome. We have ready access to the world in our pockets. I am old enough to remember the promise that this would be an enormous blessing, that it would be incredible for our society. In many ways it is, but in so many ways it is a curse. Like all of us in this place, I have talked to so many parents who are worried and who are afraid.

When I was thinking about what I was going to say today, I was taken back to the last Parliament when I was on the justice committee, and we were doing a prestudy of Bill C-63, which was a previous iteration of online harms legislation. The topic was so important that despite a filibuster going on in the House, it was important for everyone at the justice committee to discuss it. I have been through a lot of difficult bills and studies in this place at committee, and I have to say that that one was the hardest by far. We had witness after witness and parent after parent who tried, who did everything they could, but whose son or daughter is no longer with us. They were children who felt trapped and cornered in these online spaces.

We can talk about or suggest there was bad parenting, but these were parents who were paying attention. It should not matter, because our kids should be safe. We want our kids to be safe in all the spaces they occupy. I do not know that any member can stand up here today and say, and I am not suggesting that anyone has, that they are safe, because they are not.

As the previous member said, these algorithms are dangerous. They take our kids to dangerous places. It was shocking to me that the algorithm knows. If someone is inclined to an eating disorder, it will show them people who are inclined to that particular affliction. If someone is inclined to hate speech, it will show them that as well, because the goal is to keep us focused on our phones as much as possible. It is the goal of the algorithm, and it is powerful.

Having dealt with these social media companies, these big tech companies, through various bills, whether it was the Canada Elections Act, the Online Streaming Act or the various digital bills we have passed and debated over the years that I have been here, one thing has been certain to me: These companies do not care. These American tech giants do not care and have contempt for this place.

I have watched them too many times come to parliamentary committees, be evasive, not answer members' questions and have a complete disregard for what we are doing. These companies are so powerful that they can ignore a parliamentary summons. We are still waiting for Mark Zuckerberg to appear from a previous parliamentary summons. I do not think those carry over, but he was summonsed. He did not care; he did not have to. It does not matter. That was Meta.

Google was slightly better before the heritage committee. Its representatives would come and be evasive. They would do their few minutes and move on. They did not care about the safety of Canadians. They even set up an astroturf campaign over one of our bills, with a fake individual who was arguing on behalf of artists. He had no members. He was just receiving money from Google and Meta, I believe. Basically, he was an unregistered lobbyist whom we caught lying to the heritage committee. Google did not care. It denied ever being behind it, even though this person testified he was receiving money from the company.

To them, a bunch of kids dying is the cost of doing business. I hope that shocks all of us. I think it does. Having listened to many of the speeches here today, I hear there is a willingness to do something. It is important for Parliament to debate what that is, but it is shocking to see across the border the lack of willingness of our American friends and neighbours to regulate these companies, to rein them in.

I do not know about everyone here, but I am tired of the harm. I am tired of the stories. Recently, a colleague of mine asked me to stop by a reception at the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, which does incredible work, against all odds, and is based in Winnipeg. We talked to parents who feel that their backs are against the wall and who have lost kids or had kids kidnapped. One of the parents had their child kidnapped through readily available software that was accessible in the child's school. When I look to these parents, they look to us and ask what Parliament is doing. We need to act.

I hear from members of this place that we should let parents parent, that it is not for the government to step in. I can appreciate that this is coming from a good place, but these companies are so powerful. Parents are busy. It is easy to let kids have some screen time. They cannot be over their shoulder 24 hours a day. The rabbit holes they can go down are incredibly dangerous and can lead to their deaths. Whether it is extortion leading to suicide, kidnapping, or all the horrific stories we have heard, we need to step up.

We have a willingness to act, but it is shocking to me, and I hope it is shocking to everyone, having watched these companies do nothing, that we need to impose duties upon them: the duty to protect, the duty to act responsibly and the duty to make content inaccessible. They make so much money off of this. It should be shocking to all of us, to all Canadians, that Parliament needs to step up and say to these social media companies that they need to do the right thing, because they have been absent for so long.

A member from Scarborough at our committee asked a Google executive, when Google came up, about a sign on the wall at its headquarters. It said “Do no evil”, which was probably mocking Microsoft. Google took down that sign. It was too embarrassing.
I hope that we have a good debate, that we move forward with this legislation and that the committee has an excellent discussion about what moves forward next, because we owe it to our kids.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his heartfelt speech. He spoke about the importance of Bill C-34, which seeks to keep children safe online. I think this is a good example of a bill where all political parties must work together. As parliamentarians, we all need to be mindful of this issue.
Does my colleague think it is important for the government and the official opposition to vote in favour of the bill at second reading so that we can study it in committee?
Mr. Speaker, absolutely, the bill needs to get to committee.

I have been here a couple of years, and I have not seen a bill this size go through unamended. I imagine the committee will hear a lot of the same heart-wrenching stories that I heard, and I hope this compels committee members to act as quickly as possible. I do not envy them. I would not want to go through it again, but it is important work that Parliament will do. I know that every member of the House wants to protect our kids, but Parliament needs to act, government needs to step up and we need to do better for our children.

Mr. Speaker, I am assuming the bill will go to committee. When it gets there, what does the member see as the division, the line, between, on the one side, what is going to help protect our children and, on the other, free speech?

I am lucky that my daughters are both in their twenties now. I cannot really worry too much about them, but I do worry about the future, when I hopefully have grandchildren. Over 10 or 20 years, things are changing rapidly. How can this legislation be lasting and actually have a long-term future?
Mr. Speaker, to be honest, I am envious of the hon. member, and I hope I can find a way to jump my kids to that point through these difficult times.

The member keeps talking about free speech, which is fundamentally important and protected by the charter. To paraphrase, I think it was Jon Stewart who said that social media is to free speech like twinkies are to food. It is highly processed garbage. The algorithm is controlling what we see and what our kids see. We cannot just wave this away as free speech and hope the social media companies will do the right thing, because we have seen, for too many years, that dead kids are okay to them and part of their business model.
The committee will meet and do important things. Amendments will be made, and we will get to the best possible legislation we can, but we need to get the bill there as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I listened intently, and I really appreciate the concerns the member brought up. Our children's safety is paramount, and he talked about how scary it is when they go into a different world when they are online.

One of the things Bill C-34 would do is create the digital safety commission, which would allow us to make sure we are protecting our children. Can the member elaborate on some of the things the commission would have and how important it is?

Mr. Speaker, it is important to have a regulator with some teeth. Again, we can talk about letting parents parent and about the concerns about free speech, which are genuine and need to be discussed in this place, but in the absence of a regulator to enforce the bill and to hold companies to account, it is going to be a challenge. These are powerful companies that are going to do whatever they can to water down this bill. I have seen it before, but we have to do our best to provide actual concrete protections for our children, and I believe the commission would do that.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be here this evening, hearing from my hon. colleagues in this debate on this important topic, which is one that speaks to me very directly as the father of a young child.

I rise to speak in favour of the safe social media act. During debate tonight, we have heard extensively about the merits of the bill, and I echo many of those sentiments. I will speak to the legislation in a moment, but I wish to reflect first on the nature of the digital world that our children today inhabit, which is fundamentally different from that which most of the members of the chamber grew up in, in some cases just a few short years ago.

I have worked with young people since I was a young person. As a teenager and as a young adult, I worked with children and youth across Canada in after school programs, in summer camps and as a member of the Royal Canadian Army Cadets. For days and weeks at a time, we would hike, camp, swim, march, paddle, bike and climb. Endless hours were spent outdoors, in nature, interacting with our peers face to face, with nary a cellphone, touchscreen or digital device to be seen. Later in my career as an academic, a university professor and an educator, I worked with thousands of young adults pursuing post-secondary education without ever having heard the words “generative AI”, or “ChatGPT”.

I confess that I am an elder millennial, so I remember when dial-up Internet first arrived in my family home, and I remember as a late teenager getting my own first cellphone, which flipped open, could display two colours and was decidedly not smart. The hon. member for Scarborough—Woburn stole my joke about the snake game earlier, so I will move right along.

Today, at this stage in my life, it is a great joy but also a great worry to be father to an extraordinary almost 11-year-old daughter, who is growing up in a world that is not only different from the one that I was raised in but is meaningfully different even from the one the hon. generation Z members of the House experienced, as I said not long ago. The reality is that today's children are growing up in a world fundamentally different from that of previous generations. The Internet has become woven into nearly every aspect of their lives, even if they do not yet have a device.

Online is where young Canadians learn, connect with friends, explore interests, create content and engage with the world around them. It is also where they spend vast amounts of their time and attention, consume misinformation and disinformation, encounter strangers, discover pornography and experience a range of negative social experiences, including isolation, bullying, exploitation and in some cases, sexual and psychological abuse.

We know that the digital world offers tremendous opportunities, but we must also confront the difficult truth that for too many children, the online world is a place of significant risk. Data that has been widely discussed in debate this evening shows that 52% of Canadian teens have received unwanted sexual images online, while 44% report being pressured to send sexual photos. In 2023 alone, police in this country reported nearly 19,000 incidents of online child sexual exploitation, representing a 500% increase since 2014.

Clearly, this goes in tandem with the massive explosion of social media in our society, and we know that young people who experience bullying and victimization online are three times more likely to contemplate suicide. These are not just statistics. They represent real families, real children and real communities dealing with the consequences of online harms from an underregulated, corporate-controlled Internet that does not have their best interests in mind.

We know that these harms are also evolving rapidly. The rise of artificial intelligence, conversational chatbots and increasingly sophisticated digital platforms presents new opportunities but also new risks, which our laws have not fully addressed because they were not designed to do so. Parents, educators, advocates and experts are clear: Children's safety online cannot be an afterthought any longer.

As legislators, we have a responsibility to ensure that our laws keep pace with the digital world and provide meaningful protection for young Canadians. This is exactly what the safe social media act seeks to achieve. At the heart of this legislation is the simple principle that digital platforms, and the tech companies that own them, must take responsibility for protecting children who use their services.

For too long, responsibility has fallen primarily on parents, teachers and young people themselves to navigate systems that were never designed with the well-being of children in mind. This bill would change that. It would establish a clear duty to protect children that applies to regulated social media services and chatbots. Rather than waiting for harm to occur, platforms would be required to proactively design and operate their services in ways that prioritize the safety of younger users. This represents a fundamental shift in approach. Children's safety would not be optional. It would not depend on whether a company or its foreign owner chooses to act. It would become a baseline expectation for those companies to operate in Canada.

Importantly, the legislation recognizes that children are not all the same. The social and emotional development of a 12-year-old differs in meaningful ways from that of a 16-year-old. That is why, instead of a one-size-fits-all approach, the safe social media act would allow for flexible, evidence-based requirements that can evolve alongside technology and keep up with emerging online risks.

The legislation would establish important protections regarding access to social media and digital content, and I wish to highlight five, in brief, in particular. First, regulated social media services would be required to prevent children younger than 16 years old from creating or maintaining accounts unless the platform can demonstrate that it provides an appropriate, safe environment and qualifies for an exemption. This approach would create a strong incentive for companies to build safer platforms, while ensuring that children's interests remain at the centre of decision-making.

A second key aspect of the legislation is protecting children from exposure to pornographic content online. Under the bill, regulated services would be required to implement age verification or age estimation measures to ensure that individuals below the age of 18 cannot access pornographic content. At the same time, the legislation would rightly place a strong emphasis on privacy protection, requiring that any information collected for age assurance be limited, used only for that purpose and not retained any longer than necessary.

A third important feature of the bill is recognizing that social media is no longer the only digital environment where children spend their time. Increasingly, young Canadians interact with artificial intelligence systems and chatbots. While these technologies can offer certain benefits, they also present unique challenges. There have been troubling reports of chatbots promoting self-harm, encouraging harmful behaviours, providing inappropriate content, fostering unhealthy dependence and even inciting individuals to violence. A most egregious example of this is the unspeakable tragedy that occurred at the start of this year in Tumbler Ridge in my province of British Columbia. My heart still goes out to all the families affected by that horrible event.

This is why the safe social media act would extend to chatbot services. These services would be required to act responsibly by mitigating the risks of communicating harmful content and by implementing crisis intervention protocols when users express intentions to harm themselves or others.

Fourth, the legislation would address specific categories of content that can have devastating consequences for children. This includes content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor of sexual violence, content that induces a child to self-harm and content used to bully a child. The other parents in the chamber and parents watching at home will know how pernicious cyber-bullying is and how devastating it can be for our children. Simply put, social media platforms currently amplify and monetize harmful behaviour. When this happens to a young person, the effects can be severe and long-lasting.

Finally, the legislation includes strong accountability measures. The new digital safety commission would play an important role in ensuring accountability, handling complaints, strengthening protections and promoting online safety awareness across Canada.

Ultimately, the bill is grounded in a simple belief that we have overlooked for far too long: that children deserve to be safe online. The safe social media act would establish a modern framework that recognizes both the opportunities and the risks of the digital age. It would create clear expectations for platforms, introduce proactive protections, address emerging technologies and place the safety and well-being of children at the centre of our government's approach. Frankly, as a society, we should probably aim to have our children spend less time on the Internet, but as a society, we have a responsibility to ensure that when children are online, they are safe and protected from the harms that we know await them there.
I encourage my colleagues to support the bill as it moves through committee and comes before the chamber for a vote.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Wade Grant (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, like my colleague, I am a father of a young girl. She has grown up in the days of the digital age. This proposed act is one that will really be appreciated by parents like him. Why does he approve of this measure and how would it make him feel better as a parent as his daughter grows up?

Mr. Speaker, I shared this reflection earlier in response to a different question from a different colleague. At the moment, many parents across this country share these concerns. We know the dangers that await our kids on the Internet, and we are concerned in particular about increasingly young children having access to unfiltered information through the devices that are increasingly common in their classrooms.

Having parents bear the responsibility to monitor their children's Internet use, but also to control their access to digital devices, really does individualize this problem. It makes it a problem for individual families and for individual parents. As all parents know, our kids are extremely good at placing pressure on us to come to their preferred outcome or decision.

By having strong regulations at the national level, by having a national framework around social media use for young Canadians, individual families would no longer have to make this choice. As a society, we would draw a line and say that enough is enough.

Mr. Speaker, as a gen X-er who has two daughters who are gen Z, I often found myself learning from my children how to navigate social media content. Maybe we should actually be listening to some of the gen Z who have gone through this transition with us. I am wondering what kinds of benefits or protections they can offer in their transition, because they have lived this through their life. Of course, they are not the ones we are aiming this for at this point in time, but maybe the member can give me some insight on what he thinks of their contribution.

Mr. Speaker, certainly we have much to learn from Canadians of different ages on this subject. We all have different relationships to technology depending upon our age. I do think there is much we could learn from members of gen Z, but I will say that as a generation that, in many instances, perhaps most instances, would have grown up with ubiquitous Internet and ubiquitous digital technologies in their life, gen Z may not be best placed to actually reflect upon how their experience of technology has differed from those of previous generations who did not have that access and whose relationship to the Internet was very different.

That said, I will note the speech earlier tonight from the member for New Westminster—Burnaby—Maillardville, who is a member of our generation Z caucus and one of the four 21st century babies in this chamber. We have heard from the younger members of our caucus directly based on his experience, which is shared, I am sure, by many others of his age. He spoke very strongly in support of this bill, as I am sure most members of generation Z would as well.

Mr. Speaker, platforms would be able to apply to the new digital safety commission for an exemption from the age ban if they can demonstrate that their projects are safe for children. I ask my colleague if he thinks this is the appropriate approach, rather than imposing a full ban, so that children can use social media if it can be demonstrated that it is safe to do so.

Mr. Speaker, absolutely, what we have before us is really the preferred outcome of having social media platforms that were hospitable and age-appropriate for young Canadians. We understand there are benefits from social media. This is not a blanket anti social media position. The problem, of course, is that at present, those platforms have content that is not appropriate for young people. If the platforms can clean up their act and have age-appropriate content, then there is no need to ban young Canadians from social media.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is great to be here this evening and debate Bill C-34, the safe social media act, a bill that I strongly support. Before I begin, I want to ask every member of the House to think just for a moment, not as parliamentarians but as parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles, teachers, coaches and mentors, whatever position they hold in relation to younger people. Think about the young person in one's life. Think about how different their childhood is from the one many of us experienced.

A generation ago, when the school bell rang, most bullying ended for the day. If a child was having a difficult time at school, home was often a refuge. There was a chance to step away, to breathe, to reset. Today, that is no longer the case. The playground follows our children home. It travels in their pocket. It sits beside their bed. It is there when they wake up in the morning and is often the last thing they see before they fall asleep at night. The comments, the likes, the notifications, the screenshots, the videos and the conversations continue long after the classrooms have emptied out.

I know this is true not just as a member of Parliament but as a father of three girls. I am a proud father of three girls but I also take the responsibility of keeping them safe very seriously. Over the past few years, as social media has grown in influence, concerned parents throughout my community of Whitby have shared similar stories. Some have watched their children become withdrawn and anxious. Some have found themselves dealing with the aftermath of cyber-bullying. Others have discovered that their children were being pressured to share intimate images or repeatedly exposed to content that no child should ever have to encounter.

What is most striking is that these parents often feel powerless. They try but they cannot monitor devices. They set rules and have conversations, but they are operating in an online environment that changes faster than any family can reasonably keep up with. It never stops.

My wife and I have tried to keep my 15-year-old daughter off social media. She does not have a cell phone, and that is an ongoing battle in our household. We have done that for a specific reason, which is to try to keep her safe, to keep her self-esteem high and to protect her mental health, realizing that she cannot always self-regulate, and that most kids are not able to self-regulate at such a young age. I know I was not able to do that with video games when I was a kid, and my parents gently encouraged me to get off the computer games at night. Social media is a whole new reality, and that reality is what brings us here today.

We need to make social media safer for our children and grandchildren. One of the things that has struck me most in those conversations with parents is that they are not looking for government to solve every problem in their child's life. They understand that raising resilient, thoughtful young people starts at home. They know there is no substitute for parenting, for open conversations around the dinner table or for teaching children how to navigate difficult situations. What they are asking for is fairness. They are asking why the responsibility seems to fall almost entirely on families while some of the most powerful companies in the world face so little accountability for the environments that they create.

Parents can set rules. They can limit screen time. They can talk to their children about making good and better decisions but they cannot redesign algorithms that are designed specifically to target them and that are almost impossible to counteract. They cannot rewrite recommendation systems. They cannot remove harmful content from platforms or build safer products. Those responsibilities belong rightfully with the companies that create those services. I think most Canadians would agree that if a company profits from the attention of young people, it should also have a responsibility to consider their safety.

The Internet has transformed our world in remarkable ways. It has connected families, opened doors to learning and created opportunities that previous generations could never have imagined. Our children are growing up in a world where communication, education, entertainment and community increasingly exist online. The challenge is not the technology itself. The challenge is that many of the safeguards we would expect to accompany that technology have not evolved at the same pace as the technology. The evidence of that gap is impossible to ignore.

More than half of Canadian teenagers report receiving unwanted sexual images online. Nearly half say they have felt pressure to send intimate images themselves. One in four young people between the ages of 12 and 17 report experiencing cyber-bullying. Police-reported incidents of online child sexual exploitation have increased dramatically in recent years. In fact, it is up 500% since 2014. Research consistently shows that young people who experience online victimization are far more likely to struggle with serious mental health challenges. I have a very active constituency youth council. Members of my constituency youth council often cite mental health issues as their top issue. It is no doubt that online involvement and things they encounter online are contributing to the youth mental health crisis across the country. When we look at those numbers, it becomes clear that online harms are not isolated incidents. They are affecting children in communities right across our country, including in my own community of Whitby.

What is also becoming increasingly clear is that these harms are not solely the result of individual bad actors. They are often amplified by the design of the platforms themselves. Many online services are built to maximize engagement. The longer users remain on a platform, the more valuable that engagement becomes. Recommendation systems continuously serve up new content. Endless scrolling eliminates natural stopping points. Autoplay features keep videos running long after the user intended to stop. For adults, these features can be difficult enough to navigate. For children and teenagers, whose brains are still developing, the impact can be far greater.

We need to remember that young people, as they develop, do not have the same self-regulation abilities that are developed in adults and this is the challenge that we experience. Even adults become addicted to online doom scrolling. We are all probably guilty of that in this place. My daughter often says to me, “Dad, you're always on your cell phone. You're always on social media, so why can't I?” I say to her, “Because you don't know how to regulate. I know how to put it down.” The reality of it is that she is right. We are all guilty of this. We all need to do a better job regulating ourselves. I think young people are more vulnerable and susceptible to not being able to control that urge and the online platforms are designed specifically to exploit that addictive behaviour that we see in most young people when they get online.

This is why Bill C-34 represents such an important shift in how we think about online safety. Rather than responding only after a child has already been harmed, the legislation asks for a fundamental question to be answered: What responsibilities should platforms have to prevent harm in the first place? At the heart of this bill is the duty to protect children. It recognizes that children are not simply smaller adults and that services used by millions of young Canadians should be designed with their safety in mind from the outset. That safety by design is a principle that is sound and straightforward, but it represents a significant change. For years, much of the responsibility has rested with parents, educators and children themselves. While those roles remain essential, there is growing recognition that platforms must also be accountable for the environments they create.

The expectation is not perfection. No legislation can eliminate every risk and no platform can prevent every harmful interaction. What Canadians are asking for is something much more reasonable. They want companies to identify foreseeable risks, take meaningful steps to reduce those risks and be transparent about the measures they have put in place. Bill C-34 would establish those expectations and obligations, and hold online platforms accountable. It would require regulated services to consider how their products affect children and build age-appropriate safeguards into the way those products operate. It would require companies to assess risk, publish digital safety plans and provide users with practical tools that help them protect themselves.

Most importantly, the bill would focus attention on some of the most serious forms of harm that exist online today. Specifically, it would entrench a duty to make that content inaccessible. Whether it is non-consensual sharing of intimate images, the sexual exploitation of children, persistent cyber-bullying, content that encourages self-harm, or material that promotes hatred, violence or extremism, Canadians increasingly expect platforms to take responsibility when their services contribute to those harms.

I will end it there, but I just want to say I am really proud to stand with a government that has put forward this legislation. It is a really essential topic for me and the constituents in my community, and it will help keep my children safe.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Wade Grant (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it always good to listen to my friend from Whitby. I know that he has three young daughters. I only have one young daughter, and I am always worried about her.
He has been talking about the worry he has. When we move forward with laws like this, how do they ensure that he and his daughters, and any future children he may have, are protected?

Mr. Speaker, as I said, we really want assurances. My wife and I have had many conversations about how to keep our daughter safe online. We have found it challenging to keep her off these devices and platforms. With no real regulatory framework in place in Canada, it just seems like it is the wild west of online engagement.

For my daughter's digital safety, we have had to take extreme measures to try to protect her, from taking away her devices to monitoring all online activity. She can be doing her homework late at night on a laptop, but she is really online on Snapchat or some other platform. The things we see that she has been exposed to make us really concerned. Some of her friends have been exposed to intimate images, which they have been encouraged to share, and that has created problems in her friend group.
This bill would hold the social media platforms accountable. It would put in place a mechanism and a set of responsibilities that would ensure my daughter's safety in the future.
Mr. Speaker, I admire the parenting the member has done. Abstinence from social media is virtually impossible these days for most parents. Even for mine, 15 years ago, it was a bit of a challenge.

Going forward, how does the member opposite see Bill C-34 addressing the concerns with how it would apply to different social media? He said the bill would make them responsible, but how are they going to know that it applies to them if they are a small start-up or a small influencer? How are they going to know that they would be affected? We assume it is good for the big ones, but what about the other ones out there?

Mr. Speaker, the bill would put in place obligations, which would be very clear, to have online safety plans. It would put in place a digital safety commission, which would oversee and monitor things, look for any infractions and understand that there are obligations for platforms to take down or make inaccessible images that are harmful. The bill would also codify the types of online harms in many ways.

From multiple perspectives, it would create a framework that would be useful in regulating online platforms. These platforms are innovating, developing quickly and continuing to evolve, so I imagine we would have to continue amending this legislation in the future. However, it is a significant step forward from where we are at today, where I fear for young people's safety online every single day.

Mr. Speaker, the member just described the “what” and the “how”, but I am interested in the “who”. How many platforms will this bill apply to? Which platforms will it apply to? How will those platforms know that the bill is meant for them?
Mr. Speaker, it would apply to all social media platforms, as I understand it.

I do not understand the nature of the question or where it is coming from. Maybe there is a sense of skepticism on the other side, but I think this bill has been written in a way to focus on the outcome that we want, which is to keep young people safe while they engage online. It would put in place a number of different safeguards and guardrails around that, and I think that is a positive step forward.

Mr. Speaker, as a society, we absolutely have to do something about the harm being done to our kids online. Parents are struggling. Teachers are struggling. Schools are struggling. Our youth are left navigating a world where the adults have not figured out how to adult on this one yet. I think we can all agree that the kids are not all right.

Parliament's constitutional authority over communications that cross provincial and international borders gives this chamber its mandate. A school board cannot regulate a multinational platform, and parents cannot demand design changes to apps, but having the authority to act, which we have here, does not make the problems any easier to solve. We do not know yet whether this bill can deliver the protection that parents and others expect, or whether it will inevitably result in the overreach its critics fear. Too many concepts in this bill remain ambiguous, and too many of the ultimate rules depend on decisions Parliament is being asked to authorize and delegate before Canadians can know what those decisions will be.

I have held multiple well-attended town halls on child and teen use of social media in my communities. I have spoken with lawyers practising across multiple disciplines. I have consulted with experts, teachers, parents and school board officials. There are a lot of opinions out there. People are just as emphatic that this bill must pass as others are that it will be a disaster if it does. The disagreements are passionate, and there are plenty of misconceptions and misperceptions as to what will happen and what things will mean. The way this bill is currently drafted makes it impossible to validate, course correct or reassure any side.

Supporters see children being sexually exploited and online feeds pushing harmful material at vulnerable kids. They want companies held responsible for products designed to keep children engaged, and they are tired of being told to supervise their kids more closely when they cannot control what a platform does. They put forward a compelling case for online safety measures and regulations.

Critics fear that enforcing the age restriction would mean collecting more information about everyone, including adults. They fear the regulator would have excessive control over lawful expression or that the information they provide online in proving their age would be used for other things. Here in this place, where we are ultimately responsible for the unintended consequences of sloppy drafting, we do not get to just dismiss concerns like these, even for legislation with a worthy purpose.

The Canadian Mental Health Association has recognized one of the paradoxes of the blanket age provisions in this bill. While supporting the bill, the association recognizes the inherent value of an online community, particularly for rural young people or those from marginalized communities. The reality is that the same service that can expose a youth to harm can also connect them to people who can help. A blanket account restriction leaves them without both, and it does not tell us where a youth may go next. If they move to a less regulated service, parents might find it harder to supervise. The government needs evidence that its approach will reduce harm overall, including for children and youth who work around the rules.

There is nothing in the under-16 restriction that would prevent a youth from browsing without an account, where harmful recommendations can still reach them. It also excludes private messaging features from the duties on social media platforms. The bill does not expressly require government identification to be used as proof of age. Parents need to understand these limits, just as critics need to distinguish what the bill says from what they fear it might become. The legislation would fix the age for access at 16 while leaving many of the actual safety requirements undefined.

Cabinet may decide which services are covered and which face account restrictions. A new digital safety commission would have the power to prescribe mandatory design features and additional requirements for age checks. These decisions are the ones that would determine the extent to which youth are actually protected and how much information adults must disclose.

The government points to exemptions as reassurance, but not everyone is reassured by them. Others do not think there should be any exemptions. A service could admit youth under 16 if the commission accepts that it has put “adequate safeguards” in place. I do not know what that means because the detailed test remains unwritten. What adequate safeguards are at this point is anyone's guess, and I can assure everyone that if we got a group of people together to discuss what adequate safeguards are, there would be a wide range of opinions.

I cannot reassure anyone at this point as to what the criteria might be or whether the criteria would be objective. A permissive test could undermine the protection that supporters of this bill expect. An onerous or delayed process could exclude children and youth from services that could safely accommodate them. There is no automatic expiry for restrictions described as temporary and no timelines for decision-making, and the bill would not guarantee that the exemption process will even be operating when restrictions begin.

Age checks are similarly unclear. If provisions can be easily evaded, this bill gives parents false reassurance. On the other hand, a system that misclassifies an adult as a youth can shut that person out of an app that they may be perfectly entitled to use. Limits on appeals and hard-to-navigate customer service processes on social media do not help. The bill would require personal identification to be protected and deleted after age verification or estimation, but we still need to know which methods would meet the standard and how mistakes would be corrected.

The bottom line is that Canadians should not have to choose between the most reassuring interpretation of this bill and the most frightening one. The government has made an already divisive debate worse in this case by leaving central definitions and central decisions unresolved. Those who trust government may assume the regulations would deliver the protection they want. Someone who distrusts it may fear the same powers would be used against them. Unclear drafting and unresolved processes turn a debate about a law into a test of confidence in whoever administers it.

Young people should be invited to testify at committee from all perspectives so we can hear from them what they need and what they are afraid of. This bill also needs measurable safety requirements and a workable exemption process before restrictions begin. Age checks need independent testing and accessible correction when they get someone's age wrong. Victims need a clear route to urgent help when a platform fails them, while people whose lawful material is wrongfully restricted need prompt review. Parliament should require evidence showing where harm actually falls, with a firm reporting deadline so the promised review cannot drift. What I meant by that is that we should have evidence of where there is actual harm. That should be reviewable and measured, and we should be taking appropriate action to correct it.

Conservatives are willing to help. I want to be able to explain this law to the people in my communities with confidence that the outcome will match the explanation. Social media companies and others governed by this bill need to know what success looks like and what the cost of failure would be. Contrary to the remarks of my colleague, not every social media platform or app would necessarily be governed by this bill. Every social media platform may have to review the bill to determine whether it is governed by it, but it is unclear at this point whether every app would be governed.

As the bill is written right now, too much information is either fuzzy or still to come. The government ought to bring those answers to committee and either reassure Canadians or accept recommended amendments. This is about our kids, which means that it is about nothing less than the future of our country. Let us get this right.

Mr. Speaker, in her introduction, my colleague mentioned the importance of protecting our children, yet she spent the next 10 minutes criticizing just about everything that we included in Bill C-34 to achieve that objective. This is hardly surprising, given her voting record.

Members will recall Bill C-22, a bill that police forces had called for to make our communities safer, something that the official opposition claims it wants. When it was time for the vote, the official opposition's position on the matter was unclear. As for Bill C-16, which was intended to improve protection for victims, the opposition said that was important, but when the vote was held, it voted against the bill.
This time, my question is simple: Will my colleague support referring Bill C‑34 to committee for a detailed study, or will she oppose it, as we have come to expect since she was elected?

Mr. Speaker, I am not entirely sure I understand my colleague's question, or it is possible that he did not understand my speech. What I just did is what I try to do with all of the legislation that comes before us in the House. I tried to read it. I tried to understand it. Where there was a lack of clarity, I have pointed that out and invited the government to correct the record and improve the bill so we can realize the very worthy objective of it, which is to protect our kids.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. colleague for her eloquent speech. There were a lot of things in there that people need to consider. I am wondering about the implementation of some of this. It seems to me that we would be relying a lot on this online safety commission to make and implement the rules.

One thing that came to mind during her speech was false accusations. She mentioned the appeal process. Can she speak further about how she sees that as a problem that is currently absent from Bill C-34? If somebody does not like something and reports it as hate speech or something when really it is not, then a person would have to go through the whole process to get put back onto the platform. Could the hon. member elaborate a little on that?

Mr. Speaker, I also have a lot of questions about the interpretation of how this bill would work. It has been really interesting because I have held town halls on this, and sat with groups in my community to discuss it, and we have had the chance in my community to think some of these things through. It is just unclear. A lot is being left to a process that would happen after the legislation. It is a process that parliamentarians do not typically have access to.

If my community members' concerns are to find their way into the bill, if the division and questions are to be resolved, then that is something that really has to happen in this chamber. I would invite the government to take these opportunities to listen to the questions being raised, to listen to what members of my community are saying, and to answer those questions and resolve those conflicts. It would result in better legislation.

Mr. Speaker, my question for my colleague is simple. If she supports the objective of this bill, will she support sending it to committee so that members of Parliament can thoroughly examine it, or will she oppose it at second reading? Will she support the bill at second reading, yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, the very first thing I said when I started my remarks this evening was that I support the goals of the bill. There is no one in this chamber from any party who does not support protecting kids or is not concerned about what is happening with kids online. The question here is whether or not the bill is clear enough. That is something that I expect would get debated at committee and something that witnesses would be able to provide information on.

What is somewhat distressing to me is that the government did not do these consultations upfront or did not incorporate the feedback it got into the bill so that these questions did not have to be asked.

Mr. Speaker, today, young Canadians are growing up in a digital world. They spend hours every day online, watching videos, connecting with friends, exploring ideas and posting memories of their lives. It allows them to connect, to create and to access information that was simply not possible just a generation ago. However, we must recognize a difficult reality: The modern online environment is not safe, especially for children.

Children and young people face risks online that are different from those faced by adults. Children are more vulnerable when exposed to harmful content. Increasingly, they are drawn into interactions that are targeted to their vulnerabilities, which escalate into anxiety, depression and even suicide. That is why the safe social media act has been designed to prioritize the protection of children online.

At the heart of this act is a clear principle: Platforms must take responsibility for protecting children, which applies across all regulated platforms. This includes social media and chatbot services. This duty is proactive, not reactive, and the act would establish clear and enforceable obligations by building safety measures directly into their design and operations, rather than responding only after harm occurs. This is a crucial shift from the current legislation.

Child safety is not an afterthought. It is not optional. It must become part of the standard when operating in Canada. A key pillar of the duty to protect children is an obligation to prioritize age-appropriate design, including features that protect children online. These may include default safety settings for younger users, tools that limit exposure to harmful or sensitive content, and controls that allow parents or guardians to care for younger users. Rather than relying on one specific solution, the act proposes a digital safety commission to work with experts, industry and Canadians to develop appropriate measures through regulations.

An important aspect of this is to recognize that children are not a single group. A 13-year-old, a 16-year-old and an 18-year-old do not interact with online services in the same way. Different age groups require different protections. This model is grounded in the realities of childhood development. To that end, measures should be implemented to ensure that children under the age of 16 cannot create or own accounts unless exemptions occur. This recognizes that some services, especially those built around open interaction and content sharing, may not be appropriate. At the same time, incentives for services that do innovate in safe environments must be enhanced.

A key protection in the act is children's exposure to pornographic content and ensuring that children under the age of 18 cannot access it. This type of content is explicit and is not appropriate for children. Parents should not have to worry about their children stumbling across it through social media or interacting with it via a harmful chatbot. Therefore, appropriate measures must be effective at reducing exposure, while also respecting user privacy. Hence, the bill emphasizes limiting the collection of personal information, ensuring that data collected for the purpose of age is used only for the purpose of age assurance, and ensuring that information is not retained. The bill acknowledges the need to protect children from harmful exposure, while also recognizing the importance of privacy and freedom of expression.

I also want to talk about artificial intelligence, which is becoming ever more prominent. Children are spending more and more time interacting with chatbots. Chatbots can pose unique risks to children, who are acutely vulnerable to techniques that encourage an emotional connection and trust. We have heard of incidents of chatbots sending sexually explicit content to underage users and promoting suicide or anorexia. By introducing measures that create safer interactions between children and chatbots, this bill would allow children to experience technology safely.

As such, across social media and AI chatbots, the bill would identify specific categories of harmful content that disproportionately affect more profoundly, and with lasting impacts, their well-being. This includes content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor, content that induces a child to harm themselves and content used to bully a child. Under this duty, regulated services would need to follow a specific protocol to make this type of content inaccessible on their platforms.

In parallel, the act also addresses content that induces a child to harm themselves. For example, this could include a social media post that encourages a minor to injure themselves physically to cope with stress. For children who are still developing emotionally and psychologically, exposure to this indoctrination can be especially harmful. This is particularly important in the context of emerging technologies that interact directly with users, respond to sensitive situations and influence behaviour.

Another critical area of concern is cyber-bullying. Social media platforms can contribute to the spread and escalation of cyber-bullying. The viral spread of hurtful posts can magnify the emotional impact on victims and can turn a single incident into widespread public humiliation. This type of content jeopardizes the ability of a child to fully express themselves online. To be clear, the definition used for bullying a child in the act targets content where there is an intention to threaten, intimidate or humiliate a child that could cause serious harm to their physical or mental health.

The commission would provide guidelines on understanding the threshold of content that is reasonably perceived as threatening, intimidating or humiliating. For example, a group of 16-year-olds might create an Instagram account devoted to mocking a student, including posting photos or making fun of their appearance and abilities to exclude them from social events. Such content can spread through reposting. In this example, the child being bullied online could experience long-lasting humiliation, social isolation and depression. The platform would have an obligation to reduce users' exposure to that content, breaking the cycle of engagement and exposure to harm.

The safe social media act would establish a comprehensive approach to protect children online. It recognizes children's vulnerability. It would set clear expectations and obligations for platforms. It would build a system that is proactive, adaptable and accountable. This bill would take meaningful strides to create a safer online world for young Canadians.

Children are spending more of their lives on the Internet, and we accept that. This bill does not intend to prevent children from having access to valuable information or positive social experiences online. The goal is to make the online environment as safe as possible for them to explore. The duty we share, all of us in this House, is to protect children. The act would do just that.

Mr. Speaker, I heard a lot in my hon. colleague's speech. He said that the act would this and that, but from my understanding, it is the goal of the act to do those things while leaving a lot to the commission to figure out how to actually get there. Maybe the member can explain to me how he sees the bill doing these things, rather than setting goals for the commission to do them without parliamentary oversight once the legislation leaves here.

Mr. Speaker, it is important for the House to set the tone and parameters by which we should proceed, but as with any other regulatory body, we would depend upon experts and those who execute the act to provide the appropriate parameters and safeguards to protect our children.

Mr. Speaker, I know the member spent a lot of time in the Ontario legislature, and of course education is a provincial matter. Beyond the goals and aspirations of this bill, what role can provincial governments play through the education system to help increase digital literacy to help prevent harm for young people?

Mr. Speaker, I have had the pleasure of working with my colleague over many years. I know that from his time as minister of children and youth, he has an acute awareness of the vulnerability that our children have. There are a lot of predators out there. We have a lot of activity that is lawful but awful, and we must do everything we are able to do through provincial authorities to ensure that the act is implemented to protect every child throughout Canada.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague mentioned the importance of ensuring effective online protection for children, while also safeguarding data privacy and the freedom of expression.
I would like to hear his thoughts on how this bill strikes the right balance between these concerns, while ensuring that children are adequately protected from online harms.

Mr. Speaker, it is important that every determination we make in the House abides by our Constitution and the right to freedom of expression. The act would not prohibit that. It is putting forward parameters to safeguard the most vulnerable in our society, who are underage, so they are not exposed to harmful incidents that predators are taking hold of at this time. Our expressions of freedom, the freedom that is enabled through our Constitution, will always prevail.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. colleague why it is important to act now. I think there was an expectation among the Canadian population to do that. When I speak with people in my riding, some are asking how we can better protect our children. There are some concerns about what they are seeing on social media, so I would like to hear his view on what he has heard in his riding and why it is important to act now with Bill C-34.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is correct in stating what is implicit in this act, which is that the duty and responsibility for children falls to their parents, but parents are looking for support. They are looking for ways that enable them to provide support. Colleagues and individuals have called me, like lawyers in the community who are extremely engaged and affluent in what they do. One has a wife who is the president and CEO of a major corporation in Ontario. They are concerned that their 11-year-old twins are being exposed to content that they do not always have the ability to oversee. This act would be a supplement to support parents as well.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to Bill C-34, the safe social media act, and to how we can protect our children online while preserving the rights, freedoms and privacy of all Canadians.

Before entering public life, I spent 26 years as an accountant. My work required me to examine details, identify risks and ensure that decisions were supported by sound evidence. In accounting, good intentions are important but they are not enough. If assumptions are wrong, controls are inadequate and accountability is missing, the results can be very different from what was intended. The same principle applies to this legislation.

When it comes to protecting our children, we cannot afford to get the details wrong. As a member of Parliament for a rural riding, I regularly hear from parents and grandparents, educators and community members concerned about what children encounter online. These are real concerns raised around kitchen tables and in school hallways by families trying to do what is best for their children. Canadians want to know how they will protect their children from online predators and prevent harmful content from reaching them, and how technology companies can be held accountable. They also want to know how we can address these problems without creating new ones. Those are questions the House must consider as Bill C-34 moves through Parliament.

The online environment has changed dramatically over the past generation. When I was growing up, a problem at school often stayed in the schoolyard. Today, an embarrassing picture, a cruel message or a video can be shared thousands of times in minutes. Cyber-bullying can follow a child home, strangers can contact young people directly and harmful content can appear without them ever searching for it. With the growing use of artificial intelligence, children are also interacting with chatbots without necessarily understanding the risks or consequences. These experiences have a devastating effect. Statistics Canada has reported that one in four Canadian youth aged 12 to 17 has experienced cyberbullying.

The question is not whether children deserve protection; they absolutely do. The question is whether Bill C-34 would provide the protection effectively and proportionately while respecting Canadian rights. Parents can set rules and supervise device use and teach their children about online dangers but they cannot control the algorithms that determine what appears on screen, prevent every stranger from making contact or remove harmful content from platforms used by millions. Tech companies have responsibilities too. If a platform encourages endless scrolling, recommends increasingly disturbing content and fails to respond adequately when children are exposed, Canadians deserve answers. Companies should explain what they are doing, how quickly they respond and how their results are measured. Conservatives believe that technology companies must be held meaningfully accountable for the environments they create.

Bill C-34 would propose requirements relating to safe design, age verification, harmful content complaints and transparency. It would also establish a digital safety commission of Canada to oversee and enforce those requirements. These are important objectives, but many practical details will depend on regulations developed after the legislation passes. What constitutes a safe design? How would effectiveness be measured? What evidence would demonstrate that children are actually safer rather than simply that the companies have changed their policies on paper?

After 26 years in accounting, I know that accountability requires clear standards, reliable information and a way to verify results. Should we not expect the same from legislation intended to protect our children?

We must also examine the proposed restrictions on social media accounts for those under 16. Australia's experience with age-based restrictions raised important questions about compliance, workarounds and young users moving between platforms. How can the government demonstrate that Canada's approach will produce better results?

We must consider whether young people will use virtual private networks or other technologies to bypass restrictions. If the goal is to protect children, we need to know whether these measures would reduce exposure to harm or simply push it elsewhere.
