We must also consider the scope of the legislation. Children face online risks through gaming, messaging, livestreaming, and, increasingly, through artificial intelligence tools, not just traditional social media. Parents have raised concerns about online games where children can communicate with strangers. Would these environments be adequately addressed? How would the government determine which services fall within the rules? How would it prevent children from migrating to platforms with fewer safeguards? These questions deserve answers before we assume that the proposed framework would solve the problems.

Protecting children and protecting privacy are not competing goals. We must be able to do both. If platforms would be required to verify users' ages, what information would they collect? Would Canadians need to provide government identification, biometric data or other sensitive personal information? How would that be stored? How long would it be retained? What would prevent it from being used for other purposes? What would happen if it is exposed by a data breach? Canadians hear about data breaches and compromised data far too often, and a system designed to protect children must not expose children or adults to new privacy risks. We should explore age verification methods that minimize the collection and storage of personal information with strong safeguards and independent verification.

My professional background taught me that protecting sensitive information requires clear controls and accountability. Those safeguards are essential to public confidence. The same principles apply to the proposed digital safety commission. The commission would have significant authority to develop guidelines, investigate complaints, conduct inspections, issue compliance orders and impose monetary penalties.

That is considerable regulatory power, and it would need to be accompanied by strong checks and balances. How would Canadians challenge decisions they believe are unfair? What independent review would be available? How would procedural fairness be guaranteed? How would Parliament maintain actual oversight? These are not just technical questions. They concern how authority works within a free and democratic society. We need to be particularly careful when decisions about online content could affect legal expression.

Online safety cannot rest with parents alone, but neither should it be the exclusive responsibility of government bureaucrats. Technology companies need to take responsibility for the systems they build and operate. They should be transparent about the risks their services create and the steps they take to address them. Parents need practical tools to guide their children's online experiences. Law enforcement needs the tools to pursue people who exploit and abuse children. Parliament must ensure that any regulatory framework is clearly defined and proportionate, and that it has the proper mechanisms for meaningful accountability.

We should also learn from previous legislative efforts, including the stated objectives of Bill C-11 and Bill C-63. However worthwhile and grand they seem, this must never prevent us from scrutinizing a bill's mechanisms, consequences and the powers it would create.

If, as I expect, Bill C-34 proceeds to committee, we will have an opportunity to hear from a wide variety of witnesses, including parents, child safety experts, privacy specialists, social media companies, law enforcement, and legal experts. We should examine the evidence, identify gaps and pursue practical improvements. Above all, we should determine whether these measures would work, whether they could be enforced, whether they would protect privacy and whether they would make children safer in their everyday lives. We need to take the time to make sure we do this right.

Mr. Speaker, throughout the evening, we heard all of our colleagues talk about a common goal: We all want to better protect children online, on both sides of the House. Some members felt that some aspects of the bill could be improved, but I think we all agree on the objective of Bill C-34.

If we agree on the objective, which is to better protect children online, I would like my colleague to tell us clearly whether he plans to vote in favour of Bill C-34 at second reading in order to refer it to committee.

Mr. Speaker, I think the intent and the goals are agreed to by everybody in Parliament. There are a lot of questions that are still left unanswered, and I do believe we will want this bill to go to committee to answer those questions and develop what is missing. I am fully supportive of it going to committee to get those questions answered.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague said that the bill has room for improvement, but he also said that he wants it to be passed at second reading so it can go to committee.
What worthwhile improvements does he see in the bill? If he intends to support it at second reading, then he must believe it contains positive measures.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to positive things, it is addressing the concerns of many parents. We need to give them some of the tools. We need to make sure the legislation is appropriate and proportionate to what the goals are to help parents going forward.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague laid out a number of ways that the bill could be improved and a number of things that the government should pay attention to in moving forward.
I would like to ask my colleague to share a bit more about what he is hearing in his community and the concerns various groups may have.

Mr. Speaker, I have to admit this is not the major issue that I am hearing in my riding. There are a lot of concerns about everything today with regard to being in Alberta. We have had referendum issues, which have sucked all the energy out of the room for quite a while.

Parents talk to me about what we are looking at in the future, but they are always concerned that if there is going to be overreach, how these restrictions are going to affect the rest of society versus the balancing act with regard to protecting our children.
Mr. Speaker, I will ask the same question that my colleague asked our colleague earlier.
Will the Conservatives vote in favour of the bill in order to support parents who are struggling and who are concerned about the dangers children face online?

Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives are concerned about protecting children and getting this bill to committee to flesh out a lot of the details so that a lot of the questions we have will be answered and resolved going forward in this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I believe if you seek it, you will find unanimous consent to see the clock at 1:13 a.m.
Is it agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 38 deemed to have been moved.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on May 1, I asked how many food bank expansions the Liberal government needed to see before it would bring grocery bills down. The minister responded by citing the Canada groceries and essentials benefit and temporary fuel tax relief. Well, those measures do not seem to have helped. Nearly six months later, families in my community still need an answer about the price of food. Last week, Food Banks Canada released its latest “Hungercount Report”. It recorded more than 2.35 million food bank visits in March of this year, which is more than double the number in 2019 and up 9% since last year across the country. In B.C., visits rose by 14% compared to the previous March. Behind those numbers are people who are struggling to make their paycheques, pensions and disability benefits cover the essentials. The latest Statistics Canada figures show that grocery prices are 33% higher than they were in September 2020. Of course, the wages and benefits have not kept up with that increase.

I recognize that the grocery benefit does help eligible households, that fuel tax relief has been extended as Conservatives requested and that people do need that breathing room, but the government has to explain how it will reduce the underlying costs of getting food onto the shelves. The answer cannot be a never-ending stream of cheques and an ever-lengthening lineup at food banks. For Vancouver Island, that means working with us on improving the infrastructure that supports our supply chains and paying attention to freight, cold storage and distribution. It also means making it easy for local farmers and independent grocers to reach customers. It means removing unnecessary federal costs and barriers, while protecting food safety and strengthening competition.

The government has now opened applications for its $1 billion food-link fund. It says that this will improve distribution and lower food costs. Given the ineffectiveness of earlier measures, I would feel better if we had clear deadlines and measurable results.

Will the parliamentary secretary commit tonight to public reporting on whether the fund meets its approval deadlines when projects begin operating and whether they lower distribution costs for island communities? Beyond that fund, which federal costs will the government remove to make producing and transporting food more affordable?

A $1-billion commitment deserves a clear accounting of what it will deliver. Families should be able to judge the results at the grocery store. The government owes all Canadians a plan that reduces the need for that help. Once again, we find that these plans are short on details in many ways. They are short on key performance indicators, and we lack confidence that they will produce measurable results.
When will families in Nanaimo—Ladysmith and across this country finally see lasting relief in their grocery bills?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we know that Canadians are struggling with the cost of living. Of course, we also know that the oil price shock is what is driving the consumer price index up. The consumer price index would be at 2.4% if it were not for the rise in energy prices that has driven it up to 3.1%. That directly impacts the cost of food over time, and we see that the inflation of food prices is significant and elevated.

That is exactly why we have given families a boost today and a bridge to tomorrow. That includes helping both with more emergency or immediate relief and support, which includes a billion-dollar investment, and making the national school food program permanent. It also includes the groceries and essentials benefit. I am glad to hear the member opposite acknowledge that those programs really help people. Often we hear from the Conservatives that they do not acknowledge them. They call the national school food program “garbage” or claim that it does not serve any food to children, when we know in fact that is false. I have witnessed it with my own eyes when I have toured food programs in my riding.

We have also moved forward on a national food security strategy, which is significant at $3.2 billion. Previously, we never had what I would say is a medium- to long-term strategy to address the structural problems in the food system. We have had numerous reports done by the Competition Bureau that looked at corporate consolidation within the food system all along the supply chains. The reality is that this leaves our food system vulnerable to shocks in the global market.

Commodity prices affect the input costs for our farmers, the cost of transportation and distribution, and the costs for our retailers, all of whom assume some of those costs and eventually pass them down to consumers in raised prices at the grocery store. Therefore, over time, having a food system that is vulnerable and highly dependent upon global supply chains is not the most resilient strategy. What we are doing is investing in the infrastructure that communities need in order to be able to distribute food and to develop shorter supply chains and more sustainable regional food systems that have cold storage and distribution, that do value added.

On Vancouver Island, in Victoria and the surrounding areas, there is much activity in the food system. I have toured it and met with many of the groups in the past. Before I was in politics, I served on the board of Food Secure Canada, an organization that has advocated for sustainable local food systems. This national food security strategy is something I have advocated for since entering politics seven years ago.

I am very proud to stand with a government that is making a $3.2-billion investment into the structural challenges in the food system, to develop the infrastructure and capacity at the community scale, to develop more resilience and essentially create competition so independent grocery stores would be able to get access to local food and do it in a more affordable way that is somewhat insulated from the commodity price fluctuations that have made our food system quite vulnerable to shocks.

Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the parliamentary secretary acknowledge the drivers behind some of the increases in the consumer price index in this country, the CPI, but the reality is that the price of food continues to grow at an inflationary rate that exceeds the CPI. The government comes up with program after program, yet there is a lack of measurables, KPIs and clear targets they can be measured against. Given that in the parliamentary secretary's own community demand has become so intense that last year there had to be incredible expansion in the number of slots, my question is this: How will these programs work, by how much and by when, and how will Canadians know that this billion-dollar fund actually lowered their costs?

Mr. Speaker, again, it is more than just a billion-dollar fund. It is $3.2 billion. The local food infrastructure fund has already made a significant difference in my community. There are organizations, mostly non-profits and charities, in my community that offer solutions at a community scale to the food insecurity challenges we see rising in our communities. They are doing a great job. What we are doing is boosting their efforts by offering more financing and support directly from the federal government, which arguably is something we have not had before and is probably the missing piece to really addressing the root causes of food insecurity.

Every expert in the country will tell us that food insecurity is the direct result of income insecurity. Therefore, really, the long-term solution to food insecurity is to make sure we have high-paying jobs in Canada. Wages have been outpacing inflation in Canada. The Canadian economy has added twice the number of jobs—
The hon. member for Yellowhead has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to follow up on a question I asked earlier in the year about the affordability crisis facing Canadians and the government's costly decisions. When Canadians are working full-time but cannot afford a home, when families are struggling to pay for groceries and rent, and when people are forced to make impossible choices just to get by, Canadians deserve more than a government pointing to economic indicators and good news. They deserve responsible spending, meaningful actions and a government that understands the consequences of its decisions.

As a chartered professional accountant for 26 years with tax experience, I understand the importance of fiscal responsibility. Budgets must balance priorities, spending must deliver results, and every dollar of taxpayer money must be treated with respect. Responsible budgeting is not simply about cutting costs. It is about understanding what we are losing when we make those cuts.

What has been top of mind in recent days are the Liberals' cuts to national parks. We learned late last week that Parks Canada is discontinuing its search and rescue dog program in Banff National Park, a program that has been essential for more than 55 years. The program has helped locate missing people, find avalanche victims, recover those lost in the mountains and support law enforcement locally. One of these dogs, Leroy, helped find more than 57 people during his career. These are not just numbers on a spreadsheet. These are people who were brought home to their families because of the dedication and specialized skills of these dogs and their handlers.

Banff and Jasper are among Canada's most treasured national spaces. They attract visitors from across the country and around the world. As visitation grows, and demands on our parks increase, especially with the Canada strong pass, we should be strengthening the tools that help people be safe, not eliminating proven capabilities in the name of savings.

This decision raises a serious question. What is the true cost of cutting a program that helps save lives? The concerns do not end there. Parks Canada is now undertaking another round of workforce adjustments. The agency expects to eliminate the equivalent of roughly 500 full-time positions as part of its federal spending reductions, totalling nearly $145 million over the next three years. These are the people who maintain trails and facilities, protect wildlife, support visitors, preserve our national heritage and help communities recover from disasters.

In Jasper, where the community and the park continue to recover from the devastating 2024 wildfire, Parks Canada employees are still doing essential rebuilding work while facing uncertainty about their own futures. These are not positions that can be written off as cost savings measures. When experienced employees leave, specialized programs disappear. We are losing institutional knowledge, frontline capacity and the ability to respond effectively when emergencies happen.

Canadians expect their government to find savings, eliminate waste and live within its means. Conservatives believe in that responsibility. However, cutting essential services and jeopardizing skilled careers is not good management.

Affordability matters. Canadians need relief from the cost of living, and taxpayers deserve value for money, but affordability controls cannot become an excuse for decisions that put livelihoods at risk or compromise the safety—
The hon. parliamentary secretary has the floor.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I fully acknowledge that Jasper National Park and Banff National Park are real treasures in our country. I have visited Banff National Park and absolutely love Parks Canada and the work that it does to preserve natural spaces, and allow people to enjoy those spaces and experience the outdoors in Canada. Canada has so much to offer the world and visitors, as well as the people who live in our great country. In terms of geography and natural wonders, we have unlimited experiences for people to take advantage of. I am glad to hear the member opposite advocate for something that he is passionate about. I empathize with him.

At the same time, the member cannot have it both ways. He cannot have his cake and eat it too. On the one hand, the member opposite has said he wants fiscal discipline, but then he disagrees with the comprehensive expenditure review that our government has done. I think it was a demonstration of fiscal responsibility. We went through a pretty comprehensive exercise to look at ways to reduce government operational spending. It was a $60-billion savings exercise to achieve optimization within government operations, and that includes reductions that the member opposite is pointing to. He just does not like where those decisions are being made. However, I think he would agree that it is important for governments to do vertical and horizontal reviews, to review where there can be savings made and where government operations can be optimized, and that is a good practice for us to undertake.

Simultaneously, to demonstrate fiscal discipline, we have reported $11 billion less of a deficit in the spring economic update. We just recently announced that we will be meeting the target for one of our fiscal anchors a year in advance, which is to balance our operational budget or spending with revenues. That is significant progress. I understand that there is more work to do on that, but it has created some fiscal room as well for the government to take some of these tax measures and make cuts that we have made. Significantly, we have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment.

Surely the member opposite can understand the significance of those things, given his many speeches and interventions on the cost of living challenges and affordability challenges that Canadians are going through, not to mention the Conservative Party's repeated requests for cutting taxes. I am sure that he supports those measures.

Is he saying, on the one hand, that we should cut and exercise fiscal discipline but not do it in a way that impacts anybody in his riding, or is he broadly supportive of those? I cannot understand the logic here.

I think that we are demonstrating fiscal discipline. We are strategically investing in the economy. We are putting in place measures that give Canadians a boost today and a bridge to tomorrow, which is how we think about it. People need to get through the challenges they are facing today with the economic shocks that we are under, but really have hope for a future where they know that the government is working hard to create prosperity for Canadians for generations to come. That is exactly what we will stay focused on.

Mr. Speaker, I want to first say that this is all about decisions. We can look at a lot of the choices that are made with regard to Parks Canada. Last year, it gave $2 million worth of bonuses to executives and paid over $400,000 in catering. This is all about decisions. Meanwhile, the Canada strong pass reduced the amount of fees that were collected from those who were visiting, so that reduced the actual income. That is a choice that affects spending.

Regarding the rescue dog program in Banff, when I first heard about this decision, I knew immediately that this was something that needed to be addressed right now, before we have deep snow and an increased risk of avalanches. We have received dozens of emails and calls already and have thousands of signatures on an e-petition that was only started yesterday. This is not a cost-saving measure.
Will the government commit to reinstating the rescue dog program in Banff?

Mr. Speaker, our plan is focused and disciplined. We are acting where we can make the most difference, by maintaining fiscal sustainability and discipline, and making targeted investments that benefit Canadians right across the country. That means reducing the operating deficit, meeting our fiscal anchors and ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians.

I appreciate the member opposite's comments and his commitment to that particular program in his jurisdiction. As he said, quite rightly, it is about decision-making. The Government of Canada is doing its very best to make the best decisions for the greatest number of Canadians, and pursue the prosperity and the strength in our economy that all Canadians want to see.
The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, the House stands adjourned until later this day at 10 a.m., pursuant to standing order 24(1).
(The House adjourned at 1:11 a.m.)
